A shift towards earned income will inevitably impact on the capacity of arts organisations to offer a high standard of products and services at a reasonable cost, to provide the vital R&D and talent development that inspires the creative industries and to extend the reach of the arts into the lives of underrepresented communities and people. 

Crucially, it will mean that many small regional organisations and experimental companies may struggle with long term implications for both the economy and society. Tax incentives are an important part of the mixed economy. 

The increase in earned income shown by our publicly supported arts and film recipients has begun to erode the traditional distinctions between the public arts and commercial businesses, and between not-for-profit and for-profit business models. Recently introduced tax incentives for theatre and orchestras represent additional support and a shift from direct investment to incentivising growth. For commercial and public theatre organisations, these are worth up to 25% of touring costs and 20% for all other productions. Orchestras now benefit from up to 25% relief on qualifying expenditure. Tax incentives are also available to film, high-end TV, animation, video games and children’s TV as a mechanism by which to incentivise production in these sectors and create jobs. They are a major and welcome contributor to growth in the arts and creative sectors, and they complement current levels of public investment through grant-in-aid. In 2013-14, the film tax relief provided support to over 320 films being made in the UK. Since relief was introduced in 2007, over 1,200 film productions have made claims for a total of £1.3 billion 38 

Tax incentives sit alongside grant-in-aid incentivising production but they are not a strategic tool to build and maintain infrastructure, business resilience or education and outreach. This is something that only targeted investment such as grant-in-aid can do, through place making, training, experimentation and longer term support for business and artistic planning. 20 

We are all only as good as our last creative idea. If we want to be a country of innovators we need to be constantly creative. To become creative, innovative and imaginative, we need to expose ourselves to new ideas. A vibrant arts and culture community is the easiest way to make this happen. The games industry has benefited enormously from increasingly sophisticated classical music soundtracks played brilliantly by orchestras like the Philharmonia. Many games developers now pay large sums to classical composers to write scores for their games, exposing a new generation of young people to classical music while enhancing the creative experience of playing these games. We have to stop thinking about arts and culture as simply nice to have. They are just as important as well-maintained roads and bridges. By giving us the chance to stimulate our minds with new ideas and experiences, they give us the opportunity to become more creative. Arts and culture are infrastructure for the mind. 

Ian Livingstone - Co-founder Games Workshop and former Chairman of Eidos 

No one would ever want to live in a city without culture. Culture is the fuel that drives the urban metropolis. Artists, literary thinkers, designers and directors feed our souls and our imaginations, offering both a mirror and a chance to escape. 

Boris Johnson MP - Mayor of London 41 21 

# Public investment leverages private investment and earned income. 

Public investment can also be used as a means of attracting commercial interest- with successful results. In 2015, three of the six BAFTA nominees for Outstanding British Film were supported by the Film Fund and Pride won a Best Debut BAFTA. Philomena was nominated for Best Picture at the Academy Awards 39 .In some cases non-profit arts organisations have produced their own massive commercial hits - such as Matilda The Musical, War Horse, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time - as part of their portfolio of products, which has helped them to offset reduced levels of public funding and build reserves for the future. The UK’s orchestras make a substantial contribution to the commercially successful film and video games industries, which in turn enables them to leverage an additional £2 of private investment for each £1 of public investment, the equivalent to the average leverage from all NPOs. Great British orchestras, including the LSO, The Philharmonia, the LPO and the RPO, are responsible for the soundtracks of some of our most successful cultural exports, including the Harry Potter films, television shows like Downton Abbey and computer games including Halo 4 and Killzone. Orchestras in the UK are given an international edge by their funding structure- with public funds allowing them to diversify their audience, tour outside London, and continue to educate themselves and others 40 .

# The public arts are key to regional growth. 

The government recognises that regional growth is key to the future success of the economy, particularly if the creative economy is to grow in GVA and employment. A quarter of Local Enterprise Partnerships (LEPs) have stated that the creative industries are a priority sector 42 .Although there are success stories of thriving creative industries and cultural participation across England, it is not an entirely positive story. There is still a significant imbalance between London and the regions. 47.6% of creative industries jobs are in London and the South-East of England alone which, aside from agriculture and finance and insurance, makes the creative economy the most unevenly distributed part of the UK’s economy 43 .

There are strong links between cultural growth and activity and the growth of regional economies and creative industry employment. Liverpool attracted 9.7 million additional visits during its time as EU Capital of Culture, generating an economic impact of £753.8 million 44 .22 

Under 25s make up 40% of Birmingham’s population - we are young, diverse and digital. Birmingham is home to 6,000 tech firms employing nearly 40,000 people. 25% of the UK’s gaming workforce is based locally, and digital tech firms boost the region’s economy by in excess of £1.6 billion every year. Talent is brought together in initiatives and areas such as the Innovation Birmingham Campus, The Custard Factory, Fazeley Studios, Entrepreneurs for the Future (e4f ) and Oxygen Accelerator with geographical concentrations in Digbeth and the Jewellery Quarter. The city’s multicultural character and access to universities and other educational establishments provide creative employers with a steady flow of talent and our diverse and vibrant cultural scene helps us to attract and retain this talent. 

Anita Bhalla - Chair of Creative City Partnership, Board member LEP and Chair Performances Birmingham 23

The devolved nations in particular have potential for growth in the creative industries and economy. Currently Scotland has 6.9% of the Creative Economy jobs in the UK, Northern Ireland has 1.6% (the lowest of all regions) and Wales has 2.9%. With investment, we believe that recent growth can be accelerated. It is now recognised that public investment in the arts is essential to ensure that they are experienced by all, wherever they live, and for providing access to experiences and education that both benefit our least advantaged citizens and inspire individuals and communities to be creative, and in so doing contribute to local creative and cultural growth. An Arts Development: UK and Arts Council Wales study found that 90% of local authorities surveyed had partnerships with external arts and cultural organisations in 2014 compared to 82% in 2012 45 , which indicates an increasing trend towards cultural commissioning by local authorities to deliver a wide range of services including health and wellbeing as well as business and regional development. In 2013-14 Local Government invested £1.5 billion in cultural services to their communities of which £805 million was spent on libraries, which are vital cultural assets 46 . ACE distributes £611 million to the regions for arts services only 47 , but which also includes some support for libraries 48 .

Figure 4 shows that levels of local government spending, inclusive of spending on libraries, are fairly evenly distributed across England but are on a downward trajectory. ACE funding is not as evenly distributed and this makes local government support in some regions crucial for enriching the cultural lives of local communities and boosting local creative and cultural growth. But many local authorities are facing real dilemmas in maintaining levels of spending on arts and culture whilst providing core services to their most vulnerable communities and fulfilling civic responsibilities. As a result local government spending on arts and culture has fallen by 25% since 2007/08 49 .24 

On the day that Hull was named UK City of Culture the local paper carried the headline - ‘The day the city changed forever’. Some felt it was an overstatement but public investment in culture was to trigger a new confidence in private investment. With over 20 local and national companies sponsoring Hull’s bid to show private sector support alongside local authority and Arts Council cash, there was clear evidence that business saw benefits in culture changing the fortunes of a city. Hull launched a £25 million public realm strategy, now being implemented by Arups and local developer Wykeland was announced as lead partner for cultural-led regeneration on the Fruit Market, investing £15 million in a new digital centre @TheDock. The near derelict wasteland of Humber Street had seen small Arts Council grants support a jewellery gallery, a museum of club culture, music and festival activity. It is now a street full of scaffolding as private investment follows public to see the arts as the permanent solution rather than a ‘meanwhile use’. £20 million of positive media coverage has already seen a 15% increase in hotel income and a turnaround in retail. The University of Hull saw an 8% increase in students for its cultural programmes. 

Andrew Dixon - Director of Culture Creativity Place and Visiting Professor of Cultural Policy University of Hull. 

To have inspired, creative companies, Britain needs to produce an inspired, creative workforce. This is not just about school education, but involves developing communities which are able to interact with the arts at all levels. On a practical note, Hearst employees often work with the publicly funded arts - these institutions perform an important role in offering a new perspective and inspiration to all of our most successful creative industries. 

Anna Jones - Chief Executive, Hearst Magazines UK 25 

This overall downward trajectory in Local Government spending is alarming given that 

Figure 4 shows that with the exception of London, the rest of the regions are heavily reliant on Local Government spending for their arts and libraries. Hull will be the second UK City of Culture in 2017 and already has demonstrated that growth in employment, GVA and cultural confidence can flow from a city rallying around their creative and artistic heritage and future. Public investment has made it possible for the city to ‘come out of the shadows’ 50 .

# The Public arts are a source and resource for creative talent. 

Public investment supports the identification, diversification and training of creative talent. 60.5% of creative industry workers are graduates compared to a UK average of 31.8%. But 92.1% of workers were from advantaged social and economic backgrounds compared to a UK average of 66.0% 51 . In the creative media sector alone 14% of workers were educated in independent schools which represent only 7% of the population 52 .Despite an encouraging 34.3% increase in the number of BAME workers in the creative industries between 2011 and 2014, they still only represent 11.0% of the creative industries workforce, compared to 14.1% of the overall population of England and Wales and 40% in London where there is a high concentration of creative industries 53 .In England, 12% of the creative and cultural workforce is classified as disabled 54 compared to 18% of the general workforce 55 . Women held 36.7% of jobs compared with 47.2% in the whole UK economy 56 .

The range of experiences, cultures and forms of expression in the creative industries is enriched by public investment targeted on accelerating social mobility and diversity in the creative workforce. 

The UK has invested in exceptional training routes for the publicly supported arts that also support graduates who move into advertising, fashion, design, publishing and other creative economy and creative industry settings. Public investment of £60 million includes support for specialist creative Higher Education and training of proven world-class standards in terms of their graduate employment records 57 . Public investment also supports the cost-intensive training offered in our small independent schools that provide the dancers, musicians and actors needed to maintain the UK’s internationally recognised standards of artistic excellence. Budgets to support investment in our world-class HE centres of excellence are under considerable pressure, and must be maintained if we are to stimulate the supply of creative talent on which the creative industries depend 58 .26 

The vitality of the commercial sector in the visual arts depends very heavily on public investment in our art schools, galleries and museums. This vitality can be narrowly expressed as the livelihood of artists, the success of the commercial galleries and auction houses. More broadly, it includes the graphic arts, design, film and aspects of television and has a major impact on tourism and the economic success of our cities. These centres of learning and inspiration have trained and brought to public attention successive generations of artists from Moore, Riley and Hockney to Whiteread, Doig and Hirst. The art schools attract students from across the world. They are internationally recognised centres of research, developing talent that plays leading roles in the creative industries across the world. Our galleries, like Tate Modern, the Whitechapel or Nottingham Contemporary show the artists and create the public interest that stimulates an art market, in which London has become the principal centre alongside New York. 

In recent years substantial investment in institutions and people in Europe and America has attracted talent from the UK and is now quickly eroding our lead. Public investment creates the nursery for our success and future generations will not forgive us if we fail to plant seed for the next crop. 

Sir Nicholas Serota - Director, Tate 

To create an equal society we must have arts and culture that are available to everyone. This doesn’t just mean having doors open to all, but actively trying to approach and interact with those who may not feel our artistic institutions are ‘for them’. If we strip away funding, it is diversity and access programmes that suffer with knock-on effects right through society. 

Melanie Eusebe - Chair and Co-founder of the Black British Business Awards 27 

Public money has also been invested more directly into projects that help practitioners to skill up. The Creative Skillset Skills Investment Fund uses matched public/private funding to produce £32 million of support for training that provide crucial entry into the workplace and skills support in the creative industries 59 and the Creative Access organisation plays a vital role in brokering paid internships for talented BAME creatives to work in the film and media industries. The ACE Creative Employment Programme delivered by the National Skills Academy supports up to 6,500 new apprenticeships, pre-apprenticeships and paid internships (graduate and non-graduate) across the arts and cultural sector, 60 .Social objectives for public investment have merged with economic imperatives. The conditions for granting public money to arts and cultural organisations increasingly stress accountability for meeting targets that are in the national interest. These include excellence and financial sustainability but also reflect the need to ensure that the arts are diverse, inclusive and available nationwide 61 . All three of these priorities serve important national social objectives that are also economic imperatives for the creative industries and the creative economy. Creative innovation and growth in any sector depends on a diverse workforce, as McKinsey has recently demonstrated. In Diversity Matters they showed that gender-diverse companies are 15% more likely to outperform their competitors and ethnically diverse companies are 35% more likely to outperform 62 . The drive for diversity in the publicly supported arts, supported by clear links to public investment conditions, is a major initiative and exemplar for increasing the diversity of the creative industries workforce as a whole. Through public investment in projects designed to attract more socially and ethnically diverse arts audiences we ensure that the commercial potential of a diverse range of ideas and talent are realised. The publicly supported arts as well as being an important source of diverse talent and experience to the creative industries as a whole also invest in education and community outreach that nurtures tomorrow’s creative talent and consumers. 28 

There would be almost no commercially viable independent film-making in the UK without public money through BBC Films, Film 4, BFI, film production tax credit, Enterprise Investment Scheme, Creative England and Screen Yorkshire. Although at Ingenious we do not spend public money ourselves, we would not fund, whether through debt and/or equity variants or other financial instruments, films like Pride, Testament of Youth, Mr Turner, Selma and Suffragette (forthcoming) without being able to work with partners who are able to share the risk by drawing upon these vital sources of funding which, together, typically add up to between a third and half of production cost. 

Martin Smith - Special Adviser, Ingenious Media 

New Adventures makes a significant contribution to the UK’s economy, over the last decade generating over £12 million for the Treasury. Arts Council England investment enables us to take risks in creating brave new productions and touring to all parts of the UK, including to smaller theatres that otherwise would not be financially viable.. In return, New Adventure acts as R&D by building skills and expertise across the creative industries, enabling talented individuals to develop their careers. It has employed 900 dancers, musicians and creative industry professionals across 16 live productions since 2004. Musicians are employed to perform live and New Adventures provides promotional opportunities for instrumentalists and conductors. In addition, musicians are employed to record specially composed and arranged scores. Other creative industry professionals include carpenters, electricians, flymen, sound and lighting designers and operators, wig, wardrobe and makeup experts, stage and company managers, rehearsal and resident directors. New Adventures provides promotional opportunities, including for dancers moving into management and directorial roles. 

Matthew Bourne - Artistic Director, New Adventures 29 

# Intellectual property as the raw material of the creative industries. 

There is a high degree of risk of market failure in investing in the early stages of idea development; at the point at which it is not certain that an idea is commercially viable and likely to produce a return on investment. It is an inevitable corollary of creative work that there will be ideas that fail to become marketable intellectual property, for every commercially successful one. As many of the case studies in this document suggest, public investment at the high-risk stage of idea development mitigates the risk of market failure for private investors. Public investment encourages risk and experimentation in order to develop ideas to a stage where private investors are willing to accept the risk and invest in moving an idea into the supply chain. For instance, about £50,000 was spent on a series of experimental workshops at the National Theatre (NT) Studio for War Horse, and its first production at the NT in 2007 cost around £500,000. ## Overview
This is the second policy report from the Creative Industries Federation (produced in partnership with Arts Council England), arguing that public investment in the arts is crucial to the growth of the UK's creative industries. The report is authored by Professor Jonothan Neelands and Eliza Easton of Warwick Business School, with contributions from leading business figures including Melanie Clore (Sotheby's), Tom Weldon (Penguin Random House), Baroness Lane-Fox, Caroline Rush (British Fashion Council), Boris Johnson, and Matthew Bourne.

## Core Economic Argument
- The UK creative industries are booming: GVA grew 9.9% between 2012-2013 (higher than any other industrial sector including financial services), and returned £77 billion of direct GVA in 2012-2013.
- Employment in the creative economy grew 5% between 2013-2014 (vs. 2.1% UK average) and accounts for 5.8% of all UK jobs; creative economy jobs grew 13.7% since 2011.
- The public arts return 0.4% of UK GVA (a 19% increase vs. 3.3% UK average) with 9.2% employment growth.
- UK films generated £1.4 billion in exports with a £916 million trade surplus in 2013.
- The arts are linked to 42% of inbound-tourism related expenditure.

## Investment Gap
- The UK invests only 0.3% of GDP on arts and culture vs. the EU average of 0.5%, France at 0.8%, and Germany at 0.4%.
- Arts Council England grant-in-aid fell 29.4% in real terms from 2010/11 to 2014/15, accounting for only 0.1% of public expenditure.
- Total public spend on arts/culture in England represents just 0.7% of total public spend.
- Local government spending on arts and culture fell 25% since 2007/08.
- No other EU country benefits from the level of GVA the UK's public arts return.

## How Public Investment Drives Growth
- **R&D function**: Public investment mitigates risk at the high-risk idea development stage. The National Theatre spent ~£50,000 on experimental workshops for War Horse; its first production cost ~£500,000 but has now been seen by 5.5+ million people and earned a £12 million surplus.
- **Seedbed for commercial success**: The RSC's two years of publicly funded development enabled Les Misérables to become London's longest-running musical (70+ million people in 42 countries). Matthew Bourne's New Adventures received £3 million in grants but returned £12 million to the Treasury.
- **Leverage effect**: Orchestras leverage an additional £2 of private investment per £1 of public investment; NPOs leverage similar amounts.
- **Industry dependence**: 37% of video games businesses depend on public grants/government schemes. Software developers can claim tax reductions up to 225% of R&D investment.
- **Tax incentives**: Film, high-end TV, animation, video games, children's TV, theatre and orchestras benefit from tax reliefs (up to 25% for touring costs, 20% for other theatre productions, 25% for orchestras). Since 2007, over 1,200 film productions claimed £1.3 billion in relief.

## Diversity and Talent
- 60.5% of creative industry workers are graduates (vs. 31.8% UK average), but 92.1% come from advantaged social/economic backgrounds.
- 14% of creative media workers attended independent schools (7% of population). BAME workers increased 34.3% between 2011-2014 but remain only 11% of workforce (vs. 14.1% of the general population).
- Public investment supports 6,500 apprenticeships through the Creative Employment Programme and £32 million training support via Creative Skillset.
- McKinsey research: gender-diverse companies are 15% more likely to outperform; ethnically diverse companies 35% more likely.

## Regional Distribution
- 47.6% of creative industries jobs are in London and the South-East — the most unevenly distributed UK sector (after agriculture and finance/insurance).
- Scotland has 6.9% of creative economy jobs, Wales 2.9%, Northern Ireland 1.6%.
- Liverpool attracted 9.7 million additional visits as EU Capital of Culture, generating £753.8 million economic impact.
- Hull (UK City of Culture 2017) saw private investment follow public investment, including £15 million from Wykeland and a 15% increase in hotel income.
- Birmingham (Anita Bhalla): home to 6,000 tech firms employing nearly 40,000; 25% of UK gaming workforce; digital tech boosts the regional economy by £1.6 billion annually.

## Key Recommendations
- BIS (Department for Business, Innovation and Skills) should recognize the creative industries in its industrial growth data.
- A joined-up policy response is needed across HM Treasury, BIS, DCMS, DCLG and DfE, under leadership of the Secretary of State for Culture.
- The mixed economy model (public investment + tax incentives + private/philanthropic funding) should continue, but tax incentives cannot replace grant-in-aid for building infrastructure, education, and outreach.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
 

 

 

 

## Arts Council England—written evidence (CRF0043)

 

House of Lords Communications and Digital Select Committee inquiry “A creative future”

 

 

1.       How Arts Council England supports culture

 

1.1       Arts Council England is the national development agency for creativity and culture.  Between 2018 and 2022, we have invested £1.45 billion of public money from Government, and an estimated £860 million from the National Lottery.

 

1.2       The Arts Council invests through three main strands:

 

1.3       To help support organisations through the Covid-19 pandemic, Arts Council England has awarded a total of £1.14 billion through the Government’s Culture Recovery Fund, and £160 million through the Arts Council’s own Emergency Response Fund to individuals and organisations, including those within our national portfolio.

 

1.4       We invest in developing digital skills across the creative and cultural sector and encourage organisations to adopt appropriate new technologies across all aspects of their business. We plan to build on partnerships with the technology sector and with further and higher education to help drive improvement in this area.

 

1.5       The Arts Council, as an expert national sector development agency can invest strategically and at scale, working alongside local government, and other local partners including Higher Education institutions, Local Enterprise Partnerships, businesses, schools, MATs, and the voluntary sectors.

 

 

2.       Which areas of the creative industries face the greatest potential for disruption and change in the next 5–10 years, and what impact could this have?

 

a) What changes are expected in the way creative/cultural content is produced; the way audiences are engaged (for example through digital or immersive experiences); and the way business models operate?

 

2.1       We have approached this question by considering which advanced technologies have the most potential to significantly impact or disrupt the parts the creative and cultural sector we support over the next 5-10 years. We have then suggested where these impacts might be felt.

 

2.2       The interrelated technologies that we see having the greatest potential for impact are:

 

2.3       Artificial Intelligence (AI)

AI and machine learning has the potential for significant impact across many areas of arts and culture. 

 

2.4       AI requires datasets and anywhere within artistic or cultural practice that has access to significant datasets is likely to be transformed by the increasing application of AI technology. This could apply, for example, to the management and use of audience data, or to the use of data as a core component of collections management.

 

2.5       Increasingly, AI is a factor in the way that art and culture is produced, e.g. as a tool used by artists to support their creativity, or as an algorithmically programmed self-generator of forms of cultural content.

 

2.6       Potential areas of disruption relate to issues of Intellectual Property (IP), such as questions of ownership of innovations generated by AI, or the role that AI can play in helping to identify and manage IP infringements.

 

2.7       AI technologies are also an increasingly prevalent feature of how arts and culture organisations transact with their audiences online (for example, as bots embedded in websites), and AI algorithms are increasingly helping to ‘curate’ people’s online music, tv and film consumption (although there is not yet an equivalent for wider arts and culture online).

 

2.8       The many potential applications that AI has for the creative and cultural sectors have been comprehensively documented and discussed in reports such as European Commission’s 2022 report on the Opportunities and Challenges of AI for the Cultural and Creative Sectors.[[1]](#_ftn1)

 

2.9       Research on artificial intelligence in the arts and culture sector, commissioned in 2019 by the Arts Council, found that:

 

 

 

 

a)    Cost and market maturity. In some cases, such as captioning in theatres for the hard-of-hearing, the technology is highly suited to the arts sector but remains prohibitively expensive.

 

b)    Data development. Sophisticated data collection and management strategies are necessary for the uptake of these technologies. Arts organisations will be unable to make full use of their potential until they develop and refine their data management. 

 

2.10   5G  
Also related to technological advances in data-processing, the high-speed responsiveness and ultra-low latency, or lag, of 5G will revolutionise live streaming of data-rich content. Developing digital experiences over 5G networks could improve accessibility to the arts, moving rich, immersive experiences out of galleries or theatres and into the home, reaching non-traditional and potentially more diverse audiences

 

2.11   A Working Group for 5G in Arts and Heritage[[2]](#_ftn2) has over recent years tracked ‘testbed’ applications of 5G in our sector, a recent example being the 5G Festival[[3]](#_ftn3) showcase at Brighton Dome which enabled musicians in different locations to play together simultaneously, without lag, illustrating the exciting potential that 5G technology offers for remote creative collaborations as well as for providing enhanced experiences for audiences

2.12   Virtual production, extended reality, virtual worlds

The cluster of technologies which aggregate around the concepts of virtual production, extended reality (e.g. VR, AR) virtual worlds, many of which are associated with, or have developed from gaming culture, could have profound consequences both for how work is made and for where audiences might encounter it (with associated implications for business models). All promise to radically alter the way that arts and culture can be experienced.

 

2.13   Many larger arts and culture organisations have developed ambitious projects using these new technologies; prominent examples include RSC’s Dream,[[4]](#_ftn4) ROH’s Current Rising,[[5]](#_ftn5) Tate’s Modigliani VR[[6]](#_ftn6) and National Gallery’s Virtual Veronese.[[7]](#_ftn7) Some are location based, adding a new dimension to what can be experienced at traditional venues; others can be consumed at home on headsets, or sometimes within virtual online environments (e.g. on Fortnite, Roblox, or VRChat).

 

2.14   To create audience impact at scale (i.e. not bounded by the number of available headsets) such technologies are likely to evolve more social forms of immersive experience. AR already enables immersive experiences to be developed in the public realm, offering opportunities for large numbers of people to experience digital culture in a civic and social context, such as the Unreal City[[8]](#_ftn8) virtual public art trail on the Thames, or the Unboxed StoryTrails[[9]](#_ftn9) project taking place in summer 2022 at locations around the UK.

 

2.15   Online, artforms such as music are already recognising virtual worlds as a fecund site for reaching and developing audiences. Musician-led immersive start-up company Ristband[[10]](#_ftn10) exemplify the experimentation that has begun to happen in the UK, as well as internationally, in this space.

 

2.16   Web 3.0 Technologies

Potentially the most disruptive and unpredictable focus of technological development is in the area of Web 3.0. The cluster of technologies and concepts emerging in this broad area of innovation, including blockchain, crypto art[[11]](#_ftn11) DAOs[[12]](#_ftn12) and NFTs,[[13]](#_ftn13) could have profound implications for how art and culture is made, consumed, monetised and controlled.

 

2.17   Proponents of Web 3.0 technologies might emphasise their potential to change entrenched power structures in the art world, enabling artists to find new forms of economic sustainability and new audiences online, without the control of traditional gatekeepers. However, others might highlight the high degree of, largely unregulated, financial speculation associated with crypto art and NFTs and the challenges they present in terms of financial and reputational risk and in attribution and ownership of IP.

 

2.18   Cultural organisations, in the UK and internationally, have begun developing partnerships with agencies specialising in this emerging marketplace, with mixed results. In summer 2022 the Italian government suspended the creation of NFTs[[14]](#_ftn14) based on Italian masterworks in order to ‘avoid unfair contracts’.

 

 

3.       What skills will be required to meet these emerging opportunities and challenges?

 

3.1       A major challenge faced by the arts and culture sector in relation to the above technologies is inequality of access and opportunity.  Those who are currently able to experiment with the possibilities that new technologies offer tend to be:

 

 

3.2       It should be highlighted that inequality of access and opportunity applies also to the demand side of culture. Many people still do not have access to digital devices and services or, if they do, may be restricted in how they are able to use them to engage with arts and culture. A challenge for our sector in the next 10 years will be how creative and culture organisations can contribute to tackling digital exclusion, at the same time as developing digital services and experiences that make the most of what advanced technologies have to offer.

 

3.3       The most recent Digital Culture[[15]](#_ftn15) survey, commissioned in 2019 by the Arts Council and Nesta, found that: ‘larger organisations and NPOs are demonstrating some ability to adopt new digital technologies and work strategically with technology to develop audiences and, to some extent, business models, but there has not been marked progress across the sector as a whole over the six years of the study [2013-2019]. A widening gulf between large and small organisations is notable in many areas ... Whatever their scale and the resources available, organisations need to develop the right organisational structure, priorities and skills, backed up by senior level commitment, in order to create the conditions in which to benefit fully from digital technologies.’ The survey also found that ‘organisations are becoming less experimental, and more risk averse in their approach to digital technologies. Overall, there has been a downward trend in R&D behaviours.’

 

3.4       Since 2019, as has been well documented, the prolonged shutdown of live arts and culture led to widespread experimentation with digital alternatives. This greatly accelerated digital learning and skills building across the sector.[[16]](#_ftn16) However, research conducted since cultural venues have reopened has found that it remains an open question whether the digital innovation prompted by the exceptional circumstances of the pandemic will continue at scale as ‘business as usual’ is resumed. The appetite (and resource available) for continued digital R&D will be impacted also by the gathering economic crisis that is likely to see organisations focussing more on the ‘tried and trusted’ and less on risk and experimentation.

 

3.5       Broadly, the Arts Council’s approach over the last 10 years to supporting digital development across the arts and culture sector has had two strands: support for digital skills and strategy development; and encouragement for digital R&D and talent development.

 

3.6       Examples of our support for digital skills and strategy development include:

 

 

 

 

3.7       To help and encourage sector organisations to make better use of data, and contribute to a more joined up data culture across the sector as a whole, we invest in programmes such as Audience Finder[[21]](#_ftn21) and the Impact & Insight Toolkit[[22]](#_ftn22) which support arts and cultural organisations to increase their use of, and gain more insight from, audience data. We are also the UK delivery partner for Bloomberg Philanthropies’ Digital Accelerator Programme[[23]](#_ftn23) which supports a cohort of arts and cultural organisations selected by Bloomberg to develop their digital skills and capacity across a range of business areas from content production to data and insights.

 

3.8       On the R&D side, where we want to encourage and enable experimentation with more advanced and emerging technologies, examples of our support include:

 

 

 

 

3.9       The skills required to work confidently and effectively with the more advanced technologies listed in response to Question 1 are highly specialised and require expert support to develop. The Arts Council works with partners in order to make advanced digital skills (and related facilities and support expertise) available to sector organisations who have the ambition (and baseline knowledge) to undertake R&D with emerging technologies.

 

3.10   Potential partners and sources of support to help build the cultural sector’s capacity to utilise emerging technology include:

 

 

 

3.11   Arts Council funded organisations with expertise in advanced technologies also have a role to play in sharing knowledge and helping to develop skills. NPOs such as the Royal Shakespeare Company, Serpentine Galleries, Watershed and Furtherfield, have all developed programmes and projects deliberately devised to support sector peers in their understanding of how advanced technologies can be relevant to arts and culture. 

 

3.12   Beyond the NPO portfolio there are several other small arts organisations that specialise in supporting sector practitioners to undertake creative R&D with emerging tech and have received Arts Council project funding to assist their work. These include Collusion[[32]](#_ftn32) and York Mediale.[[33]](#_ftn33)

 

 

4.       What actions are needed from the Government and local authorities to ensure there is an appropriate talent pipeline equipped with these skills?

 

a) How can this be sufficiently flexible to take account of the pace of change in the sector?

 

4.1       A key measure for Government is to continue its investment in R&D and advanced digital skills development in the creative industries and to set criteria for future funding (or for access to the support that this funding enables) that makes it possible for arts and culture organisations that are not primarily commercial, profit-oriented businesses to benefit.

 

4.2       Relevant templates for this could be the Creative Industries Clusters Programme: £39m Industrial Strategy Challenge Funding, administered via UKRI/AHRC, to support nine creative R&D partnerships across the UK, three of which created significant opportunities for arts and culture organisations in the respective cluster areas: Yorkshire & the Humber (XR Stories), Bristol and Bath (B+B), and Gateway and Greater London (StoryFutures); and the Audiences of the Future Challenge: £33m Industrial Strategy Challenge Funding, via UKRI/AHRC, to invest in five large-scale immersive technology products, services and experiences, two of which (Dream, and Dinosaurs and Robots) had several arts and culture organisations as part of the collaborative delivery team.

 

4.3       Since forming their cluster in 2018, StoryFutures[[34]](#_ftn34) (SF) and StoryFutures Academy[[35]](#_ftn35) (SFA) have developed a significant track record of working with arts and culture sector. Examples are: SFA’s UK-lead delivery role in the Arts Council supported UCIE (UK-Canada) programme; SFA also played a partnership role in the third cohort of CreativeXR[[36]](#_ftn36); 50 funded opportunities for ‘the next generation of UK creative talent’ to work on the major SFA-led UNBOXED 22[[37]](#_ftn37) commission StoryTrails.[[38]](#_ftn38) The London SF cluster has worked with the National Gallery on its StoryLab[[39]](#_ftn39) programme, and SF has also produced and published a significant body of research[[40]](#_ftn40) on topics related to immersive economy and culture.

 

4.4       Based at the University of York, since 2018 XR Stories[[41]](#_ftn41) has also supported significant R&D with new tech by arts/culture sector organisations in the Yorkshire region. As with the other Creative Clusters, XR Stories has a remit to be ‘a bridge between industry and academic partners’ and, like the other clusters, it has regarded the not-for-profit sector of the culture/creative industries as within its scope. Development support has been facilitated in particular by R&D funding[[42]](#_ftn42) for immersive and interactive storytelling projects,[[43]](#_ftn43) many of which are from the arts/culture sector. XR Stories has proved a useful resource/ source of knowledge transfer for Arts Council NPOs in the York area (e.g. York Museums Trust, Pilot Theatre, Theatre Royal York) and has been an important partner for Project Grants-funded organisation York Mediale.

 

4.5       Bristol + Bath Creative R&D[[44]](#_ftn44) (B+B) is a partnership aiming to improve the performance of the Creative Industries in the Bristol and Bath region. Unlike SF and XR Stories, it does not have a specific focus on XR storytelling. B+B brings together Arts Council NPO Watershed and the four B+B universities, working with a range of industry partners. The core proposition is to partner with industry to gain understanding about user engagement in new platforms. The partnership is working ‘at sites where 5G connectivity, XR technologies and live arts overlap’ and it ‘offers a suite of support to the region’s businesses, creatives, artists and thinkers to experiment with new and emerging technologies, conduct research, and develop prototype products and experiences to share with the public.’ Beneficiaries have included arts/culture sector organisations and individual practitioners.

4.6       Audience of the Future[[45]](#_ftn45) (AotF) has also enabled large scale collaborative R&D and knowledge exchange in the arts/culture sector through the Dream[[46]](#_ftn46) and Dinosaurs and Robots[[47]](#_ftn47) demonstrator projects. A number of Arts Council NPOs (RSC, Punchdrunk Philharmonia, Almeida Theatre), plus the Science Museum Group, have played leading roles within these projects –– working alongside partners from HE (Goldsmiths, Portsmouth University) and the wider creative industries (e.g. Magic Leap, Epic Games, Factory 42, Marshmallow Laser Feast). While these projects have captured and shared learning that could benefit the sector, it is unclear that they have provided specific practical skills development or production opportunities beyond the core participants.

 

4.7       To help stimulate R&D and advanced digital skills development in the arts and culture sector, the Arts Council would strongly endorse some of the key recommendations to Government listed in the 2021 Boundless Creativity[[48]](#_ftn48) report published jointly by UKRI/AHRC and DCMS, which set out to ‘Recommend specific research and policy interventions to drive engagement with the issues highlighted in this report, including those which will allow the sector to maximise the potential of new digital and immersive technologies in engaging and diversifying audiences.’ Two of the resulting recommendations are aimed to increase creative R&D with new tech by the cultural sector. These recommendations were:

 

 

 

4.8       The recommendations: ‘capitalise on the new ways of working that have characterised cultural life during COVID-19 and the shared commitment of the AHRC and DCMS to work more closely together for the benefit of cultural organisations and creative technology.’

 

4.9       The Arts Council would advocate that any new programmes should be for a minimum of 5-years (justified by the successes of the UKRI/AHRC industrial strategy funded programmes) to ensure ecologies are given time to develop and skills and approaches have the time and resources to embed.

 

4.10   One of the purposes of such funding would be to incentivise collaborations and knowledge exchange across sectors, especially between HEIs and culture sector partners. Overall, there seems more scope for creative technology to be foregrounded as a priority locus for knowledge exchange between HEIs + the arts; currently HEI/culture sector knowledge exchange tends to focus more on other agendas, such as health, place-making and climate change (as exemplified by the current NCACE[[49]](#_ftn49) priority activity areas, which highlight ‘technologies for social good’, but not the use of advanced technologies for creative production and distribution). 

 

4.11   Regarding ‘recommendation 3’ of the Boundless Creativity report, the Arts Council would suggest that DCMS conversations with HMRC should include consideration of whether additional Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes could be introduced in order to support creative R&D in the arts and culture sector, alongside existing successful tax relief schemes such as those for Film, and for Museums and Galleries Exhibitions.

 

4.12   Combined and local authorities have an important role in ensuring that the appropriate support exists to grow creative industry clusters in place.  Both can provide local leadership and convene partners to ensure that the needs of the creative sectors are considered, and evidence collated, as local strategies are developed.  This is particularly relevant as regards skills, where growth in the creative industries is a local or a regional priority combined and local authorities should engage creative sector stakeholders in the development of Local Skills Improvement Plans, and ensure that they are represented in the employers consulted. Local and combined authorities can broker partnerships between the local creative industrial sector, FE, HE and schools to this end.  This will also be important to ensuring that access to careers in this sector is equitable. 

 

4.13   Where they are negotiating a devolution deal with the Government, combined authorities seeking to grow the local cultural sector should consider how the full suite of powers they request, including but not limited to skills, can support this growth.  We would also recommend that government thinks in the round about how devolution asks of departments other than DCMS may be fundamental to ensuring that devolution deals can effectively support creative sector growth. Skills is an immediate and obvious example.

 

4.14   Where the local creative sector lacks capacity to engage with local strategy and planning, local and combined authorities should facilitate engagement through the development of models such as cultural compacts, which can help build the local strategic and partnership capacity within the creative sector necessary for its full participation in setting out local ambition and contributing to the actions necessary to realise that.

 

4.15   University and other industry training courses for arts and culture should also include within their curriculum programmes and modules that reflect the latest (and upcoming) technological developments, as they pertain to different arts and cultural disciplines.

 

4.16   Regarding the clause in Question 3 about Government interventions that are flexible and responsive to the rapid rate of change, we would advocate that any future programmes should be accompanied and informed by ongoing evaluation, research and periodic points of consultation (across a range of stakeholders) which will help to ensure that emerging themes and technologies  can be identified and that existing programmes can be adapted, or new ones introduced, where new opportunities or priorities emerge.

 

 

5.       What actions are needed from industry to support the talent pipeline development?    
 

a) What actions are needed from organisations in the creative industries to prepare for and accommodate the requirements of the future workforce?

 

5.1       The tech industry can support talent development in the arts and culture sector by providing access to new technologies for learning and experimentation at all professional levels. For example, recognising that a workforce with expertise in technology development and storytelling techniques will benefit both the creative and tech sectors, the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) partnered with Magic Leap, maker of augmented reality hardware and platforms, to provide fellowships[[50]](#_ftn50) to recent university graduates. Working across these organisations, the Fellows developed their skill and expertise in using spatial computing to create new theatrical experiences.

 

5.2       The tech industry can also support talent to develop through less intensive methods of skill building and knowledge exchange. For example, Arts Council partnered with Google Arts to deliver a range of workshops on topics such as ecommerce, web design, content and streaming, data & analytics, email marketing, CRM and SEO.  Access to Google’s software and expertise shaped by Arts Council to be applicable in the arts and culture sector allows existing talent to continuously improve.

 

5.3       Arts Council has been approached by several tech sector leaders in gaming and immersive technology seeking to develop programmes for children and young people. A number have pointed to BFI Academy and BBC Academy as models of what is needed in terms of scale and impact.

 

5.4       The tech sector can also play a role in upskilling the existing leadership in the arts and culture sector by advocating that staff join the boards of arts organisations. The Arts Council 2019 Digital Culture Survey found: “At board level, a similar picture emerges. 57% of organisations told us they don’t have board members who make a significant contribution to their digital strategy, while only 19% report that they do (the latter figure is down from 21% in 2017).”  The National Gallery has a digital advisory board comprised of thought leaders from across the tech sector who support the Gallery in embedding digital innovation into planning and practice. Arts Council receives many requests for support in identifying tech sector experts to join their boards.  Board appointments are significant leadership development opportunities which tech companies could use to develop their internal talent pipelines. New models of board ‘banks’ should be considered to fulfil this need.

 

5.5       Storytelling is critical for broad consumer/audience adoption of technologies, particularly AR/VR and other immersive technologies. Furthermore, numerous studies have identified creativity[[51]](#_ftn51) as a top soft skill[[52]](#_ftn52) needed in the tech industry.[[53]](#_ftn53) On the other hand, Arts Council has found a drop in knowledge of digital technology among its senior leadership: In 2013, 22% of respondents felt their senior management were knowledgeable about digital technology, but this figure dropped to just 13% in 2019. Developing multiple channels of knowledge exchange, cross-functional training and lifelong learning between the tech and creative sectors will be key to the health of both workforces.

 

5.6       Given the pace of digital change, arts and culture organisations will need to create new methods of skills acquisition.  Not only will continuous digital upskilling need to be embedded into core operations, new types of roles and working methods will need to be developed.  For example, Arts Council decided to adopt a new recruiting method and structure for its Digital Culture Network team.  The ‘Tech Champions,’ who provide advice and support to the organisations Arts Council funds, where specifically recruited for their experience outside of the subsidised arts. Arts Council wanted their fresh perspective to help disrupt thinking in arts and culture organisations regarding use of new technologies. Furthermore, the intention is that there will be continuous churn of Tech Champions so that new knowledge is replenished. Other methods of bringing tech knowledge into an organisation should be adopted. For example, The National Gallery has a number of tech residencies associated with its National Gallery X[[54]](#_ftn54) experimental lab. 

 

5.7       Arts and culture organisations will also need ensure digital is embedded in its financial and strategic planning.  Future workforces will expect digital innovation to be included in core operational budgets and for digital to play a central role in the delivery of organisational mission and purpose. According to Arts Council’s 2019 Digital Culture Survey the most frequently cited barriers to organisations realising their digital aspirations are lack of funding to allocate to digital (70 per cent in 2019). Studies need to be conducted on the impact of Covid on these attitudes. Anecdotally, interest in funding for digital infrastructure has grown over the last two years, suggesting that digital is increasingly seen as important for core operations. 

 

5.8       Arts and Culture organisations will also need to become more data savvy and invest in data management system and tools. According to Arts Council’s 2019 Digital Culture Survey, in terms of commercial uses of data, 15 per cent of organisations in the sector are using data to develop new products or services and 31 per cent are personalising campaigns for marketing, sales and fundraising. This contrasts with the commercial use of customer or end-user data in many other sectors such as retail, healthcare, transport and banking.  Research indicates that the future workforce is data literate[[55]](#_ftn55) and will expect data to be at their fingertips to enable rapid decision making.

 

 

6.       What role do innovation and research & development play in addressing the future challenges facing the creative industries?

 

a) What actions are needed from the Government, funding bodies and sector organisations to support innovation, and research & development?

 

6.1       The Arts Council’s position on the role that Government could play in stimulating R&D in the arts and culture sector is largely covered in the response to Question 3, and supports the recommendations from the Boundless Creativity report. Namely, to: continue to fund creative innovation and R&D programmes; review how current Government definitions of R&D could be amended to better reflect the role and value of R&D in the creative industries; and to consider whether additional tax relief schemes could be introduced to support and incentivise creative R&D with advanced technologies.

 

6.2       As the principal funding body for arts and culture in England the Arts Council aims to support and incentivise innovation and R&D in a number of ways.

 

6.3       Firstly, a commitment to supporting and encouraging R&D is signalled in the Investment Principles[[56]](#_ftn56) (IPs) which underpin our 10-year strategy, Let’s Create. The second of our IPs, Dynamism, notes the importance of ‘new technological opportunities’ and states that: ‘We want to see the development of a more informed and effective data culture within the organisations that we fund, and the adoption of appropriate new technologies across all aspects of their businesses. We know that the cultural sector has yet to fully utilise the power of data to understand its audiences and the impact of its work. We will build partnerships with the technology sector and with further and higher education to help drive improvement in this area.’ 

 

6.4       The third of three essential pillars[[57]](#_ftn57) that we identify as underpinning Dynamism is ‘Using technology and information’. Our ambition is that ‘Cultural organisations are committed to using data and appropriate technology to develop and improve their businesses. The ongoing development of digital skills and data literacy is prioritised.’ Organisations are advised to ‘Embed the use of appropriate technology and tools across your activities and seek to understand and exploit the opportunities technology can provide’; and to ‘Build confidence and skills to use technology across your organisation and regularly review to ensure that knowledge and skills and systems are up to date and match business needs.’

 

6.5       The Arts Council is currently in the decision process of determining its next NPO portfolio for 2023 to 2026. Within this portfolio of regularly funded organisations, there will be a new category of NPO called Investment Principles Support Organisations (IPSOs).[[58]](#_ftn58) Some of these IPSOs will provide services which help other arts organisations to embed the Dynamism IP. We expect that some IPSOs will have specific knowledge and expertise in digital technologies that they will share with the sector (e.g. through training opportunities and online resources). The 2023-2026 portfolio is also expected to include some NPOs (not in the IPSO category) which have a strong focus within their public-facing programmes on R&D and on creating and distributing new work made using advanced technologies. 

 

6.6       Our National Lottery Project Grants (NLPG) programme will continue to welcome applications using digital technologies,[[59]](#_ftn59) including ‘Projects that involve interactive or immersive digital elements and can give users a new, interactive or immersive experience using technology.’ Examples of the types of projects that we say we will fund include VR, AR, MR, location-based and online interactive games or web-based projects, immersive digital exhibitions and immersive or interactive work within wider film, media arts or other festivals.

 

6.7       The strand of NLPG for applications for over £100,000 has priority Areas of Focus, which include: ‘Building new partnerships across technology and research that support innovation in practice’ and ‘Utilising using new technologies to develop new, forms of arts and cultural content and ways of, reaching audiences’. 

 

6.8       We will also look to continue to use our Development Funds to invest in programmes that specifically support creative R&D and talent development with advanced technologies, such as the Creative XR and the UK-Canada Immersive Exchange programmes.

 

6.9       Additionally, we will continue to form partnerships, and to strengthen existing ones, that can help us to support the sector to experiment with and gain new skills in advanced technologies. The types of partners we will work with will cover a range of different sectors, including HE, public sector development agencies with an innovation and technology remit, the commercial creative industries and other funders with an interest in supporting innovation and technology. Some examples of these partners are provided in our response to Question 2.

 

6.10   To support the sector to improve digital and data skills in specific business areas (e.g. web design or digital marketing) we will continue to invest in the Digital Culture Network and in data-focussed resources such as Audience Finder. 

 

6.11   In terms of other funders, we will advocate for innovation and R&D funding that is not routed directly via the Arts Council (e.g. industrial strategy funding administered by AHRC/UKRI) to include eligibility criteria that make it possible for the (generally not-for-profit) organisations that make up our sector to benefit. Where practicable, we will look to develop co-funding partnerships with agencies that can contribute relevant, research, technological and innovation expertise, as well as match funding, to help develop the advanced digital capabilities and outputs of our sector.

 

6.12   We will expect that sector organisations with advanced digital expertise that are funded by the Arts Council, either as IPSOs or as public-facing NPOs, will play a leadership role to help the sector to understand and engage with the opportunities presented by advanced technologies. Examples from the current portfolio include the Serpentine Galleries’ Arts Technologies[[60]](#_ftn60) programme and R&D Platform[[61]](#_ftn61) and the learning and resources generated by the RSC’s Dream[[62]](#_ftn62) project.

 

6.13   We support the government’s ambition, as set out in the Levelling Up White Paper, to increase funding for R&D outside of London and the South East, and suggest that policies such as the three Innovation Accelerators might be able to support growth in the creative industries.

 

 

7.       How effective are the Government’s existing strategies at supporting the creative industries to meet the challenges and opportunities ahead?

 

7.1       We believe that the programmes initiated by UKRI/AHRC with Government industrial strategy funding have been effective and influential in supporting the development of ecologies and networks of expertise, production activity and skills development within the creative industries. The current programmes are scheduled to end in 2023 and, in line with the Boundless Creativity report recommendations, we would advocate for further innovation programmes of this kind to be introduced, backed by Government investment, in order to capitalise on and amplify the achievements of the last four years.

 

7.2       We would further advocate that any future programmes should: seek to address current geographical gaps in provision/opportunity (i.e. extend beyond the current nine creative industries cluster locations which, for example, do not support activity in the Midlands); have eligibility criteria which make it clear that not-for-profit arts and culture organisations can benefit from funding and development opportunities; run for a minimum of 5-years, to enable networks to form and ecologies to mature, allowing sufficient time for development impacts to accrue and embed.

 

7.3       In order to ensure that the benefits of any future Government funded creative innovation and R&D programmes are appropriately targeted to bring benefits to the not-for-profit arts and culture sector, the Arts Council would wish to be considered as a stakeholder that has knowledge and expertise to contribute to any consultations regarding ideas and proposals for future Government creative R&D programmes.

 

7.4       There is evidence of positive impact from Government creative industries Tax Relief schemes that encourage risk and innovation in areas such as Film, Theatre and Museum and Galleries Exhibition. It should be considered whether similar Tax Relief mechanisms should be developed, or existing ones adapted, to help stimulate innovation and production in practices using advanced technologies, such as XR storytelling.

 

 

8.       What lessons can the UK’s creative industries learn from other countries, and other sectors?

 

8.1       The Arts Council recognises that cutting-edge technological innovation in the creative industries happens in a highly collaborative space that is not limited by national boundaries. Creative teams applying to the Arts Council/Digital Catapult Creative XR fund, for example, regularly include members or partners working in different territories. On the other hand, creative industries practitioners in different territories may operate within regulatory, fiscal, financial and legal frameworks and consumer markets that are different from those in the UK.

 

8.2       In order to benefit from creative R&D developments happening elsewhere in the world and also to identify opportunities for new collaborations, different sources of investment, and new routes to market, it is important for practitioners working creatively with advanced technologies to be exposed to international influences, working cultures and technological and creative innovations.

 

8.3       The Arts Council currently supports international exchange and showcasing for practitioners working creatively with advanced technologies through two specific programmes: the Future Art and Culture[[63]](#_ftn63) (FAC) programme at the annual South by Southwest (SXSW) conference and festivals in Austin, Texas; and the UK-Canada Immersive Exchange[[64]](#_ftn64) (UCIE) programme, an international talent development and XR co-production initiative jointly devised and resourced by arts funders and creative tech development agencies based in Canada and England.

 

8.4       SXSW is recognised as the preeminent international culture and technology event. It is a showcase and marketplace where creatives can meet with pioneers and investors from a wide range of innovation sectors (not just arts and culture) resulting in significant cross-disciplinary collaboration, media and export outcomes.

 

8.5       The FAC programme, funded by the Arts Council and produced by NPO British Underground, introduces cultural practitioners from England to creative industry (and wider innovation) professionals from over 100 countries creating opportunities for targeted, qualitative engagement with key international decision makers. SXSW is unique as a showcase where creative tech professionals come into contact with pioneers and investors from other innovation fields, enhancing opportunities for collaboration, development and investment.

 

8.6       British Underground works in close partnership with key UK organisations with an international focus such as the Department for International Trade (DIT), UKRI, and British Council to deliver a ‘UK House’; a joined-up presence at SXSW that amplifies the profile and impact of the UK creative tech delegation.

 

8.7       Tom Fleming Associates independent evaluation of FAC found that: ‘FAC 2022, alongside previous editions, is having a significant and varied impact on the practice and position of arts and tech programmes, organisations and individual professionals who have participated. It is also boosting the profile of the UK as a champion of boundary-crossing creative practice and positioning Arts Council investment to the heart of this embrace with creative technology.’

 

8.8       The UCIE pilot programme culminated in March 2022 with a ‘world premiere’ showcase of co-production immersive prototypes[[65]](#_ftn65) developed by teams of UCIE participants working across boundaries between the UK and Canada, with all the creative activity being delivered remotely due to Covid restrictions.

 

8.9       Other major creative industries initiatives working with advanced technologies (such as the UKRI/AHRC creative clusters and Audience of the Future programmes and the UNBOXED project) have also had a significant presence at SXSW and at other major international festivals in recent years, highlighting the importance of international exchange and profile-raising to practitioners working in this field. A significant number of immersive projects that received prototype funding through Creative XR have subsequently been selected to participate in high profile international showcases, such as Tribeca (New York), Venice Immersive and LFF Expanded (the immersive strands of the Venice and London international film festivals), often leading to additional production investment and opportunities for further distribution and commissions.

When handling different types of content:

- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

This document is the written evidence (CRF0043) submitted by Arts Council England to the House of Lords Communications and Digital Select Committee inquiry "A creative future" (September 2022). It covers how the Arts Council supports culture, disruptions facing the creative industries, skills needs, talent pipelines, R&D policy, and international lessons.

**Arts Council funding**: Between 2018-2022, the Arts Council invested £1.45 billion of public money plus an estimated £860 million from the National Lottery. During Covid-19, it awarded £1.14 billion through the Government's Culture Recovery Fund and £160 million through its own Emergency Response Fund.

**Key disruptive technologies (next 5-10 years)**:
1. **AI** – significant impact on audience data management, collections management, artistic production, IP ownership questions, and audience curation. Arts Council's 2019 commissioned research found barriers include cost/market maturity (e.g., theatre captioning) and the need for sophisticated data management.
2. **5G** – ultra-low latency will revolutionise live streaming of data-rich content, improve accessibility, and enable remote creative collaborations (e.g., 5G Festival at Brighton Dome).
3. **Virtual production, extended reality, virtual worlds** – could radically alter how work is made and where audiences encounter it. Examples include RSC's Dream, ROH's Current Rising, Tate's Modigliani VR, National Gallery's Virtual Veronese. Social forms of immersive experience are likely to evolve (e.g., Unreal City AR trail on the Thames, Unboxed StoryTrails). Online, projects like musician-led start-up Ristband are using virtual worlds.
4. **Web 3.0 technologies** (blockchain, crypto art, DAOs, NFTs) – potentially the most disruptive, with implications for how art is made, consumed, monetised and controlled. Proponents cite potential to change power structures; critics note unregulated financial speculation and IP/attribution challenges. In 2022, Italy suspended NFT creation based on Italian masterworks.

**Skills challenges**: A major challenge is inequality of access and opportunity; many lack digital devices. The 2019 Digital Culture survey (Arts Council/Nesta) found "a widening gulf between large and small organisations," organisations becoming "less experimental and more risk averse," with a downward trend in R&D behaviours. Senior management knowledge of digital technology fell from 22% (2013) to 13% (2019). Only 19% of organisations have board members contributing to digital strategy. In 2019, 70% cited lack of funding for digital as a barrier. Pandemic shutdowns accelerated digital learning, but it's unclear whether innovation will continue at scale amid economic crisis.

**Arts Council support mechanisms**: Digital Culture Network, Audience Finder, Impact & Insight Toolkit, Bloomberg Philanthropies' Digital Accelerator Programme, Creative XR, UK-Canada Immersive Exchange, Digital R&D Fund for the Arts. NPOs like RSC, Serpentine Galleries, Watershed, Furtherfield share expertise; small organisations like Collusion and York Mediale support practitioner R&D.

**Government/talent pipeline recommendations**: Continue investment in R&D and advanced digital skills; set funding criteria enabling not-for-profit arts organisations to benefit. Templates include the Creative Industries Clusters Programme (£39m, via UKRI/AHRC – XR Stories, B+B, StoryFutures) and Audiences of the Future Challenge (£33m – Dream, Dinosaurs and Robots). Programmes should run a minimum of 5 years. Supports Boundless Creativity report (2021, UKRI/AHRC & DCMS) recommendations, including considering new Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes. Combined/local authorities should engage creative stakeholders in Local Skills Improvement Plans and cultural compacts. Universities should reflect latest tech developments in curricula.

**Industry actions needed**: Tech industry should provide access to new technologies (e.g., RSC-Magic Leap fellowships, Google Arts workshops), support board-level tech expertise (with board 'banks' considered), recognise creativity as a top soft skill. Organisations need continuous digital upskilling embedded in operations (e.g., Arts Council's 'Tech Champions' recruitment model), embed digital in financial/strategic planning, and become more data savvy.

**R&D role**: Arts Council's "Dynamism" Investment Principle underpinning its Let's Create strategy emphasises "new technological opportunities," data culture, and technology adoption. New 2023-2026 NPO portfolio will include Investment Principles Support Organisations (IPSOs) sharing digital expertise. National Lottery Project Grants welcome digital/immersive projects; funds over £100,000 prioritise technology partnerships and new forms of content/audience reach.

**Government strategies effectiveness**: UKRI/AHRC industrial strategy programmes have been effective but end in 2023; future programmes should address geographical gaps (e.g., no current cluster in the Midlands), ensure not-for-profit eligibility, run 5+ years. Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes (Film, Theatre, Museums & Galleries) have shown positive impact; similar schemes should be considered for advanced tech practices.

**International lessons**: Cutting-edge innovation is highly collaborative and cross-border. The Arts Council supports international exchange via the Future Art and Culture (FAC) programme at SXSW (produced by British Underground) and the UK-Canada Immersive Exchange (UCIE). SXSW provides cross-disciplinary collaboration, investment and export outcomes. Creative XR prototypes have been selected for showcases at Tribeca, Venice Immersive and LFF Expanded.

**Social Evaluation System, Economic Treatment, and IP Protection for Art Graduates in China (Dimensions 2 & 3)**

Please research the following two interconnected dimensions:

**Dimension 2: Social Evaluation System and Its Impact**
1. How do Chinese societal attitudes, family expectations, and institutional recognition affect the career development and income levels of art graduates? Include analysis of the traditional "face culture" (面子文化) and the perception of art as a "unstable" or "impractical" career.
2. Specific barriers and biases art graduates face in China: hiring discrimination, glass ceilings in non-art industries, credentialism, the "professional title" (职称) system's impact on art professionals, and regional disparities (first-tier cities vs. smaller cities).
3. How the Chinese educational system (Gaokao, art examination system) and the classification of "art students" (艺术生) shapes social perceptions.
4. Market valuation of art skills in China compared to STEM fields - income gaps, social prestige rankings.

**Dimension 3: Economic Treatment and Protection Mechanisms**
1. Intellectual property protection for artists in China: current state of copyright law enforcement, trademark protection for visual artists, challenges in digital copyright (NFTs, AI-generated art), and recent IP litigation cases involving artists from 2021-2026.
2. Cultural consumption upgrades in China: how has the growth of China's cultural and creative industry, museum economy, art market, and cultural tourism affected the income and economic opportunities for art professionals? Include data on China's cultural industry GDP share, art market size, and growth trends.
3. Specific policy initiatives: the Chinese government's copyright protection reforms, the "Cultural Confidence" (文化自信) policy, cultural industry development plans in the 14th Five-Year Plan, and any pilot programs supporting artist income.
4. Analysis of whether improved IP protection and cultural consumption growth have actually translated into better economic outcomes for individual art professionals, with data on income trends.

Prioritize Chinese-language sources for data. Include both quantitative data (income statistics, employment rates, IP litigation data, cultural industry GDP figures) and qualitative analysis.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in the Journal of Education Research and Practice (JERP) titled "艺术类专业毕业生就业影响因素的多维解析与路径优化" (Multi-dimensional Analysis and Path Optimization of Factors Influencing Employment of Art Graduates). The study investigates employment challenges faced by art graduates in China, using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from 3,847 graduates across 150 higher education institutions (2022-2024), plus qualitative interviews with 126 participants.

Key findings: Overall employment rate is 86.7% (52.3% contracted, 34.4% flexible, 13.3% pursuing further study). Employment concentrates in first-tier (42.8%) and new first-tier cities (31.6%). Design graduates earn highest average monthly salary (7,500 RMB) vs. pure art (5,800 RMB). Only 38.4% work in fields directly matching their major.

The study uses structural equation modeling (SEM) and finds that human capital (skills and practical experience) has the strongest direct effect on employment quality (β=0.372, p<0.001), followed by social capital (β=0.298). Environmental factors (regional economic development and cultural industry policy support) positively influence employment outcomes, while labor market competition has a negative effect. Gender effects are not significant. Family socioeconomic status positively impacts employment quality indirectly through better internship opportunities. Design/art graduates are constrained by skill-market mismatch, while other art graduates are constrained by social networks.

Recommendations include: optimizing education with practice-based teaching and industry-academia integration; government support through art entrepreneurship funds and talent policies; career guidance expanding into "art+tech" and "art+business" domains; and targeted support for disadvantaged students to compensate for cultural capital gaps.
</summary>

**Key Reforms:**

1. **Tiered System:** Establishes a unified 4-tier system (Level 4 = Junior, Level 3 = Intermediate, Level 2 = Associate Senior, Level 1 = Senior) across 4 professional categories: Art Performance (actors, instrumentalists), Art Creation (directors, screenwriters, composers, photographers, designers, fine artists, literary writers), Art Management (performance supervisors), and Technical Support (stage technicians, sound engineers, editors).
