# Artists and Other Cultural Workers: A Statistical Portrait

Connecting the Dots – #YesThisIsAnArtsStory Repost from the National Endowment for the Arts

This report was published in April 2019.

The authors, editors and designers can be found on **page 4** of the report.

**About the Report**

This omnibus report, Artists and Other Cultural Workers: A Statistical Portrait, extends the range of statistics that the National Endowment for the Arts historically has tracked as part of its decades-long research function. Although the agency periodically reports facts and figures about 11 distinct artist occupations (based on U.S. Census data), this report brings in other job characteristics, other data sources, and even other kinds of cultural workers. Among key findings are:

1. Regardless of occupation, over 5 million workers are employed in arts and cultural industries. They are all wage-and-salary workers.

• There are nearly 2.5 million artists in the U.S. labor force (either self-employed or wage-and-salary workers). • Approximately 333,000 (self-employed or wage-and-salary) workers hold secondary jobs as artists.

• Another 1.2 million (self-employed or wage-and-salary) workers hold a primary job in a cultural occupation other than artist.

2. Artists are 3.6 times as likely as other workers to be self-employed.

• In 2012-2016, roughly 34 percent of all artists were self-employed. This compares with 9 percent of all workers.

• Most self-employed artists seem to like their work arrangement: 79 percent say they would not prefer to work for someone else, while 58 percent cite flexible schedules and independence as the main reasons they are self-employed.

3. Artists are becoming a larger share of the U.S. labor force.

• In 2006, artists composed 1.42 percent of the labor force; by 2017, they were 1.55 percent, representing a 6.1 percent increase.

• In 2017, the artist unemployment rate hit an 11-year low.

• As a group, artists currently experience unemployment rates similar to those of all U.S. workers.

4. Faster-than-average growth in employment is projected for set and exhibit designers, actors, producers and directors, and film and video editors.

• Between 2016 and 2026, annual job openings will have averaged 7,400 for actors and 14,100 for producers and directors. Employment growth in these occupations stems from strong demand for new movies and television shows.

• Employment of film/video editors is projected to grow at a 17 percent clip. A contributing factor is the number of shows increasingly produced by Internet-only sources and streaming services.

Chapter by chapter, this report builds a cohesive statistical summary of artists and other cultural workers in the United States. In doing so, it complements the National Endowment for the Arts’ regular measurements of two other key segments of the arts ecosystem: arts industries and organizations, and levels of arts participation nationwide.

args.summary:
This page is a Dance Data Project (DDP) repost of a National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) report titled "Artists and Other Cultural Workers: A Statistical Portrait," published in April 2019. The report is part of DDP's "Connecting the Dots – #YesThisIsAnArtsStory" series.

Key findings from the report include:
1. Over 5 million workers are employed in arts and cultural industries. There are nearly 2.5 million artists in the U.S. labor force, approximately 333,000 workers hold secondary jobs as artists, and another 1.2 million hold a primary job in a cultural occupation other than artist.
2. Artists are 3.6 times as likely as other workers to be self-employed. In 2012-2016, roughly 34% of all artists were self-employed versus 9% of all workers. Most self-employed artists like their arrangement: 79% would not prefer to work for someone else, and 58% cite flexible schedules and independence as the main reasons.
3. Artists are becoming a larger share of the U.S. labor force. In 2006, artists composed 1.42% of the labor force; by 2017, they were 1.55% (a 6.1% increase). In 2017, the artist unemployment rate hit an 11-year low and is currently similar to all U.S. workers.
4. Faster-than-average employment growth is projected for set and exhibit designers, actors, producers/directors, and film/video editors. Between 2016-2026, annual job openings will average 7,400 for actors and 14,100 for producers and directors. Film/video editor employment is projected to grow at a 17% clip due to streaming services and Internet-only content sources.

The page also lists upcoming funding deadlines (including Bronx Cultural Visions Fund, DRIFT Open Call, Culture Forward Grant, New England Dance Fund, Community Arts Grant, Shubert Foundation Dance Grant, Howard Fellowship, and National Dance Project grants) and provides navigation links to DDP's research, interviews, resources, and advocacy sections.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

<webpage_content>
136 Irving Street  
 Cambridge, MA 02138



Art Is Work

# Introduction

[Back to table of contents](/publication/art-is-work)

Project

Commission on the Arts

Share

* [Introduction](#introduction)
* [The Value of Artists](#the-value-of-artists)
* [Artists and Creative Workers: The Details](#artists-and-creative-workers-the-details)

“This is the only real concern of the artist, to recreate out of the disorder of life that order which is art.”  
**—James Baldwin[1](#footnote__lWfZpICnkopLoCUxs---oLepL9nr98e2YynQaWbhwI_1)**

“Hell! They’ve got to eat just like other people.”  
**—Harry Hopkins, Director of FDR’s Works Progress Administration during the Great Depression**

Art can be many things, but it starts as work. Sadly, that work is consistently undervalued in American society. While a recent national survey found that 81 percent of Americans believe the arts are “a positive experience in a troubled world,” a separate survey conducted for this report found only 22 percent of Americans believe artists contribute “a lot” to the general good of society.[2](#footnote__Mo4EzGLSGFAvi9bHmc5YZmnuj44MAR-BoJcZHyA2jOU_1) This gap between American feelings about the personal value of the arts and their perceptions about the value of those who create that art undermines the work artists and cultural workers are able to do, the value they are able to contribute to the health of our communities, and who is able to make a life as an artist. In this report, we address a central question: **How can we better recognize the value of artists in our national policy in order to enable the essential work they do?**

The report is a product of the Commission on the Arts, a multiyear project of the American Academy that brought together artists, scholars, advocates, and leaders from across the country. The forty-four members of the Commission identified central issues related to the arts and their role in American life and society, including how artists are often undervalued even when their art is rightly considered essential. To build this report, the Commission held virtual listening sessions with experts in the field, commissioned a field scan of community and economic development–focused artist programs around the country, and built partnerships with advocacy groups, experts, and creatives involved in similar efforts.

We discovered that artists desperately need a better system. In the middle of our work, the COVID-19 pandemic struck, deeply impacting the arts and culture sector. Venues shuttered, organizations lost revenue, and artists had gigs and shows canceled, were furloughed, or lost their jobs entirely. Despite such hardships, artists of all kinds, including musicians, dancers, writers, actors, and visual artists, stepped up to help their communities through their artistic abilities. Still, the moment is one of crisis for arts and culture—and also reveals existing cracks in the sector. For some, the pandemic has underscored the precarious nature of their work. Many artists had access to unemployment insurance for the first time in their careers because of the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance program. For others, the crisis highlighted glaring racial and gender inequities in the field, as the loss of income and the consequences of lost income were not distributed evenly.[3](#footnote__ixFt5yUQQlivxx6yDPAYVmbLhBsnH8OaGyu1NiXB8g_1) The precarity of the present moment reflects the severe lack of supports that were in place before the pandemic. Artists need help now, but simply addressing the immediate crisis will not shore up artists’ lives and protect them from the next shock or from the smaller crises of the everyday.

“The United States needs to recalibrate its market values and support systems to justify an inclusive attitude toward professional artists as essential workers of society.”  
**—Felix Padrón (Commission member, visual artist, curator, and arts management professional)**

We arrived at four key principles that ground our recommendations to build a better system:

1. **Name and include artists in federal policy.** Artists need representation at a federal level, preferably at the executive level, and they need to be explicitly named as a category in legislation and policy. That is the only way to ensure that new federal policies aimed at building our workforce, supporting the economy, and strengthening society will include artists as vital members of the workforce, builders of the economy, and maintainers of community.
2. **Recognize how creative work happens.** Many work-related policies and safety nets are written for a long-lasting single employment relationship that is no longer standard for the general workforce and was never standard for artists. Artists need policy that recognizes *as standard* independent contract work, multiple employers, entrepreneurship, and inconsistent income—and supports workers accordingly.
3. **Center equity.** The value of artists to America will never be realized without the full participation of Black, Indigenous, and other artists of color. Yet they have been under­resourced and underrecognized. Women artists, artists with disabilities, and rural artists have likewise often been underrecognized. Artists need anti-racist policies that equitably fund, train, and support them.
4. **Think locally, share nationally.** Much of artists’ vital work is locally rooted and supported. Policy and funding solutions must recognize this. Funding mechanisms at the national level need to be shaped in a way that supports and amplifies local mechanisms and programs. However, increased national-level sharing of successes and supports is clearly also needed.

To make the case for these policies and practices, we start by articulating the value of artists and cultural workers in American society and dig deeper into the challenges that limit their full participation in those roles. We then build out the four principles above into a set of recommendations to enable an America where the people who make art are as valued as the product of their labors.

Artists are dynamic contributors to the small-business sector. The Torpedo Factory Art Center, a reclaimed World War II facility in Alexandria, Virginia, provides studio space for artists such as Christine Cardellino.

## The Value of Artists

Arts are essential to many areas of American life, as attested by the already numerous reports, research papers, and paeans to the value of the arts. In the present report we touch on only two main areas—the economic and the civic—while acknowledging that the value of the arts and the artists who make arts possible extends far beyond. (A separate report by this Commission, on the arts in K–12 education, examines many of these other values.)[4](#footnote__6oRS-5cgbXUwr2I7xbPKdUyJh8xUNvajdVZqjqONgbM_1)

That a large share of Americans fails to see the value of the creative sector to society is disappointing, because arts and culture play a tangible role in the American economy, supplying approximately 4.3 percent of the gross domestic product (at least in times undistorted by the pandemic). In 2019, the sector was larger than construction, travel and tourism, and agriculture.[5](#footnote__uGcSf3A1JOw6yVKIOTkWCKH7OEvNtBmjMaXZW-J62k_1) But creating this value is possible only because millions of Americans are employed in the creative economy.[6](#footnote__FILLlDTGeiWOK7OxP0Pxa89EdiBlpkUWk9JhP6jUoRY_1)

Prior to the pandemic, the arts and culture sector was growing. Adjusted for inflation, production of arts and cultural goods and services grew by more than 35 percent from 1998 to 2016, and the sector provided a nearly $33 billion trade surplus to the U.S. economy in 2019.[7](#footnote__ETTweSjrePqOpjCXOETx2kwLdVuzIcsoohG9iixjPRg_1) Research suggests that the arts and culture sector can also be a key area of state-level economic growth following periods of economic shock (such as a recession) by facilitating sector diversification and general employment growth.[8](#footnote__7Vnh5aga8M0toBTTNbbIChI0hIrAaT6fRFe59hyCW-E_1) And greater inclusivity can make room for even more growth. For instance, a recent study indicates that addressing barriers for Black creatives in film and television could increase annual revenues by $10 billion.[9](#footnote__7kd5lNdiNH2Ia5JxliXUotUYVMUbvIrBH29V0dds2Ng_1)

**“I would love for every biotech company to have a creative director.”**  
  
Christina Agapakis is the creative director at Gingko Bioworks, a biotech company valued at $15 billion.[10](#footnote_0_Ok5vASAPXNJyTPky8NlVngoerJyIFU53z7XrrnijZQ_1) She leads a small team of creatives who work on the company’s storytelling and branding, among other things.  
  
Christina trained as a biologist, receiving a doctorate in bioengineering, but she had always been interested in the social dimensions of science. “I liked art, as a kid, but I have immigrant parents. How am I going to have a job as an artist? What does that mean? I’m going to be a scientist, obviously.” After following artists who produce science-engaged art during her graduate studies and writing about them, Christina was hired as Gingko’s first creative director and given license to shape how the company talks about itself and its technologies, starting with social impact.  
  
One of the ways she does this is through art. Artists, she says, “put on a show, and all of a sudden people are thinking about science differently.” For a company that does synthetic biology, an often-controversial area, the question of how to tell its story is a vital one. Under Christina’s direction, the company has explored these issues through projects such as producing the scents of extinct flowers.  
  
Gingko’s three-month creative residency program has invited artists such as Natsai Audrey Chieza (now a curator and mentor in the program) to work on experimental dyeing and printing on fabric using bacteria. According to Christina, time and the space to fail are essential to involving artists and creatives in the work: “Letting people play and fail. It’s rare to find a space where people can do that.”  
  
Convincing some people that creativity is not just the “fun part”—that, in fact, it is part of the real work of the company—has been challenging. Christina says, “I would love for every biotech company to have a creative director.” They can affect how companies make choices about projects, how they shape their teams, and how they envision the company’s story unfolding into the future. “We want to make a different kind of technology: we have to do it differently. And it has to be well-designed.”

The economic benefits go beyond the broad national impact. For instance, artists and culture workers can also be an essential part of the work of building community wealth.[11](#footnote_1_FY2yfJx-UBWyqXLQsnAAeRZM2A740ezDSx80db8HFN8_1) Other evidence shows that arts and culture have been an important resource for community revitalization and development across the country.[12](#footnote_2_6itWDbwWlaBjWC0xhMoGNtkpnfp7e0GOHjg6veyWJvw_1) Native arts can be an essential component of community economic development on reservations.[13](#footnote_3_eGAa5dNkQCpJxCQ7UdPRDDKoh8Wh81V9i8fxNgIDek_1) Rural counties with performing arts organizations have higher population growth than the average for all rural counties, and they are more likely to host innovative companies in all sectors.[14](#footnote_4_ERhcKf0SAV2uHyCwLvBQviX0WbviNpP-3eMAQpz88t8_1) Other research shows that arts and crafts experience correlates with the production of patentable inventions and the founding of companies.[15](#footnote_5_KXgTen27SfLrJxIBFdwlnOTwT-Z6sto7EwXm1LgtDYs_1)

Artists also bring immense value to the building of communities and the essentials of our civic infrastructure. As Erik Takeshita, a community development and arts practitioner, told the Commission in one of our listening sessions, “artists’ core competencies are imagining that which doesn’t exist and helping to manifest and make it real.” Artists have long been employed in civic beautification projects, but city and state governments are also coming to recognize that the skills and talents of artists can be applied to developing vibrant and equitable cities and towns. This work is often done at a small scale, but it can have significant impact.[16](#footnote_6_9l5nIGgRIzNOYChZc0REviDd44l0N2RA8Z3Oe9Zy0Ag_1) For instance, the City Artist program at Public Art Saint Paul, which has been active since 2005, employs artists to engage members of the public in urban planning. Pop Up Meeting, an initiative designed by artist Amanda Lovelee through the program, uses an artistically retrofitted city truck to bring urban planning into neighborhoods in an engaging fashion.[17](#footnote_7_BdAFHYXgfLe8sTqrlPNQLSS4M4LDPmIwuY6nNaJloh4_1) At a slightly larger scale, Smart Growth America’s Transportation for America program has been connecting “arts-friendly insiders in city and state transportation agencies to local artists or local arts agencies” across America.[18](#footnote_8_dEDj-mXRSuyOzlD9jylXcIc8LtFlSQP22YEScrNjcYI_1) In 2020, the program enabled an artist to work on Oakland, California’s “slow streets” program (a project to mitigate the risks of COVID by enabling greater pedestrian use of streets), helping to make the program work better for residents in low-income and commuter neighborhoods. Calandra Childers, acting director of the Seattle Office of Arts and Culture, described programs like these as a way to fund (and thus enable) work that some artists are doing already.

“If the 20th century was about the allocation and distribution of resources, the 21st century is about the distribution of belonging, the renewal of shared purpose, creative placemaking, democratic reform, and the innovation and imagination necessary to advance as a species in the face of urgent climate challenges. . . . We need the tools of artists—their methods of public engagement, their capacity to build empathy and connection, their ability to reimagine spaces and processes and institutions, their power to facilitate and, ultimately, help people and communities adjust to disruptive change.”  
**—Steven Tepper, Commission member, Dean of the Herberger Institute for Design and the Arts at Arizona State University**

Beyond the economic and the civic, artists create immense, if less easily measurable, value for everyone in American society. The most obvious example is the joy, interest, and challenge many of us find in engaging with a new play, attending a local concert, or putting a small print up on our walls. In 2017, three-quarters of U.S. adults consumed artistic or arts-related content through electronic media, and more than half attended artistic, creative, or cultural activities.[19](#footnote_9_stLItJ2zXmAgOgxI24FsHcmwYkkylWPDd5Yt4qc1VE_1) Specific communities also find vital meaning in heritage art forms, from gospel music to beadwork to step dance, that closely intertwine with cultural maintenance. Some scholars, for instance, argue that artistic creativity is a space through which Afro-diasporic people can work against anti-Blackness and innovate community development.[20](#footnote_0_S2BjVySmKP4kbIRFHLVv1tT2iygllOQ3wCUt3-54A1g_1) And the State Department has long recognized the value of artists in cultural diplomacy, organizing trips abroad by musicians such as Dizzy Gillespie and Louis Armstrong in the 1950s and 1960s as part of the Jazz Ambassador program and funding current programs such as Arts Envoy and American Music Abroad.[21](#footnote_1_9gbu0Boh2modURbISPUo1jqQeEN6854gSmBhXjHIdag_1)

Artists and culture workers are essential to America’s economy, communities, and everyday life and well-being, even if their efforts are not often recognized by the broader public. For the nation to benefit fully, however, we need policies that support and empower artists and cultural workers in their creative work.

The Washington National Opera’s Pop Up Truck brought socially distanced opera performances into the DC community.

**“Honestly, almost all the departments want one.”**  
  
In 2018, the Los Angeles (LA) County Department of Arts and Culture began a Creative Strategist/Artist-in-Residence program to address complex civic issues. The program, a recommendation of the county’s Cultural Equity and Inclusion Initiative, sends a few artists each year to work with hosts like the Department of Mental Health, the Office of Violence Prevention, and the Department of Parks and Recreation. Together, they tackle persistent civic challenges and support equity and inclusion.  
  
In 2019–2020, one of those artists was Deborah Aschheim, who worked with the LA County registrar-recorder/county clerk in efforts to get out the vote for the 2020 election. LA County was rolling out a new voting system, and engaging and informing voters, especially underrepresented ones, was a priority. Focusing on the next generation of voters, Aschheim worked with instructors in arts departments at six community colleges and four California state universities to create projects involving students in civic art-making.  
  
Community engagement is often a key part of artist-in-residence programs. Aschheim wore her tires down driving all over LA County. She met students where they were and listened to them. “They were used to being messaged to. This was a dialogue,” she said. Aschheim, the instructors, and the students cocreated engagement projects to encourage voting. They made voter trading cards, posters in English and Spanish, and airbrushed bags and T-shirts with slogans at events. “It was,” Aschheim said, “a way in to thinking of government as being made up of people like you.”  
  
As director of the county’s Department of Arts and Culture, Kristin Sakoda sees the program “as a way for the County to employ artists for the value they bring to the table.” The program brings together artists and bureaucrats: “There have been studies that show that when you have teams that include artists with non-artists, you see a high degree of innovation and creativity. But the bureaucrats bring something too; they bring a high degree of know-how. You want both at the table.” Aschheim agreed: “Artists are comfortable with problems. Problems are creative jumping off points. It’s healthy to have someone that’s bought into the mission, is on payroll, but is allowed to question things.”  
  
The Department of Arts and Culture works with host departments to determine what challenges they want to address, make sure they are ready to work with an artist, and help facilitate the position’s full course. The position allows artists to pursue their independent projects concurrently. Both the artists and the government find a lot of value in these innovative positions. “Honestly, almost all the departments want one,” Sakoda said. “They think it’s a great opportunity, and we think it’s a great way to employ artists and introduce arts-based civic engagement and problem solving.”

## Artists and Creative Workers: The Details

One challenge for forming policy to support artists and creative workers is the complexity of defining and understanding the workforce. Even a simple question, such as “How many artists are there?” is difficult to answer. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the U.S. workforce includes 2.6 million artists—1.6 percent of all workers—but other estimates conclude that as many as five million are employed in the larger creative economy.[22](#footnote_2_frWBu2c7rJoEl5aUB6qMg07pbligEAsueVxqdRe25Q8_1) This disparity is influenced by two main factors: the definition of the creative workforce, and the structures of employment in the arts and culture sector.

Who “counts” as an artist? Most broadly, the creative workforce includes all those involved in the production and dissemination of creative work. The National Endowment for the Arts, for instance, defines two categories: *artist occupations*, which range from animator to choreographer to author; and *other cultural occupations*, which range from curators, sound engineers, tour guides, and ushers to printing press operators.[23](#footnote_3_SsGYuRxcMQ3NDsNLEiQ1gr4c91fwEadrqPnoONRJu28_1) The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics spreads artists and cultural workers across several occupational categories, with “Arts and Design” including occupations such as craft and fine artist, fashion designer, and special effects artist and animator, while entertainment and sports occupations are grouped together, as are media and communication occupations.[24](#footnote_4_oIbnXR0n8n6EXR0xLfx9FMyiOmPq5g1UwLDC96Aaw_1) While a broad definition is essential for a full picture of the creative economy, in this report we narrow the focus to artists who are attempting to gain an income from their art at least part-time, in part because the workforce needs of a choreographer and a printing press operator are distinct.[25](#footnote_5_CB9lS1aqAa3cbpLRXsaqLO-M9TfUrrRKF0NDbUmzQx4_1)

“Artists and culture workers are essential to America’s economy, communities, and everyday life and well-being.”

How are creative workers employed? Another challenge in creating policy for the creative workforce is the wide range of employment structures and arrangements. Many artists do not practice their art as their primary, wage-earning job. Yet many counts of the workforce focus only on those employed full-time by organizations. For instance, a 2019 study estimates that 12.3 percent of artists held their occupation as a second job (the high was 34.8 percent for musicians, and the low was 7.4 percent for producers and directors).[26](#footnote_6_eSjN7pfLySK22TRAYahWpCbU19IWJgYxYZ1PV8fgL0_1) In addition, artists are “3.6 times as likely as other workers to be self-employed,” with around 34 percent of artists self-employed in 2012–2016.[27](#footnote_7_6Cc26sSv39YhSwejHsTNnhb0yeK3mIBaCof6KePY_1)

A more recent analysis points to the wide variation among creative occupations. Actors, in particular, were much more likely to be unemployed or out of the labor force than their counterparts in other creative occupations (even in the year before the pandemic), with approximately 16 percent unemployed and another 29 percent not in the labor force in 2019. In comparison, the shares for all creative workers were 4 percent and 15 percent respectively, which were similar to the shares among all those sixteen or older who had been employed in the previous five years (3 percent and 14 percent).[28](#footnote_8_IgbpPiFx8rRXwM8yNIO9mpDWFIWN0TQwQOg3CbojEac_1)

**Source:** U.S. Census Bureau, “[ACS 1-Year Estimates-Public Use Microdata Sample, 2019](https://data.census.gov/mdat/#/search?ds=ACSPUMS1Y2019&cv=ESR&rv=SOCP&wt=PWGTP).”

This range of employment arrangements complicates efforts to evaluate artists’ income. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, “the median annual wage for arts and design occupations was $48,130 in May 2019, which was higher than the median annual wage for all occupations of $39,810.”[29](#footnote_9_SRZ6pZjl77ZIqOLTrEP6t93CJIYLiUpwdedhzWlrnc_1) But this conceals a wide and diverse array of employment characteristics in this area. For instance, artists and creative workers are less likely than workers overall to be working full-time/full-year. For example, at the low end of the range among artists, only 22.8 percent of actors were employed full-time for the entire year.[30](#footnote_0_E1TrNb4IUbn5cKTIo7xsA6gEJTwVG4l6L8vdBoX0-sE_1) The average salary for artists is lower than that of other professional workers, and median salaries vary widely across the creative occupations, with dancers/choreographers earning $31,150 and architects earning $76,680.[31](#footnote_1_R-evMuEyk1Q1nYEVtOB7Iv2nSIrt1A1obCw-OZlkEXk_1) And such averages capture only those working full-year/full-time, thus missing many working artists.

Finally, addressing policy to an undifferentiated category of “artists” can overlook the significant differences within the category. The demographics of the creative workforce differ widely by occupation. For instance, while women account for 46 percent of the total artistic workforce, they are overrepresented among dancers/choreographers (81 percent of total) and underrepresented among musicians (only 33 percent).[32](#footnote_2_7EU5m1NAdZcqYuOa3JcOnSFW555t3eZoFRjfWB87ng_1) Reflecting the physical toll that some creative work can take on participants, the median age for musicians is forty-five, while that of dancers/choreographers is just twenty-six.[33](#footnote_3_GP29nXVMF4TrvNNYJ1X9Cqwmc3593ZrtSPyAPRTX4Y_1) Artists are also less likely than the general population of workers to be non-white or Hispanic, at only 25 percent (compared to 36 percent overall). Like the other demographic differences, however, this varies by occupation; for instance, 44 percent of dancers/choreographers are non-white or Hispanic.[34](#footnote_4_rivVhKUINmBMv1xeapTn0M0KrrE--zX8x1Kuo-0kEY_1) All of these statistics likely undercount and underrepresent artists and culture bearers from marginalized communities. Research cited by First Peoples Fund estimates that around 40 percent of those on some Native reservations are practicing artists.[35](#footnote_5_p33UHQ3dduI1jkV8u6ufS6XxXjvhXKOL52NzZUb4nO0_1)

The same systemic barriers that contribute to inequities in income, representation, and recognition also impact who is counted as an artist and who sees cultural work as a viable career path. Understanding the shape and diversity of the arts and creative workforce is thus essential to understanding the workforce challenges and possible areas of need in the sector.

args.summary:
This webpage presents the "Art Is Work" report by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences' Commission on the Arts (a multiyear project with 44 members including artists, scholars, advocates, and leaders). The report addresses the central question: "How can we better recognize the value of artists in our national policy in order to enable the essential work they do?"

Key findings and statistics:
- While 81% of Americans believe the arts are "a positive experience in a troubled world," only 22% believe artists contribute "a lot" to the general good of society.
- Arts and culture supply approximately 4.3% of U.S. GDP (larger than construction, travel/tourism, and agriculture in 2019), providing a nearly $33 billion trade surplus in 2019.
- Production of arts and cultural goods/services grew by more than 35% from 1998 to 2016 (inflation-adjusted).
- Addressing barriers for Black creatives in film/TV could increase annual revenues by $10 billion.
- BLS counts 2.6 million artists (1.6% of all workers), but other estimates put creative economy employment as high as 5 million.
- 12.3% of artists held their occupation as a second job (up to 34.8% for musicians); artists are 3.6 times more likely than other workers to be self-employed (34% self-employed in 2012-2016).
- Median annual wage for arts/design occupations was $48,130 (May 2019) vs. $39,810 for all occupations; dancers/choreographers earned $31,150 while architects earned $76,680.
- Only 22.8% of actors worked full-time for the entire year.
- Women are 46% of the artistic workforce but 81% of dancers/choreographers and only 33% of musicians.
- Artists are less likely to be non-white/Hispanic (25% vs. 36% overall); 44% of dancers/choreographers are non-white/Hispanic.
- Around 40% of those on some Native reservations are practicing artists.
- In 2017, three-quarters of U.S. adults consumed artistic content electronically, and over half attended artistic activities.

The report outlines FOUR key principles for building a better system:
1. Name and include artists in federal policy (federal representation, explicit naming in legislation).
2. Recognize how creative work happens (independent contract work, multiple employers, entrepreneurship, inconsistent income as standard).
3. Center equity (anti-racist policies equitably funding, training, and supporting Black, Indigenous, and other artists of color, plus women, artists with disabilities, and rural artists).
4. Think locally, share nationally (national funding shaped to support local mechanisms).

The COVID-19 pandemic underscored artists' precarity—venues shuttered, gigs canceled, job losses—while also revealing racial and gender inequities; many artists accessed unemployment insurance for the first time via Pandemic Unemployment Assistance.

The report also includes case studies: the LA County Creative Strategist/Artist-in-Residence program (Deborah Aschheim's voting engagement work), the City Artist program at Public Art Saint Paul (Amanda Lovelee's "Pop Up Meeting"), Transportation for America's arts integration, and Christina Agapakis's role as creative director at biotech company Ginkgo Bioworks ($15 billion valuation).

# Artists and Other Cultural Workers

**Domain A: Artists and Other Cultural Workers** provides a comprehensive description of artists and individuals whose employment involves supporting artists or the arts industry (the latter referred to as *other cultural workers*). Indicators in this domain will explore artists and other cultural workers by demographic characteristics and background, the types of art they create, and their means of employment and income.

For more information on Domain A, [**view our infographic**](/sites/default/files/naserc_infographic_domaina_6.24.2026.pdf) and access short papers and data for each indicator below. **New indicators and updated statistics for current indicators will be released as data become available.**

## Explore the Indicators

[**A.1 Who are the artists?**](/sites/default/files/a1-report-202605.pdf)

*This indicator highlights the number of artists, by occupation, demographic group, and other individual characteristics**.*** (See [A.1 Tables](/sites/default/files/a1-tables-202605.zip) for related data). This indicator is annually updated in July.

[**A.2 Who are other cultural workers?**](/sites/default/files/a2-report-202605.pdf)

*This indicator highlights the number of other cultural workers, by occupation, demographic group, and other relevant individual characteristics.* (See [A.2 Tables](/sites/default/files/a2-tables-202605.zip) for related data). This indicator is annually updated in July.

[**A.3 Where are artists and other cultural workers located in the United States?**](/sites/default/files/a3-report-202605.pdf)

*This indicator highlights the number of artists and other cultural workers, by occupation and geographic location.*(See [A.3 Tables](/sites/default/files/a3-tables-202605.zip) for related data). This indicator is annually updated in July.

[**A.4 What do artists and other cultural workers study as undergraduates?**](/sites/default/files/a4-report-202606.pdf)

*This indicator reports what artists and other cultural workers study for their bachelor’s degrees and the occupations of those with bachelor’s degrees in visual and performing arts.* (See [A.4 Tables](/sites/default/files/a4-tables-202606.zip)  for related data). This indicator is annually updated in September.

[**A.5 What is the labor market status of artists and other cultural workers?**](/sites/default/files/a5-report-202509.pdf)

*This indicator explores employment and unemployment rates among artists and other cultural workers, comparing them with the national labor force, and examines employment characteristics such as hours worked, multiple job holdings, and reasons for part-time work.* (See [A.5 Tables](/sites/default/files/a5-tables-202509.zip)  for related data). This indicator is annually updated in October.

[**A.6 Who are the arts managers?**](/sites/default/files/a6-report-202505.pdf)

*This indicator presents demographic characteristics of managers in selected arts-related industries.* (See [A.6 Tables](/sites/default/files/a6-tables-202505.zip)  for related data). This indicator is annually updated in September.

[**A.7 What are the earnings for artists and other cultural workers?**](/sites/default/files/a7-report-202606.pdf)

This indicator is annually updated in July.

[**A.8 What are labor market outcomes for young artists and other cultural workers?**](/sites/default/files/a8-report-202606.pdf)

*This indicator highlights labor force status and earnings information for young artists and other cultural workers, supplemented with analysis of their household income.* (See [A.8 Tables](/sites/default/files/a8-tables-202606.zip) for related data). args.summary:
This is a webpage from the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) describing "Domain A: Artists and Other Cultural Workers" of the National Arts and Social Engagement Research Consortium (NASERC). This domain provides a comprehensive description of artists and individuals whose employment supports artists or the arts industry (referred to as "other cultural workers"). Indicators explore artists and other cultural workers by demographic characteristics and background, types of art created, and means of employment and income. New indicators and updated statistics are released as data become available.

The webpage lists 8 indicators (A.1 through A.8), each with linked reports and tables (PDF and ZIP formats):
- A.1 Who are the artists? (number of artists by occupation, demographic group, and other characteristics; updated annually in July)
- A.2 Who are other cultural workers? (number by occupation, demographic group, and characteristics; updated annually in July)
- A.3 Where are artists and other cultural workers located in the United States? (by occupation and geographic location; updated annually in July)
- A.4 What do artists and other cultural workers study as undergraduates? (bachelor's degrees and occupations of visual/performing arts degree holders; updated annually in September)
- A.5 What is the labor market status of artists and other cultural workers? (employment/unemployment rates compared to national labor force, hours worked, multiple job holdings, reasons for part-time work; updated annually in October)
- A.6 Who are the arts managers? (demographic characteristics of managers in selected arts-related industries; updated annually in September)
- A.7 What are the earnings for artists and other cultural workers? (earnings supplemented with household income analysis; updated annually in July)
- A.8 What are labor market outcomes for young artists and other cultural workers? (labor force status and earnings for young artists/cultural workers with household income analysis; updated annually in September)

Additional resources include datasets available at the National Archive of Data on Arts & Culture (NADAC). An infographic for Domain A is also available for download.

This Report The intended purpose of the National Survey of Artists is to understand and make visible the lives and livelihoods of artists practicing in the United States today. This report presents topline findings from the survey, providing the distribution of artists’ responses to a series of questions about their artistic practices, work and jobholding, earnings, wellbeing, and personal characteristics. The results are representative of a population of artists and culture bearers who have a dedicated professionalized practice. This survey was conducted using methods that allow us to estimate the characteristics of this group of artists across the U.S. adult population. This report shares descriptive statistics about artists’ survey responses, but does not analytically explore the causes of the response patterns that we observe. However, we hope that it will encourage readers to notice and ask questions. As part of this survey project, we offer companion resources to enable deeper exploration, including a technical report describing the survey and its methods, a public use data file and accompanying user guide, and additional analytic and interpretive reporting to come. Introduction: Understanding the Artist Workforce Survey Background and Rationale Why We Did This Survey Artists are understood to play beneficial social and economic roles within their communities,1,2,3 but many artists’ lives are marked by economic precarity, due in part to their tendency to have work arrangements that differ significantly from traditional employment. For example, artists are more likely than other workers to be self-employed4,5 and to switch between self-employment and working for an employer.6 Such nontraditional career paths and employment structures may have substantial impacts on artists’ economic stability, access to health care and other benefits, and overall wellbeing. Artists’ nontraditional work arrangements also make it difficult to identify and locate artists within the labor force, and thus to study them as a distinct class of worker.7,8 Moreover, current data sources that do provide information on the artist workforce have notable limitations. National Survey of Artists – Findings Report 3 Final Report | October 2025 into two categories: 1. Non-Representative Data Sources. Several data sources on artists are not meant to be representative of the full artist population in the U.S. but rather provide information on specific segments of the artist population, such as artists who hold certain credentials,9 artists who have engaged with specific programs,10 or artists who reside within defined geographies.11 This work is valuable in the context of the programs and policies it was designed to assist, and complements the current survey. 2. Representative Data with Definitional Constraints. Other studies utilize nationally representative samples but are constrained by specific definitions of who qualifies as an "artist.” The American Community Survey (ACS) enables us to identify individuals who engaged in specific artistic occupations as their “primary occupation” (that is, the one at which they spent the most time) in the prior week. The Current Population Survey (CPS) captures data on those who engaged in certain artistic occupations as their primary or secondary occupation in the prior week. Such data sources can only be used to make observations about the lives and livelihoods of artists who held formal employment within specific occupational types as their primary or secondary job during a given week. For example, the National Endowment for the Arts used CPS data to estimate that in 2022 approximately 1.6% of the U.S. labor force qualified as an artist.12 However, these data sources are unable to provide information about artists who (1) may not identify with the set of “artistic” occupations provided on the survey, (2) may have worked within those occupations, but not during the prior week, (3) may have worked within those occupations during the prior week, but not as their primary or secondary job, or (4) may have worked in occupations unrelated to their artistic practice. Thus, these data sources may exclude some unknown number of individuals who create art, sell art, teach art, and/or understand themselves as artists. Conversely, other national data sources on artists provide expansive conceptualizations of who qualifies as an artist for the purposes of data collection. The Survey of Public Participation in the Arts (SPPA) and the Annual Arts Basic Survey (AABS) collect information on the number of American adults who create art, engage in artistic performance, or produce creative writing. This means that they have limited utility in providing information about practicing artists as a distinct group. Our Approach Our study addresses these limitations by surveying a nationally representative sample14 of practicing artists in the U.S., including artists who are not currently represented in other national data sources. We do so by using a nuanced and multidimensional process for identifying artists that includes factors such as (1) which creative practices they engage in, (2) how they engage with those practices, (3) how much time they spend on their practices, (4) who they share their creative work with, and (5) how others see them. In this way our study moves beyond conceptualizing artists by their employment arrangements or stated occupation and instead accounts for the varied means artists have of supporting themselves financially while pursuing their creative practices. The survey findings presented in this report provide a comprehensive national15 snapshot of the lives and livelihoods of artists working in the U.S. today, including detail about their creative practices, work arrangements, finances, health and wellbeing, and personal characteristics.16 This descriptive data is intended to inform policies and support systems that reflect the lived experiences and needs of the artist workforce and of individuals with a dedicated artistic practice in America. 13 Sunil Iyengar et al., “Arts Participation Patterns in 2022: Highlights from the Survey of Public Participation in the Arts” (Washington, DC: National Endowment for the Arts, October 2023), https://www.arts.gov/sites/default/files/2022-SPPA-final.pdf. 14 NORC at the University of Chicago, “Panel Design | NORC at the University of Chicago,” https://amerispeak.norc.org/us/en/amerispeak/about-amerispeak/panel-design.html. By nationally representative, we mean that the sample of artists we surveyed accurately reflects the U.S. population along several key characteristics. This enables us to make observations about the entire population of U.S. artists using the survey responses from our sample of artists. 15 In addition to surveying a nationally representative sample, the survey findings were adjusted using weights at the person-level so that the descriptive results reflect the U.S. population. The characteristics used to calculate the weights were determined by the latest data from the American Community Survey (ACS), the Current Population Survey (CPS), and the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). 16 Despite our efforts to be all-inclusive, the survey will potentially exclude artists who were temporarily inactive outside the reference period (past 12 months) and those who could not complete the survey in English or Spanish. Conceptually, these criteria were meant to identify individuals who engage in creative practices in a substantial and sustained manner— that is, with professional intent, but without necessarily working as an artist as their primary or secondary job. To qualify as an artist for our study, an individual must have met five criteria: 1. “Practice” criterion. The study team created a list of creative practices falling under five broad artistic discipline categories – Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Writing, Craft Arts, and Other Arts – that would be considered eligible for this study. To capture information on respondents’ creative practices, we asked respondents about activities in the past 12 months that they do “at work, at home, as part of a community, with friends, or on your own.” We indicated that these are activities they might do for “enjoyment, to make money, to honor your culture or heritage, as a form of activism, or for other reasons.” The intent was to elicit this information without priming respondents on the concept of being an artist. In all, we asked respondents about their participation in 37 distinct activities (artistic subdisciplines) that we categorized as activities in the Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Writing, Craft Arts, Design, or Other Arts disciplines. As shown in Exhibit 1, 97% of respondents had participated in at least one activity other than Design activities, which made them eligible to continue the screener.18 Respondents who engaged exclusively in Design activities were considered ineligible for the purposes of this study. This exclusion of design-only respondents is not a statement on who is or is not an artist—rather, it was a decision about prioritizing data collection from a particular set of individuals who practice art in ways that we wanted to make visible through this survey. Note that this report does include detail on some artists who practice design and hold design jobs—this is because our screening criteria excluded only those individuals who reported that they engaged in design activities and no other arts activities. 2. “Engagement” criterion. We next asked respondents about potential ways they could engage with each of their selected arts activities. Specifically, for each activity they indicated participating in, we asked them if they engaged in that activity in any of six different ways: as a hobbyist, a student, a teacher, a professional, a former professional, or as a culture bearer. Respondents could select more than one way of engaging in each activity. When a respondent indicated that they engaged with an activity as a teacher, professional, former professional, or culture bearer, they remained potentially eligible to be included in the artist sample for that activity, provided that they also met the audience criterion for that activity below. When a respondent indicated that they exclusively engaged in an activity as a hobbyist or student, they were no longer eligible for the artist sample through that activity. Twenty-nine percent of respondents met the engagement criterion for at least one arts activity (Exhibit 1). 3. “Audience” criterion. Next, we asked respondents about their intended audience(s) for most of their work in each of their selected arts activities. Respondents could select all that apply from six audience options: myself, people I know personally, my community, clients, other people who are active in this field, and/or the general public. When a respondent indicated that audiences for a given activity included their community, clients, other people who are active in that field, and/or the general public, they remained potentially eligible for the artist sample for that activity. When a respondent indicated their only intended audience for an activity was themself and/or people they know personally, they were no longer eligible for the artist sample through that activity. As shown in Exhibit 1, 46% of respondents met the audience criterion for at least one arts activity. args.summary:
This report presents topline findings from the National Survey of Artists, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago with funding from The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation. The survey was designed to make visible the lives and livelihoods of artists practicing in the United States, addressing limitations in existing data sources that either only capture artists in specific occupations or use overly broad definitions. The survey used a nuanced, multidimensional screening process to identify practicing artists rather than relying on employment arrangements, considering creative practices, engagement methods, time spent, audiences, and recognition by others.

The survey was fielded September-November 2024, offered in English and Spanish, and included a final sample of 2,618 artists. It drew from three sample sources: NORC's AmeriSpeak probability-based panel, the Lucid non-probability panel, and a list sample of arts and design school graduates from the Strategic National Arts Alumni Project (SNAAP).

To qualify as an artist, respondents had to meet five screener criteria: (1) Practice—participated in at least one of 37 artistic activities across five disciplines (Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Writing, Craft Arts, Other Arts); (2) Engagement—engaged as a teacher, professional, former professional, or culture bearer (not just hobbyist or student); (3) Audience—intended audiences included their community, clients, other active field members, or the general public; (4) Recognition—others (beyond just friends/family) think of them as an artist; and (5) Hours—spent more than 0 hours per week on eligible arts activities. 97% of respondents participated in at least one activity, 29% met the engagement criterion, 46% met the audience criterion, 22% met all three criteria, and 18.38% met the recognition criterion. Design-only respondents were excluded to prioritize capturing data on artists with less traditional work arrangements.

The report includes findings across sections covering: artists' creative practices and identities; work arrangements (including up to four jobs; income sources; paid, temporary, and part-time work; self-employment; arts vs. non-arts occupations); finances (household income, assets, debts, financial support, and vulnerability); health needs and benefits (health insurance, dental and vision coverage, healthcare precarity); and artist demographics (gender, sexual orientation, age, geography, race, education, military service, and legal system experience). The report also contains detailed portraits of four specific artist groups: teaching artists, culture bearers, fully self-employed artists, and 3+ job holders.

The purpose of the report is to provide descriptive statistics to inform policies and support systems reflecting the lived experiences of the artist workforce. It does not analytically explore causes of observed patterns but offers companion resources including a technical report, public use data file, and user guide.

# Basic Income Changed My Life

Anne van Dalen describes the positive impact that the freedom and security of basic income had on her life.

Author: Anne van Dalen

Anne van Dalen was the first woman in the Netherlands to receive a basic income, (Universal Basic Income or UBI) as part of ground-breaking crowdfunded social experiment. Here she describes how it works and the impact it had on her life.

#### How did my UBI come about?

It all started in 2014 after donating €5 to a crowdfunding initiative called [OnsBasisinkomen.nl](https://onsbasisinkomen.nl "OnsBasisinkomen") (transl. our basic income) which aims to raise funds to provide someone a basic income in order to gain insight in what it means to actually live on UBI. It turned out to be feasable and the first ever experimental guinea pig, Frans Kerver, kicked it off in July 2015. The moment the call for a second UBI sounded I again donated €5 and in addition I put my name down as a possible recipient not thinking I’d ever be so lucky.

#### Before and after

I was all but surviving in a dried-up relationship in a menial part-time job in a rented flat in a social housing estate plagued by noisy anti-social neighbours. Life at 53 was stiflingly average, depressingly boring and at the same time indisputably stressful. When on Monday the 25th of April 2016 I opened a message in my mailbox reading “Hello Anne, you are the lucky recipient of the 2nd UBI. Should you choose to accept you shall receive an unconditional €1000 a month for 12 months".

I jumped at the chance! I immediately ditched the part-time job, the partner and the flat. I am now working as an autonomous artist, occupying a classroom in a former primary school (EDM) which serves both as my art studio and living quarters. I couldn’t be happier.

Having basic needs taken care of makes all the difference in the world. Living on €1,000 a month covers the rent, fixed costs, food, art supplies and not much else. It suits me just fine. As for my work as an artist, UBI allows me to focus on the actual producing of art. Not having to consider saleability, not having to waste creative energy has freed me up no end. UBI allows me to create without limitations. Not having to occupy myself with money-matters is a huge relief. Having (enough) money does not by itself create happiness but the opposite, not having enough money, does result in anxiety and feelings of depression. I have now regained a great deal of independence. It’s huge!

#### Resistance is futile

The majority of response has been positive. On discussing UBI’s merit or detriment some people focus on economic issues like government expenditure, taxation, costs vs profit. Others ask themselves who’s going to want to do the dirty jobs, won’t the world grind to a halt? Some resort to personal attacks telling me “You’re nothing but a scrounger. I’m not paying taxes for you to sit on your arse all day. Get a fucking job”. Such comments signal fear of change and lack of factual information. Misgivings prevent people from considering the idea of UBI let alone embracing it. Whenever I am given the chance to sit people down, talk to them face to face and explain UBI’s tenets these objections tend to vanish.

#### Confronting silliness

Basic income confronts us with the ridiculousness of the current system of job-slavery, any system that ties existence and self-worth to having a job is nothing but silly. Everybody knows it, but admitting it equals calling yourself an idiot. This is one of many reasons why this UBI experiment by OnsBasisinkomen.nl is valuable. It needs real people to experience day-to-day living on a basic income to grasp the extent in which the current system has taken hold. To those who have convinced themselves being a wage slave is the only way of life, I say: you’ve no idea. Honestly, you’ve no idea. In experiencing the difference lies the change. That is why I would like every single person on the planet to be given the opportunity to live it. To coin a shitty phrase: “because we’re worth it”.

#### Conclusion

Basic income has greatly improved my life. It empowers me as a woman, as an artist and as a human being.

> Therefore I say: “Go for it!”

This article was first published on [Citizen's Basic Income Network Scotland's website](https://cbin.scot "Citizen's Basic Income Network Scotland").
