--- SOURCE 14: CIF_Arts and Growth_v7.indd ---
URL: https://www.artscouncil.org.uk/sites/default/files/CIF_Arts_and_Growth.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Overview
This is the second policy report from the Creative Industries Federation (produced in partnership with Arts Council England), arguing that public investment in the arts is crucial to the growth of the UK's creative industries. The report is authored by Professor Jonothan Neelands and Eliza Easton of Warwick Business School, with contributions from leading business figures including Melanie Clore (Sotheby's), Tom Weldon (Penguin Random House), Baroness Lane-Fox, Caroline Rush (British Fashion Council), Boris Johnson, and Matthew Bourne.

## Core Economic Argument
- The UK creative industries are booming: GVA grew 9.9% between 2012-2013 (higher than any other industrial sector including financial services), and returned £77 billion of direct GVA in 2012-2013.
- Employment in the creative economy grew 5% between 2013-2014 (vs. 2.1% UK average) and accounts for 5.8% of all UK jobs; creative economy jobs grew 13.7% since 2011.
- The public arts return 0.4% of UK GVA (a 19% increase vs. 3.3% UK average) with 9.2% employment growth.
- UK films generated £1.4 billion in exports with a £916 million trade surplus in 2013.
- The arts are linked to 42% of inbound-tourism related expenditure.

## Investment Gap
- The UK invests only 0.3% of GDP on arts and culture vs. the EU average of 0.5%, France at 0.8%, and Germany at 0.4%.
- Arts Council England grant-in-aid fell 29.4% in real terms from 2010/11 to 2014/15, accounting for only 0.1% of public expenditure.
- Total public spend on arts/culture in England represents just 0.7% of total public spend.
- Local government spending on arts and culture fell 25% since 2007/08.
- No other EU country benefits from the level of GVA the UK's public arts return.

## How Public Investment Drives Growth
- **R&D function**: Public investment mitigates risk at the high-risk idea development stage. The National Theatre spent ~£50,000 on experimental workshops for War Horse; its first production cost ~£500,000 but has now been seen by 5.5+ million people and earned a £12 million surplus.
- **Seedbed for commercial success**: The RSC's two years of publicly funded development enabled Les Misérables to become London's longest-running musical (70+ million people in 42 countries). Matthew Bourne's New Adventures received £3 million in grants but returned £12 million to the Treasury.
- **Leverage effect**: Orchestras leverage an additional £2 of private investment per £1 of public investment; NPOs leverage similar amounts.
- **Industry dependence**: 37% of video games businesses depend on public grants/government schemes. Software developers can claim tax reductions up to 225% of R&D investment.
- **Tax incentives**: Film, high-end TV, animation, video games, children's TV, theatre and orchestras benefit from tax reliefs (up to 25% for touring costs, 20% for other theatre productions, 25% for orchestras). Since 2007, over 1,200 film productions claimed £1.3 billion in relief.

## Diversity and Talent
- 60.5% of creative industry workers are graduates (vs. 31.8% UK average), but 92.1% come from advantaged social/economic backgrounds.
- 14% of creative media workers attended independent schools (7% of population). BAME workers increased 34.3% between 2011-2014 but remain only 11% of workforce (vs. 14.1% of the general population).
- Public investment supports 6,500 apprenticeships through the Creative Employment Programme and £32 million training support via Creative Skillset.
- McKinsey research: gender-diverse companies are 15% more likely to outperform; ethnically diverse companies 35% more likely.

## Regional Distribution
- 47.6% of creative industries jobs are in London and the South-East — the most unevenly distributed UK sector (after agriculture and finance/insurance).
- Scotland has 6.9% of creative economy jobs, Wales 2.9%, Northern Ireland 1.6%.
- Liverpool attracted 9.7 million additional visits as EU Capital of Culture, generating £753.8 million economic impact.
- Hull (UK City of Culture 2017) saw private investment follow public investment, including £15 million from Wykeland and a 15% increase in hotel income.
- Birmingham (Anita Bhalla): home to 6,000 tech firms employing nearly 40,000; 25% of UK gaming workforce; digital tech boosts the regional economy by £1.6 billion annually.

## Key Recommendations
- BIS (Department for Business, Innovation and Skills) should recognize the creative industries in its industrial growth data.
- A joined-up policy response is needed across HM Treasury, BIS, DCMS, DCLG and DfE, under leadership of the Secretary of State for Culture.
- The mixed economy model (public investment + tax incentives + private/philanthropic funding) should continue, but tax incentives cannot replace grant-in-aid for building infrastructure, education, and outreach.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Arts Council England—written evidence (CRF0043) ---
URL: https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/111119/html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the written evidence (CRF0043) submitted by Arts Council England to the House of Lords Communications and Digital Select Committee inquiry "A creative future" (September 2022). It covers how the Arts Council supports culture, disruptions facing the creative industries, skills needs, talent pipelines, R&D policy, and international lessons.

**Arts Council funding**: Between 2018-2022, the Arts Council invested £1.45 billion of public money plus an estimated £860 million from the National Lottery. During Covid-19, it awarded £1.14 billion through the Government's Culture Recovery Fund and £160 million through its own Emergency Response Fund.

**Key disruptive technologies (next 5-10 years)**:
1. **AI** – significant impact on audience data management, collections management, artistic production, IP ownership questions, and audience curation. Arts Council's 2019 commissioned research found barriers include cost/market maturity (e.g., theatre captioning) and the need for sophisticated data management.
2. **5G** – ultra-low latency will revolutionise live streaming of data-rich content, improve accessibility, and enable remote creative collaborations (e.g., 5G Festival at Brighton Dome).
3. **Virtual production, extended reality, virtual worlds** – could radically alter how work is made and where audiences encounter it. Examples include RSC's Dream, ROH's Current Rising, Tate's Modigliani VR, National Gallery's Virtual Veronese. Social forms of immersive experience are likely to evolve (e.g., Unreal City AR trail on the Thames, Unboxed StoryTrails). Online, projects like musician-led start-up Ristband are using virtual worlds.
4. **Web 3.0 technologies** (blockchain, crypto art, DAOs, NFTs) – potentially the most disruptive, with implications for how art is made, consumed, monetised and controlled. Proponents cite potential to change power structures; critics note unregulated financial speculation and IP/attribution challenges. In 2022, Italy suspended NFT creation based on Italian masterworks.

**Skills challenges**: A major challenge is inequality of access and opportunity; many lack digital devices. The 2019 Digital Culture survey (Arts Council/Nesta) found "a widening gulf between large and small organisations," organisations becoming "less experimental and more risk averse," with a downward trend in R&D behaviours. Senior management knowledge of digital technology fell from 22% (2013) to 13% (2019). Only 19% of organisations have board members contributing to digital strategy. In 2019, 70% cited lack of funding for digital as a barrier. Pandemic shutdowns accelerated digital learning, but it's unclear whether innovation will continue at scale amid economic crisis.

**Arts Council support mechanisms**: Digital Culture Network, Audience Finder, Impact & Insight Toolkit, Bloomberg Philanthropies' Digital Accelerator Programme, Creative XR, UK-Canada Immersive Exchange, Digital R&D Fund for the Arts. NPOs like RSC, Serpentine Galleries, Watershed, Furtherfield share expertise; small organisations like Collusion and York Mediale support practitioner R&D.

**Government/talent pipeline recommendations**: Continue investment in R&D and advanced digital skills; set funding criteria enabling not-for-profit arts organisations to benefit. Templates include the Creative Industries Clusters Programme (£39m, via UKRI/AHRC – XR Stories, B+B, StoryFutures) and Audiences of the Future Challenge (£33m – Dream, Dinosaurs and Robots). Programmes should run a minimum of 5 years. Supports Boundless Creativity report (2021, UKRI/AHRC & DCMS) recommendations, including considering new Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes. Combined/local authorities should engage creative stakeholders in Local Skills Improvement Plans and cultural compacts. Universities should reflect latest tech developments in curricula.

**Industry actions needed**: Tech industry should provide access to new technologies (e.g., RSC-Magic Leap fellowships, Google Arts workshops), support board-level tech expertise (with board 'banks' considered), recognise creativity as a top soft skill. Organisations need continuous digital upskilling embedded in operations (e.g., Arts Council's 'Tech Champions' recruitment model), embed digital in financial/strategic planning, and become more data savvy.

**R&D role**: Arts Council's "Dynamism" Investment Principle underpinning its Let's Create strategy emphasises "new technological opportunities," data culture, and technology adoption. New 2023-2026 NPO portfolio will include Investment Principles Support Organisations (IPSOs) sharing digital expertise. National Lottery Project Grants welcome digital/immersive projects; funds over £100,000 prioritise technology partnerships and new forms of content/audience reach.

**Government strategies effectiveness**: UKRI/AHRC industrial strategy programmes have been effective but end in 2023; future programmes should address geographical gaps (e.g., no current cluster in the Midlands), ensure not-for-profit eligibility, run 5+ years. Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes (Film, Theatre, Museums & Galleries) have shown positive impact; similar schemes should be considered for advanced tech practices.

**International lessons**: Cutting-edge innovation is highly collaborative and cross-border. The Arts Council supports international exchange via the Future Art and Culture (FAC) programme at SXSW (produced by British Underground) and the UK-Canada Immersive Exchange (UCIE). SXSW provides cross-disciplinary collaboration, investment and export outcomes. Creative XR prototypes have been selected for showcases at Tribeca, Venice Immersive and LFF Expanded.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Art Is Work | American Academy of Arts and Sciences ---
URL: https://www.amacad.org/publication/art-is-work/section/2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the "Art Is Work" report by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences' Commission on the Arts (a multiyear project with 44 members including artists, scholars, advocates, and leaders). The report addresses the central question: "How can we better recognize the value of artists in our national policy in order to enable the essential work they do?"

Key findings and statistics:
- While 81% of Americans believe the arts are "a positive experience in a troubled world," only 22% believe artists contribute "a lot" to the general good of society.
- Arts and culture supply approximately 4.3% of U.S. GDP (larger than construction, travel/tourism, and agriculture in 2019), providing a nearly $33 billion trade surplus in 2019.
- Production of arts and cultural goods/services grew by more than 35% from 1998 to 2016 (inflation-adjusted).
- Addressing barriers for Black creatives in film/TV could increase annual revenues by $10 billion.
- BLS counts 2.6 million artists (1.6% of all workers), but other estimates put creative economy employment as high as 5 million.
- 12.3% of artists held their occupation as a second job (up to 34.8% for musicians); artists are 3.6 times more likely than other workers to be self-employed (34% self-employed in 2012-2016).
- Median annual wage for arts/design occupations was $48,130 (May 2019) vs. $39,810 for all occupations; dancers/choreographers earned $31,150 while architects earned $76,680.
- Only 22.8% of actors worked full-time for the entire year.
- Women are 46% of the artistic workforce but 81% of dancers/choreographers and only 33% of musicians.
- Artists are less likely to be non-white/Hispanic (25% vs. 36% overall); 44% of dancers/choreographers are non-white/Hispanic.
- Around 40% of those on some Native reservations are practicing artists.
- In 2017, three-quarters of U.S. adults consumed artistic content electronically, and over half attended artistic activities.

The report outlines FOUR key principles for building a better system:
1. Name and include artists in federal policy (federal representation, explicit naming in legislation).
2. Recognize how creative work happens (independent contract work, multiple employers, entrepreneurship, inconsistent income as standard).
3. Center equity (anti-racist policies equitably funding, training, and supporting Black, Indigenous, and other artists of color, plus women, artists with disabilities, and rural artists).
4. Think locally, share nationally (national funding shaped to support local mechanisms).

The COVID-19 pandemic underscored artists' precarity—venues shuttered, gigs canceled, job losses—while also revealing racial and gender inequities; many artists accessed unemployment insurance for the first time via Pandemic Unemployment Assistance.

The report also includes case studies: the LA County Creative Strategist/Artist-in-Residence program (Deborah Aschheim's voting engagement work), the City Artist program at Public Art Saint Paul (Amanda Lovelee's "Pop Up Meeting"), Transportation for America's arts integration, and Christina Agapakis's role as creative director at biotech company Ginkgo Bioworks ($15 billion valuation).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: National Survey of Artists – Findings Report ---
URL: https://www.norc.org/content/dam/norc-org/pdf2025/National%20Survey%20of%20Artists%20-%20Findings%20Report.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report presents topline findings from the National Survey of Artists, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago with funding from The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation. The survey was designed to make visible the lives and livelihoods of artists practicing in the United States, addressing limitations in existing data sources that either only capture artists in specific occupations or use overly broad definitions. The survey used a nuanced, multidimensional screening process to identify practicing artists rather than relying on employment arrangements, considering creative practices, engagement methods, time spent, audiences, and recognition by others.

The survey was fielded September-November 2024, offered in English and Spanish, and included a final sample of 2,618 artists. It drew from three sample sources: NORC's AmeriSpeak probability-based panel, the Lucid non-probability panel, and a list sample of arts and design school graduates from the Strategic National Arts Alumni Project (SNAAP).

To qualify as an artist, respondents had to meet five screener criteria: (1) Practice—participated in at least one of 37 artistic activities across five disciplines (Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Writing, Craft Arts, Other Arts); (2) Engagement—engaged as a teacher, professional, former professional, or culture bearer (not just hobbyist or student); (3) Audience—intended audiences included their community, clients, other active field members, or the general public; (4) Recognition—others (beyond just friends/family) think of them as an artist; and (5) Hours—spent more than 0 hours per week on eligible arts activities. 97% of respondents participated in at least one activity, 29% met the engagement criterion, 46% met the audience criterion, 22% met all three criteria, and 18.38% met the recognition criterion. Design-only respondents were excluded to prioritize capturing data on artists with less traditional work arrangements.

The report includes findings across sections covering: artists' creative practices and identities; work arrangements (including up to four jobs; income sources; paid, temporary, and part-time work; self-employment; arts vs. non-arts occupations); finances (household income, assets, debts, financial support, and vulnerability); health needs and benefits (health insurance, dental and vision coverage, healthcare precarity); and artist demographics (gender, sexual orientation, age, geography, race, education, military service, and legal system experience). The report also contains detailed portraits of four specific artist groups: teaching artists, culture bearers, fully self-employed artists, and 3+ job holders.

The purpose of the report is to provide descriptive statistics to inform policies and support systems reflecting the lived experiences of the artist workforce. It does not analytically explore causes of observed patterns but offers companion resources including a technical report, public use data file, and user guide.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The intended purpose of the National Survey of Artists is to understand and make visible the lives and livelihoods of artists practicing in the United States today."

--- SOURCE 9: Basic Income Changed My Life ---
URL: https://citizen-network.org/library/basic-income-changed-my-life.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Anne van Dalen, the second person in the Netherlands to receive a Universal Basic Income (UBI) through the crowdfunded initiative OnsBasisinkomen.nl, describes how receiving an unconditional €1,000 per month for 12 months transformed her life. She was 53 years old, working a menial part-time job and living in a stressful social housing situation when she received the UBI in April 2016. Design/art graduates are constrained by skill-market mismatch, while other art graduates are constrained by social networks.

Recommendations include: optimizing education with practice-based teaching and industry-academia integration; government support through art entrepreneurship funds and talent policies; career guidance expanding into "art+tech" and "art+business" domains; and targeted support for disadvantaged students to compensate for cultural capital gaps.

**Key Reforms:**

1. **Tiered System:** Establishes a unified 4-tier system (Level 4 = Junior, Level 3 = Intermediate, Level 2 = Associate Senior, Level 1 = Senior) across 4 professional categories: Art Performance (actors, instrumentalists), Art Creation (directors, screenwriters, composers, photographers, designers, fine artists, literary writers), Art Management (performance supervisors), and Technical Support (stage technicians, sound engineers, editors).

4. **Management Improvements:** Shifts from direct government oversight to random inspection and supervision. Implements a personal integrity commitment system and streamlines application materials.

**Implementation:** The policy applies nationwide across all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities, with regional standards allowed as long as they meet national minimum requirements.    - Connect evaluation with talent training and employment

--- SOURCE 14: 毕业生行业收入差距呈扩大趋势 是什么原因导致？-新华网 ---
URL: http://www.xinhuanet.com/politics/2018-06/25/c_1123028875.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Xinhua News Agency (published June 25, 2018) analyzes the widening income gap among college graduates across different industries in China, based on data from the "National College Graduate Employment Survey" conducted by Peking University researchers Zhou Liping and Yue Changjun.

**Key Findings:**

- **Income disparity is widening:** The ratio of highest to lowest industry average wages for urban employees rose from 1.76:1 in 1990 to 3.64:1 in 2016. Among graduates specifically, the income gap ratio peaked at 1.89 in 2015 before slightly declining to 1.85 in 2017.

- **Top-paying industries:** Information Technology (IT) and Financial services lead with average starting monthly salaries of 5,386 yuan and 5,098 yuan respectively in 2017. The lowest-paying sectors were wholesale/retail (3,255 yuan) and accommodation/food services (2,854 yuan).

- **Only IT and Finance show significant "income premium":** After controlling for personal characteristics, family background, human capital, and job nature, only IT (11.3% higher) and Financial services (7.3% higher) showed statistically significant wage premiums compared to manufacturing.

- **Education and school prestige matter most:** Human capital differences (education level and institution reputation) are the strongest explanatory factors for inter-industry income gaps. Higher human capital also has positive externalities—raising overall industry wages through improved productivity.

- **Industry choice is more valuable than education investment:** Similar graduates entering emerging service industries earn at least 9% more (about 900 yuan/month on a 10,000 yuan base), with returns exceeding education investment returns.

- **Graduates are flocking to high-paying sectors:** Financial sector employment rose from 6.3% (2009) to 15.2% (2015), while manufacturing employment dropped from 18.2% to 10.4% over the same period.

**Concerns and Recommendations:**
1. The government should develop strategic emerging industries and upgrade traditional manufacturing to create more suitable graduate jobs.
2. Universities should adjust curriculum and enrollment based on market demands, particularly following the "Made in China 2025" initiative.
3. Graduates should improve their human capital but also rationally choose industries based on interests and skills, not just salary.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: 知识产权案例选——版权 ---
URL: https://ipr.mofcom.gov.cn/zhuanti/cases/copyright.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a copyright law resources page from the China Intellectual Property Protection Network (中国保护知识产权网, ipr.mofcom.gov.cn), hosted by China's Ministry of Commerce. It provides an educational overview of China's copyright (著作权) law provisions, organized into several thematic sections, each accompanied by links to related legal case news articles.

**Key Content Sections:**

1. **Objects Protected by Copyright (著作权保护的客体):** Under China's Copyright Law, copyright protects literary, artistic, natural science, social science, and engineering/technical works including: (1) written works; (2) oral works; (3) music, drama, quyi (folk art), dance, and acrobatic art works; (4) fine art and architectural works; (5) photographic works; (6) cinematographic works and works created by methods similar to filmmaking; (7) graphic works such as engineering design drawings, product design drawings, maps, schematic diagrams, and model works; (8) computer software; and (9) other works stipulated by law and administrative regulations.

2. **Copyright Ownership and Exhaustion Doctrine (著作权归属与权利穷竭):** Copyright belongs to the author. Natural persons who create works are authors. Works created under the direction of a legal person or organization, representing their will, and for which they bear responsibility, are deemed to be authored by that legal person/organization. China's Copyright Law has no explicit provision on exhaustion of the distribution right, but in practice, copyright holders generally cannot continue to control the circulation of their works after exercising their rights once.

3. **Protection Period and Statute of Limitations (权利的保护期与诉讼时效):** The author's rights of attribution, modification, and integrity are protected without time limit. For a citizen's work, the right of publication and related rights are protected for the author's lifetime plus 50 years (ending December 31 of the 50th year after death); for collaborative works, this extends to 50 years after the death of the last surviving author. Some countries provide a protection period of lifetime plus 70 years. Under China's General Principles of Civil Law (Article 135), the statute of limitations for civil rights is 2 years (unless otherwise provided by law); some countries, such as the US, use a 3-year statute of limitations.

4. **Limitations on Rights (权利的限制):** Under China's Copyright Law, works may be used without the copyright holder's permission or payment of remuneration (provided the author's name and work title are indicated and other rights are not infringed) in 12 specific situations, including: personal study, research, or appreciation; appropriate quotation for commentary or explanation; unavoidable reproduction/citation in news reporting; republication of political, economic, or religious editorial articles by media; use for classroom teaching or scientific research (translation or limited reproduction without publication); official use by state organs within reasonable scope; reproduction by libraries/archives/museums for archival purposes; free performances (no fees charged to public or performers); copying/drawing/photographing/video recording of artworks in outdoor public spaces; translation of Chinese-language works into minority languages for domestic publication; and publication of works in Braille. These limitations also apply to rights of publishers, performers, record producers, and broadcasters.

5. **Infringement Determination Under New Technologies (新技术下的侵权认定):** The rapid development of the internet has brought technological innovations that raise new questions regarding copyright infringement determination.

**Related Case News Links Featured:**
- Oracle v. Google (Java copyright case, US) — Oracle defeated Google
- Monkey selfie photograph copyright dispute (photographer vs. Wikipedia)
- European Court ruling that downloading pirated movies and music is no longer legal in the Netherlands
- Garcia v. Google (plaintiff won; could change US copyright rules)
- US Circuit Court ruling on Sherlock Holmes copyright case
- US Supreme Court ruling that laches doctrine cannot prevent copyright holders from bringing infringement suits (Raging Bull case)
- European libraries may digitize books without permission
- US Circuit Court rejected the standard for determining fair use (Cambridge v. GSU)
- European Court ruling on parody raises new issues
- US Supreme Court ruling that Aereo (internet TV service) infringed copyright
- European Court: technical protection measures are only protected by law when used to prevent piracy (Nintendo/PC Box case)
- European Court ruling that browsing webpages does not constitute copyright infringement
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: 法庭之上：艾德·希兰在音乐版权侵权案中胜诉，但事情还没有结束…… ---
URL: https://www.wipo.int/zh/web/wipo-magazine/articles/in-the-courts-ed-sheeran-succeeds-in-music-copyright-infringement-case-but-its-not-over-yet-56446

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This WIPO Magazine article (Sept 7, 2023) by Hayleigh Bosher, Associate Professor at Brunel University London, examines Ed Sheeran's victory in a US music copyright infringement case and the broader impact of music copyright litigation. The case concerned Sheeran's song "Thinking Out Loud" (co-written with Amy Wadge in 2015) alleged to have copied Marvin Gaye and Ed Townsend's 1973 song "Let's Get It On."

The article sets context with the landmark "Blurred Lines" case (2013-2018), where Robin Thicke and Pharrell Williams were found liable for copying Marvin Gaye's "Got To Give It Up," initially awarded $7.3 million (later reduced to $5.3 million plus 50% of future royalties). That ruling, which focused on stylistic similarities, proved controversial—a dissenting judge warned it impermissibly granted copyright over a musical style, and Pharrell Williams feared the entertainment industry would "freeze in litigation."

Sheeran's prior disputes are noted: a £16 million settlement in 2016 over "Photograph" versus Matt Cardle's "Amazing," a 2018 settlement over "The Rest of Our Life," and a 2022 UK High Court win in the "Shape of You" case where the court found no deliberate or subconscious copying.

The "Let's Get It On" vs. "Thinking Out Loud" case was filed in July 2017 by Kathryn Townsend Griffin (who inherited Ed Townsend's song share), Helen Mcdonald, and Cherrigale Townsend's estate, following a July 2017 suit. A separate lawsuit was brought by Structured Asset Sales (owned by David Pullman). The trial ran April 2023 in Manhattan federal court after 6 years of litigation, with both sides presenting dueling music expert reports—Alexander Stewart for the plaintiffs (citing bass melody, drum parts, harmony, and the four-chord progression rhythm), and Lawrence Ferrara for Sheeran (finding no substantive similarities, with any similarities being common pre-existing expression).

The key issue was whether the harmonic progression in "Let's Get It On" was common and thus unprotected. Townsend conceded Sheeran's experts found at least 13 prior songs using the same chord progression, which also appeared in at least 2 guitar tutorials. The jury deliberated less than 3 hours and ruled Sheeran's song was independently created, so no infringement occurred. On May 16, 2023, Judge Louis Stanton dismissed the second suit by Structured Asset Sales, finding the copied elements were commonplace and ineligible for copyright protection, emphasizing that chord progressions and harmonic rhythms are "common building blocks of music creation."

However, Townsend filed a notice of appeal on June 1, 2023, so the matter is not fully concluded. The article emphasizes that copyright must balance preventing copying against allowing creators to draw inspiration from prior works, and questions whether the trend toward expensive expert-heavy litigation has drifted from copyright principles.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Any loss of our freedom to be inspired, we're going to end up in a world where the entertainment industry that we all know will freeze in litigation." — Pharrell Williams, on the Blurred Lines ruling. "Copyright must strike the appropriate balance between preventing copying and allowing creators to draw inspiration from previous works." "The key in this case was that, while some parts of the two songs were similar, those parts were unprotected elements that anyone can use free of charge." "The judge emphasized that chord progressions and harmonic rhythms are common building blocks of music creation." — Judge Louis Stanton, on dismissing the Structured Asset Sales lawsuit.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: AI时代知识产权司法迎来新挑战 ---
URL: https://ipc.court.gov.cn/zh-cn/news/view-4513.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Intellectual Property Court of the Supreme People's Court of China (最高人民法院知识产权法庭), specifically a news/feature article published on 2025-07-18 titled "AI时代 知识产权司法迎来新挑战" (AI Era Brings New Challenges to IP Justice). Written by 王健 (Wang Jian), sourced from 《民主与法制》周刊 (Democracy and Legal System Weekly) 2025 Issue 25.

The article examines how Chinese courts are addressing emerging intellectual property challenges posed by generative AI (AIGC) and artificial intelligence technologies. It features interviews with judges from courts in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Sichuan.

**Key cases discussed:**

1. **AI-generated image copyright case (China's first):** In 2023, plaintiff 李昀锴 (Li Yunkai) used Stable Diffusion to generate the image 《春风送来了温柔》 and posted it on social media. The image was used without permission by a defendant (刘女士). In November 2023, Beijing Internet Court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, finding copyright infringement (ordering an apology and ¥500 compensation). The court held that the plaintiff's multiple adjustments of parameters and prompts demonstrated "personalized expression and intellectual input" satisfying originality requirements. Judge 朱阁 noted AI models themselves are not legal subjects and cannot be "authors" under copyright law, but human-generated AI content can be protected.

2. **"幻之翼透明艺术椅" (Fantasy Wing Transparent Art Chair) case:** Zhangjiagang City People's Court ruled that simple prompts input to Midjourney with no preserved creation process records did not demonstrate originality, so the images could not be recognized as works. This contrasted with the Beijing Internet Court approach, showing divergent judicial views.

3. **AI training data copyright case (first of its kind):** Four illustrators sued Xiaohongshu's AI product "Trik AI" (operators 伊普 and 行吟科技 companies) for unauthorized use of their artworks in AI model training. A hearing occurred June 20, 2024 at Beijing Internet Court; as of June 2025, the case was still ongoing. A technical witness (梁楚盟, PhD student at University of Southern California) explained AI training doesn't directly copy images but learns features through mathematical modeling.

4. **iQiyi v. MiniMax:** In January 2025, iQiyi sued MiniMax in Shanghai Xuhui District People's Court, alleging unauthorized use of copyrighted material in model training, seeking about ¥100,000 in damages. Still in proceedings.

5. **Overseas parallel:** The New York Times and 7 other US media outlets sued Microsoft and OpenAI for using articles in AI training; both defended based on "fair use of public data," showing this is a global challenge.

6. **"奥特曼" (Ultraman) AI image cases - two divergent rulings:** 
   - Guangzhou Internet Court held a platform (operating "Tab" website AI drawing) directly liable for infringing reproduction and adaptation rights, ordering cessation and ¥10,000 compensation, citing platform control over model training data and outputs.
   - Hangzhou Internet Court (September 2024) adopted a "phased responsibility" approach: platform wasn't directly liable for users uploading infringing materials (input stage), but constituted contributory infringement for failing to take necessary measures on output content (¥30,000 compensation). This was the first ruling clarifying generative AI platform responsibility boundaries.

7. **Douyin v. B612 (AI special effects model):** Beijing IP Court (final ruling March 31) found network structure, convolutional layers, and parameters of models had 91.7% similarity; upheld unfair competition finding. The court clarified AI model structure and parameters constitute "competitive interests" protected by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. Downloaded ¥1.5 million economic loss + ¥100,000 reasonable expenses. Judge 李迎新 noted models could also be protected under trade secret rules if meeting value/confidentiality/secrecy requirements.

8. **Open-source voice data case (first data IP registration certificate case):** A company registered "1505-hour Chinese Mandarin voice data" under data intellectual property registration. A competitor (隐某公司) illegally obtained the dataset subset. Beijing IP Court (second instance) held: public disclosure removed secrecy (no trade secret), and dataset lacked originality (not a compilation work), but substantial labor created competitive interests protected under Article 2 of Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The defendant violated the CC open-source license's non-commercial purpose rule. The case established: (1) data IP registration certificates serve as preliminary evidence of legitimate holding; (2) "classified protection, tiered application" rules for datasets; (3) open-source data users must strictly comply with license terms.

**Expert opinions:**
- 李明德 (Li Mingde, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences researcher): Copyright law requires authors to be natural persons; AI-generated content essentially should not receive copyright protection. He emphasized more attention should be paid to whether front-end training infringes; commercial use of copyrighted works in AI training should constitute infringement.
- 张凌寒 (Zhang Linghan, China University of Political Science and Law professor): Suggested referencing Locke's labor theory re: whether to grant AI copyright; recommended "AI-assisted creation" recognition standards; proposed platforms follow "safe harbor rules" with "knowledge" standards, model providers be examined from "foreseeability" perspective, and users from "subjective fault" perspective.
- The 《人工智能法（学者建议稿）》 (AI Law Scholar Draft) by 7 institutions proposed fair use for AI training data with different purposes if not affecting normal use and rights holders' interests, but requiring data source labeling.

**Regulatory context:** The 2023 《生成式人工智能服务管理暂行办法》 (Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services) requires model training use "data and foundational models with legal sources."

The court's contact information is provided: Beijing Fengtai District, Auto Museum East Road No.2 Building 3; postal code 100160; litigation service phone 12368; email ipc@court.gov.cn.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"利用人工智能生成内容是否构成作品，应当根据具体情况进行分析，而非一概而论。关键在于人类使用AI模型的技术原理是否给人创作空间、生成的内容是否体现了人类的独创性。" — 朱阁 (Judge Zhu Ge, Beijing Internet Court)

"著作权法明确作者为自然人，AI生成内容因缺乏人类创作主体资格，本质上不属于作品，不应获得著作权保护。...至少在目前看来，著作权的集体许可是一个可行的路径。" — 李明德 (Li Mingde)

"人工智能产业的发展，不能以牺牲著作权人的利益为代价。既要保证人工智能训练可以使用充足的语料，又要充分保障著作权人的合法权益。" — 李明德 (Li Mingde)

"大模型平台的训练中对他人作品的使用属于商业性使用。如果将商业性使用受到著作权法保护的作品认定为不侵权，则著作权法保护作品、鼓励创新的宗旨将在很大程度上失去意义。" — 李明德 (Li Mingde)

"杭州互联网法院创新性提出'分阶段责任'，判决首次明确生成式AI平台的责任边界：平台对用户输入内容无审查义务，但对输出内容需承担合理注意义务。技术中立原则不再成为侵权借口。"
</key_excerpts>

9. 趙無極 30.09.65 - Christie's, 11/7, RMB 64,570,000.

The report, focused on the auction category, reveals that in 2024, amid economic uncertainty, the national cultural relics and art auction hammer price reached 18.354 billion yuan (excluding buyer commissions), a decline of 35.38% year-over-year. The annual auction transaction volume was 307,100 pieces/sets, down 10.35% from the previous year, indicating the market entered a deep adjustment phase. This webpage from GBA知识产权律师 (GBA IP Lawyer) discusses a landmark Chinese court case regarding copyright protection for AI-generated works, known as the "Spring Breeze Brings Tenderness" (春风送暖) case. The case was decided by the Beijing Internet Court under case number (2023)京0491民初11279号.

The court addressed three key issues:

1. **Whether the AI-generated image qualifies as a copyrighted work**: The court examined the plaintiff's creative process, including designing how to represent characters, selecting prompt words, arranging prompt order, setting technical parameters, and choosing images that matched the intended result. The court found these activities constituted meaningful intellectual input. It held that AI models lack free will and legal personality, and are merely technical tools—the creative process is fundamentally "humans using tools to create." As long as AI-generated images reflect original human intellectual contribution, they can be recognized as protected works. The image was classified as a work of fine art (美术作品) rather than falling under the "other works" clause.

2. **Whether the plaintiff owns the copyright**: Since AI models are not individuals or legal entities, they cannot be considered authors. Copyright belongs to the person making the creative intellectual contribution. Because the plaintiff conceived the idea, designed and arranged the prompts, adjusted parameters, and selected the final result, the plaintiff was recognized as the author and copyright owner.

3. **Whether the defendant's conduct constituted infringement**: The court found the defendant used the image without permission and removed the watermark linking to the plaintiff, violating the plaintiff's copyright. No statutory defense applied. The court ordered the defendant to stop infringing, issue a public apology, and compensate the plaintiff 500 RMB in economic damages.

**Conclusion**: The case provides important guidance for AI-generated work copyright protection in China, confirming that: (1) AI-generated works can be protected if they reflect user originality; (2) users who control the creative process can be recognized as authors; and (3) unauthorized use can lead to civil liability including damages and apology obligations. The ruling reinforces a human-centered approach to copyright protection, reflecting China's efforts to adapt traditional legal principles to emerging technologies.

**Case Background:** On February 24, 2023, plaintiff Li used the open-source software Stable Diffusion to generate an AI image by inputting prompts, then published it on Xiaohongshu (Little Red Book). **Court Ruling:** The court ordered the defendant to (1) publish an apology statement on the platform, (2) compensate the plaintiff 500 yuan in economic damages, and (3) dismissed the plaintiff's other claims.

**Key Findings on the Three Disputed Issues:**

1. **AI-generated images qualify as "artistic works":** The image met the four requirements for a work (belongs to literature, art, or science; originality; tangible form of expression; intellectual achievement). The originality derived from the creator's process—inputting prompts, adjusting parameters, and selecting results based on personal aesthetic choices. Stable Diffusion was compared to a paintbrush that provides tools, while the user's design determines the final output. The model doesn't assemble preset elements or retrieve existing images, making identical outputs nearly impossible.

2. **The AI software user holds the copyright:** Under China's Copyright Law, authors are limited to natural persons, legal persons, or unincorporated organizations—excluding AI software itself. Software designers' contributions end with the model creation; the final image content depends on the user's prompts. The court affirmed that copyright belongs to human creators despite AI being the tool.

3. **Using the image without author information constitutes infringement:** The defendant infringed the plaintiff's authorship right (signature right) and right to network dissemination by failing to attribute the author and publishing without permission. The article advises AI creators to clearly label their works (e.g., "AI illustration" tags) per good-faith principles and public transparency requirements.

**Damages Assessment:** The court awarded 500 yuan based on creators' difficulty in measuring actual losses (cost inputs are hard to quantify), citing Copyright Law Articles 52-54 which allow courts to award between 500 yuan and 5 million yuan when damages cannot be precisely calculated.

- **For software designers:** Ensure lawful/compliant outputs, check originality, inform users through agreements, auto-generate watermark signatures, save creation history, and enhance privacy and content protection.
- **For creators:** Understand their rights (signature, publication, network dissemination, reproduction, distribution, exhibition, adaptation, modification rights); take preventive measures (watermarks, clear authorization statements); preserve creation process records (videos, operation logs, copyright registration with China Copyright Protection Center); and keep records of use during value development.
- **Vindication procedure when infringed:** Verify infringement; preserve evidence (screenshots, videos, notarization); contact the infringer or send lawyer's letters; negotiate to minimize losses; file complaints with authorities or sue in court; seek remedies of cessation, elimination of impact, and damages.

**Case Facts:** In February 2023, the plaintiff used the open-source AI image tool Stable Diffusion, inputting prompts (24 positive and 120 negative prompts), made 4 rounds of parameter/prompt modifications, and generated an image titled "春風送來了溫柔" posted on Xiaohongshu. On March 2, 2023, the defendant used the image without permission (after removing the plaintiff's watermark) with original poetry on Baijiahao. The plaintiff sued for infringement of attribution rights (署名權) and information network transmission rights (公開傳輸權).

**Beijing Internet Court Ruling (November 27, 2023):**
1. **Whether the AI image qualifies as a "work":** The court found it meets all four criteria under Article 3 of China's Copyright Law — it belongs to the artistic domain, possesses "originality" (determined case-by-case; the plaintiff's prompts reflected personal choices, arrangements, aesthetic selections, and personality), has a certain expression form, and constitutes a human "intellectual achievement" reflecting the natural person's intellectual input (AI served as a tool to present human creativity tangibly).
2. **Copyright ownership:** AI cannot be an "author" (Article 11 limits authors to natural persons, legal persons, or unincorporated organizations). AI model designers are not authors either — they are "producers of creation tools" whose intellectual input lies in tool production, not image generation. The plaintiff, whose intellectual input directly generated the image, is the author and holds copyright.
3. **Infringement:** The defendant infringed the information network transmission right (public transmission) by publishing the image, and the attribution right (name indication) by removing the watermark. Defendant ordered to pay 500 RMB compensation and publish an apology on Baijiahao.
4. **AI cannot be a copyright subject:** The court emphasized that unlike commissioning a human artist (who exercises personal will and judgment), AI image generation still involves humans creating with a tool, so humans remain the creators.

**Comparison with Other Countries:** Most countries (South Africa, Australia, Japan, US) deny copyright protection to AI-generated content, arguing copyright law protects only human creation. Interestingly, China's 2019 Beijing Higher People's Court guidelines originally took a restrictive view, but China changed course. Three reasons for China's contrasting approach:
- China interprets "human participation" broadly (even preparation-stage participation counts) and fails to clearly distinguish "computer-assisted" vs. "AI-generated" creation — unlike the US "Zarya of the Dawn" case where the Copyright Office denied protection because prompts could not be controlled or predicted.
- China applies an objective standard for "originality" rather than the subjective standard (author-work connection) used elsewhere.
- China's 2017 "Next Generation AI Development Plan" aims to make China the global AI leader by 2030, and protecting AI-generated works promotes the AI industry.

**Implications:** As a non-precedent country, one ruling can't fully predict future Chinese court attitudes, though more scholarly discussion may shift views. The ruling is unlikely to affect other countries (especially Anglo-American jurisdictions emphasizing author rights and human participation), but could influence developing countries if China's AI industry flourishes. Risks include a surge of copyright infringement suits from copyright owners against AI training uses, and potentially suppressing human creativity. China's August 15, 2023 "Interim Measures for Generative AI Services Management" still lacks specific AI intellectual property provisions.

--- SOURCE 1: 徐冰：家长和社会对艺术教育的偏见几乎毁了艺术 阿特网—最即时的艺术新闻资讯 ---
URL: https://www.ccartd.com/news/detail/2021-8/132736369980000000.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Chinese-language article from the art news site "阿特新闻" (Art News), titled "徐冰：家长和社会对艺术教育的偏见几乎毁了艺术" (Xu Bing: The Prejudice of Parents and Society Against Art Education Has Almost Destroyed Art), published on August 17, 2021, sourced from 無悠藝 (Wu You Yi). The article presents the views of Xu Bing (徐冰), a renowned independent artist based in New York, on art, creativity, and art education.

Xu Bing is described as one of the most internationally influential contemporary Chinese artists, known for exploring the essence of Chinese culture and modes of thinking through imagery and symbolism. He graduated from the Printmaking Department of the Central Academy of Fine Arts (中央美术学院), where he later taught, and moved to the United States in 1990 as an honorary artist invited by the University of Wisconsin.

Key arguments from Xu Bing in the article:
- Art's core is not about form or material but about valuable thinking and being rooted in one's social context. He states "有问题就有艺术" (where there are problems, there is art), and that one's circumstances and problems are the source of artistic creation.
- Chinese society is criticized for overemphasizing drawing fundamentals while neglecting the foundation of thinking ability.
- Creativity doesn't come from IQ but from "the energy of the social field" (社会现场的能量), and China is a place with great potential energy for creativity.
- He criticizes Western art education for overemphasizing creativity in a simple, formulaic manner rather than exploring the actual mechanisms of creativity, which paradoxically damages students' natural creative abilities.
- He advocates for "大美术" (Great Fine Arts), a broad concept of art education that includes design, fashion, advertising, and architecture, rather than purely "fine arts."
- He discusses the artist's role: an artist must be able to say what others haven't said in a language others haven't used, producing something unprecedented.
- He reflects on traditional culture, noting that tradition is largely "dead" unless activated by contemporary problems ("随时代" - keeping up with the times).
- He critiques the current art education system, which he says is based mainly on 19th-century Western training methods combined with fragments of traditional lineage methods and half-digested Western contemporary art education, leaving students with fragmented skills but no understanding of their purpose as artists.
- He mentions that art education should raise the quality of a person, turning a "rough person into a refined, capable person."
- On artistic creation, he describes it as a confrontation between the creator and their own character and inner self, emphasizing the delicate care needed for student creativity (comparing it to a snail's fragile tentacles).

The article references several of Xu Bing's notable works, including 《天书》(Book from the Sky), 《凤凰》(Phoenix), 《英文方块字书法教室》(English Calligraphy Classroom, 1995-1998), 《鬼打墙》(Ghosts Pounding the Wall, 1990-1991), 《背后的故事》(Background Story, created 2004 during a visit to Berlin using three Chinese paintings from the German East Asian Art Museum's WWII-lost collection), 《荣华富贵》(Rong Hua Fu Gui, 2011), 《鸟飞了》(Birds Fly - composed of 400+ "bird" characters in different scripts), 《地书》(Book from the Ground - a book readable in any language using symbols), and the "木林森" (Forest) project. In 1999, he made an "art for the people" banner in English square-word calligraphy for MoMA.

The article concludes with his observation that Eastern painting reflects the eye's natural aperture adjustment (a planar construction process), while Western painting trains the eye to be like a camera with a locked aperture. The core message is that art's depth lies not in art itself but in how it connects with social reality and the critical problems of civilization.
</summary>

My attitude is to face problems—where there are problems, there is art.), "艺术的创造力，本质不来自于IQ，而真正来自于社会现场的能量。中国可是个可以创造巨大能量的地方，就看谁有这个本事，懂得吸纳这能量，用在你觉得值得用的事情上。" (The essence of artistic creativity does not come from IQ but truly from the energy of the social field. --- SOURCE 2: 将心比心：论中国社会学的田野调查-中国社会科学网 ---
URL: https://www.cssn.cn/dkzgxp/zgxp_zgshkx/2021nd12q/202208/t20220822_5479797.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic article titled "将心比心：论中国社会学的田野调查" (Putting Oneself in Others' Shoes: On Fieldwork in Chinese Sociology) by 周飞舟 (Zhou Feizhou), a professor at Peking University's Department of Sociology, published in the journal 《中国社会科学》 (Social Sciences in China) 2021 Issue 12 (dated 2021-12-28). The article examines the history, methodology, and challenges of fieldwork (田野调查) in Chinese sociology.

The article's core argument is that field investigation is the central method in Chinese sociology's development and reconstruction. It advocates for inheriting and developing Fei Xiaotong's (费孝通) "将心比心" (putting oneself in others' shoes/empathy-based) approach to field investigation to advance "sociology for the people" and better grasp the pulse of the new era of Chinese modernization.

Key sections and arguments:

1. **History of fieldwork ("从实求知")**: Traces the development from European "social surveys" (typified by Booth's surveys in London) to Chinese "社会调查运动" (social survey movement) of the Republican era (represented by Tao Menghe, Li Jinghan, Yan Jingyao), and the subsequent "社区研究" (community studies) promoted by Wu Wenzao (吴文藻) at Yenching University, which formed the "Yenching School" advocating for the sinicization of sociology. Fei Xiaotong distinguished "社会调查" (social survey) from "社会学调查" (sociological investigation), with 《禄村农田》 being his most representative community study. After the 1980 reconstruction of sociology, Fei conducted extensive research on rural enterprises, identifying models like "苏南模式" (Sunan model), "珠江模式" (Pearl River model), and "温州模式" (Wenzhou model). His studies were guided by "志在富民" (the aspiration to enrich the people), involved repeated visits ("行行重行行"), and followed the principle of "从实求知" (seeking knowledge from practice).

2. **Social bedrock ("社会底蕴")**: Argues that Chinese social structures rest on deep cultural foundations—relationships (关系), ethics, and informal institutions that are rarely examined by social science. Examples include research on township enterprise property rights (Liu Shiding's "两次嵌入" or double embedding of relationships in contract enforcement), government use of "关系控制" (relationship control) to resolve conflicts, and Xu Zongyang's study of capital going to rural areas where villagers steal corn from outside enterprises due to "内外有别" (distinction between inside and outside). Yang Shanhua and Sun Feiyu's concept of "社会底蕴" refers to those "constant" features that persist beneath social change, while Fei Xiaotong noted that the "只能意会" (only comprehensible by intuition/ tacit) aspects of culture are the real keys to understanding regional development differences.

3. **Methodological challenge of "将心比心"**: Addresses Edmund Leach's two critiques of Fei's 《江村经济》—representativeness of micro-community studies and the appropriateness of studying one's own society. Fei reflected that his earlier work was "只见社会不见人" (only seeing society, not people), focusing on social structure but not on "心态" (mentality), "道义关系" (moral relations), and the ethical dimensions of action (what the author calls "行动伦理" or action ethics). The article advocates for the "漫步" (strolling/walking) perspective over "鸟瞰" (bird's-eye view), which enables three effects in fieldwork: "机缘效应" (serendipity effect), "追踪效应" (tracking effect), and most importantly, "感通效应" (empathetic resonance effect). Using the author's 2014 Chengdu study of "农民上楼" (farmers moving to high-rise buildings), the article demonstrates that there are multiple layers of "facts" in fieldwork—surface statistics cannot capture the underlying "被上楼" (being moved up) mentality. True objectivity requires researchers to open themselves to understanding subjects' subjective mentalities, using one's heart to sense the other's heart—this is "将心比心."

The article concludes that this empathy-based field investigation is essential for creating a distinctly Chinese sociology with Chinese characteristics, style, and disposition, connecting China's living social reality with its deep historical traditions.

This webpage contains the full text of Chinese President Xi Jinping's speech "Talking at the Forum on Literature and Art Work" (在文艺工作座谈会上的讲话), delivered on October 15, 2014. The speech was published by the official Chinese news source on October 16, 2024. It is a foundational policy document for Chinese cultural policy, addressing the role of literature and art (文艺) in national rejuvenation and the guidance for Chinese artists and writers.

The speech is organized around five main questions (problems):

1. **Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires the prosperity and development of Chinese culture.** Xi argues that culture is vital to a nation's survival and development, citing the "Axial Age" concept from German philosopher Karl Jaspers (800-200 BC). He emphasizes that China's global standing historically came from cultural appeal rather than military expansion ("以德服人、以文化人"). He reviews great literary and artistic figures from Greece, Russia, France, Britain, Germany, the US, India, and China. He declares that "without the prosperity of Chinese culture, there can be no great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" (没有中华文化繁荣兴盛，就没有中华民族伟大复兴), and that literature and art are the clarion call of the times, can best represent an era's features, and best lead an era's trends. He quotes Lu Xun that literature and art are the first step in transforming the nation's spiritual world.

2. **Creating excellent works worthy of the era.** Xi stresses that the fundamental measure of an era's literary achievement is its works. He criticizes problems in current creation: quantity over quality, "plateaus without peaks" (有'高原'缺'高峰'), plagiarism, mechanical production, fast-food consumption, works that mock the sublime, distort classics, subvert history, or demonize heroes. He identifies "restlessness/impetuousness" (浮躁) as the most prominent problem reported by artists. He cites Flaubert (writing one page of Madame Bovary in 5 days) and Cao Xueqin (revising Dream of the Red Chamber for ten years) as examples of dedicated craftsmanship. He emphasizes that innovation is the life of literature and art, citing Liu Xie's "Wenxin Diaolong" and calligrapher Li Yong: "Those who imitate me are clumsy, those who resemble me die" (学我者拙，似我者死). He calls for building a large team of accomplished artists and adapting to new internet/new media forms and new artistic groups (network writers, freelance authors, independent producers).

3. **Adhering to a people-centered creative orientation.** Socialist literature and art is essentially the people's art. He traces this through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, and Hu Jintao. He elaborates three points: (a) the people need art (including for telling China's story to the world and letting foreigners understand China); (b) art needs the people (people are the source of creative lifeblood, citing Lenin: "Art belongs to the people"); and (c) art must love the people. He uses the example of writer Liu Qing, who resigned as deputy county party secretary to live among farmers for 14 years to write "The Builders" (《创业史》), and recalls the advice of writer Wang Yuanjian before Xi went to work in Zhengding in 1982. He states a good work must stand up to evaluation by the people, experts, and the market, putting social benefit first while pursuing social and economic benefit unity — "art cannot be a slave to the market" (文艺不能当市场的奴隶).

4. **The Chinese spirit is the soul of socialist literature and art.** Xi connects this to cultivating and practicing socialist core values, which he had promoted across various speaking engagements throughout 2014. He warns of the prominent problem of value loss in society (no good/evil distinctions, no behavioral bottom lines). The deepest, most fundamental, most eternal element in core values is patriotism (爱国主义), citing Fan Zhongyan, Lu You, Wen Tianxiang, Lin Zexu, Yue Fei's "Man Jiang Hong", and Fang Zhimin's "Lovable China". The eternal value of art is the pursuit of truth, goodness, and beauty. He stresses inheriting excellent traditional Chinese culture, which is the spiritual lifeline of the Chinese nation, but warns against "Western worship" (以洋为尊), "de-ideologization", "devaluation", "de-Chineseization". He mentions Hollywood films "Kung Fu Panda" and "Mulan" drew from Chinese cultural resources. Inheritance should mean creative transformation and innovative development, not simple restoration or blind exclusion. He calls for strengthening literary and art criticism — criticism must genuinely criticize, not flatter, must not use Western theory to tailor Chinese aesthetics or replace artistic standards with commercial standards (not "red envelope thickness equals review height"). Critics should do "cutting rotten apples" work as Lu Xun said, being guided by Marxist literary theory while inheriting Chinese critical heritage and critically borrowing from modern Western theory.

The speech concludes with Xi expressing the Central Committee's high expectations that the literary front will create more fine works and contribute to cultural development and building a strong socialist culture. The webpage includes several photographs with captions showing Xi at cultural events between 2014 and 2024 (the 2021 Congress of China Federation of Literary and Art Circles, the 2024 National Day concert, a 2024 state honor ceremony awarding Tian Hua the "People's Artist" title, and inspection visits to Gansu, Guangxi, Jiangsu, and Xinjiang).

Key points:

# National Endowment for the Arts Grant Process

[In This Section](https://americanorchestras.org/learn/development-fundraising/nea-funding/nea-funding-opportunities/tips-for-your-nea-grant-application#section-nav)
_Updated July 15, 2026_

On August 7, 2025, a new executive order on [**Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking**](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/08/improving-oversight-of-federal-grantmaking/) was announced, which urges advancement of the President’s policy agenda, expresses preference for a broader range of recipients, seeks more interagency coordination to reduce duplication of grants, and calls for certain procedural measures placing more responsibility in the hands of senior appointees and designees. A [**memorandum from the Department of Justice**](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-releases-guidance-recipients-federal-funding-regarding-unlawful) at the end of July “clarifies the application of federal antidiscrimination laws to programs or initiatives that may involve discriminatory practices, including those labeled as Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (“DEI”) programs.”. The NEA meets regularly with its Office of General Counsel, which determined its existing grant language (as of October 2025) to be in compliance with both directives.

On February 6, 2025, the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) [**announced**](https://www.arts.gov/news/press-releases/2025/updates-national-endowment-arts-fy-2026-grant-opportunities)it was reviewing recent executive orders and related documents to ensure compliance and provide the required reporting.Both the scope of what will be funded by the NEA and the compliance requirements for awardees are significantly changed.The NEA has not yet provided information about how new rules may or may not apply to NEA funding administered by states and localities.

On May 2, 2025, the NEA sent notifications to many FY24 and FY25 grantees, terminating awards in progress, effective May 31, 2025. The agency also withdrew many offers of new FY25 grant awards that had already been publicly announced and were awaiting final grant confirmations. This is an extreme disruption in the typical [**life cycle of an application and grant award**](https://www.arts.gov/grants/grant-review-process). Approximately 100 appeals to reconsider grant termination were approved by the NEA after extensive review, and those grantees were reportedly notified over summer 2025.

In the sections below, please find up to date information about disruption to prior grant awards and applications and the process for applying for FY27 awards (further updated from changes begun in FY26).

## FY2025 and Open Grant Awards

**On May 2, 2025, the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) sent notifications to many FY24 and FY25 grantees, terminating awards in progress, effective May 31, 2025. The agency also withdrew many offers of new FY25 grant awards that had already been publicly announced and were awaiting final grant confirmations.**

The notifications cite the agency’s intention to instead prioritize projects _“that elevate the Nation’s HBCUs and Hispanic Serving Institutions, celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, foster AI competency, empower houses of worship to serve communities, assist with disaster recovery, foster skilled trade jobs, make America healthy again, support the military and veterans, support Tribal communities, make the District of Columbia safe and beautiful, and support the economic development of Asian American communities.”_

Grantees that received a termination letter have until June 30, 2025 to request final payment of any “actual, allowable, approved costs” incurred before the new project end date of May 31, 2025. This end date overrides the project end dates that had been previously approved, but **grantees should be sure to keep checking the grant portal in the event that the project end date shifts earlier, since email notification is not always being issued**. Federal Financial Reports (FFR) for awards must be submitted by July 31, 2025. The FFR must reflect actual, allowable, approved costs incurred during the revised period of performance. While all other final and/or interim performance reporting requirements, including the Final Descriptive Report and the Geographic Location of Project Activity (GEO), are waived, policy experts recommend that grantees complete these reports so that they can assert full technical compliance with the original terms of the grant awards.

Grantees were permitted to appeal the determination within 7 calendar days of receiving the notice if they could provide documentation that the project supports one of the Administration’s specified new priority areas. Notices withdrawing offers of FY25 grants were also given a 7 calendar day appeal period. Approximately 100 appeals to reconsider grant termination were approved by the NEA after extensive review, and those grantees were reportedly notified over summer 2025.

The League collected information to assist orchestras in navigating the grant termination and withdrawal process and continues to field questions about drawing down funds and reporting requirements. Grantees may find helpful the following resource: [**A Nonprofit Checklist: What to do When Your Federal Grant or Contract is Terminated | National Council of Nonprofits**](https://www.councilofnonprofits.org/nonprofit-checklist-what-do-when-your-federal-grant-or-contract-terminated).

A number of FY2025 grants were publicly announced and offered, and many received final grant approval notifications or withdrawal notices in early-mid November 2025. The NEA has not yet publicly shared these respective outcomes.

The NEA also has not announced plans for moving forward with the FY2025 GAP Round 2 applications that have undergone review by the agency, are awaiting final approval, and were due to be announced to grantees soon. Typically, these grants are announced in late Spring, but due to the federal government shutdown at the beginning of FY26, it is likely some unspent funds were redirected to keep essential functions of the agency operational, such as allowing grantees to continue drawing down funds.

There is also not yet clarity about which assurances of compliance with executive orders would apply to ongoing FY2025 grantmaking, or successful termination appeals.

## FY2026 Grant Application Process

**On February 6, 2025, the National Endowment for the Arts [announced](https://www.arts.gov/news/press-releases/2025/updates-national-endowment-arts-fy-2026-grant-opportunities) that it is reviewing the recent executive orders and related documents to ensure compliance and provide the required reporting.****Both the scope of what will be funded by the NEA and the compliance requirements for awardees are significantly changed.****The NEA has not yet provided information about how new rules may or may not apply to NEA funding administered by states and localities.****In an update to its Grants for Arts Projects summary page, the NEA now strongly encourages “applications for arts projects that incorporate one or more**[**agency funding priorities**](https://www.arts.gov/grants/priorities)**.” It is unclear how these posted priorities intersect with funding priorities that had been articulated in termination letters that went to grantees this spring.**

The NEA launched the FY2026 grant process in December 2024, and has now revoked the prior grant guidelines. Applicants that initiated an application under the prior guidelines must re-submit their request under the new guidelines. There are two new initial [**application deadlines**](https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.arts.gov_grants_grants-2Dfor-2Darts-2Dprojects&d=DwMFaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=ITNqzxRGmOV1gHiCZCea9fLL_i6gddeUAH8noq_bCTQ&m=5PJK00J7F7bHlZNOqsz9TXB7Dpy9rnaWBFxnLqWmzzEWZa2PttTp_YLioFO9WGtF&s=XgB59SqnVF_Wl24rMrUvhYu7m4cUJHA9LeIHI8EKiAQ&e=) of **March 11 (March cycle of GAP) and July 17****(July cycle of GAP)**.

On February 7, 2025, the NEA issued revised FY26 grant guidelines in response to recent directives and to “streamline and simplify the application process and align with the agency’s [**mission**](https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.arts.gov_sites_default_files_Legislation.pdf&d=DwMFaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=ITNqzxRGmOV1gHiCZCea9fLL_i6gddeUAH8noq_bCTQ&m=5PJK00J7F7bHlZNOqsz9TXB7Dpy9rnaWBFxnLqWmzzEWZa2PttTp_YLioFO9WGtF&s=2hDscgC9GRRdaXA3DvuW9tMB2X84OIOCDwWGUe41SVE&e=).”

The Challenge America grant opportunity is canceled for FY2026 and prospective applicants are instead encouraged to apply to Grants for Arts Projects.

**Please read ALL of the following material when considering next steps in applying for NEA support:**

*   [**Revised FY26 NEA Grant Guidelines**](https://www.arts.gov/grants/grants-for-arts-projects)
*   [**Assurance of Compliance**](https://www.arts.gov/grants/legal-requirements-and-assurance-of-compliance#assurance)

In a February 18 webinar, the NEA stated “In accordance with Executive Orders, we will not fund projects that include DEI activities.”

While applicants will be required to certify that they will comply with “all applicable Executive Orders,” the NEA has not yet specified all of the current or future full array of orders that would apply. The National Council of Nonprofits has provided an[**overview of court action**](https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.councilofnonprofits.org_files_media_documents_2025_chart-2Dexecutive-2Dorders.pdf&d=DwMFaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=ITNqzxRGmOV1gHiCZCea9fLL_i6gddeUAH8noq_bCTQ&m=4wdhmKVJCDKZvCxAfPhQN4PfKUG5DX2nfMXFNtYURkJBwZYWTji_JO6mNxX_4Iac&s=nFAdIjjc1lVqWzPFvyBr0SdAuH-HWRcJadqsLKq20Bc&e=) in response to a range of orders. 

The NEA’s new Assurance of Compliance required applicants to certify compliance with **[Executive Order No. 14173, Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/ending-illegal-discrimination-and-restoring-merit-based-opportunity/)** and **[Executive Order No. 14168, Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/defending-women-from-gender-ideology-extremism-and-restoring-biological-truth-to-the-federal-government/)**.

On Friday, February 21, a federal judge issued a [**preliminary injunction**](https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__storage.courtlistener.com_recap_gov.uscourts.mdd.575287_gov.uscourts.mdd.575287.44.0-5F2.pdf&d=DwMFaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=ITNqzxRGmOV1gHiCZCea9fLL_i6gddeUAH8noq_bCTQ&m=4wdhmKVJCDKZvCxAfPhQN4PfKUG5DX2nfMXFNtYURkJBwZYWTji_JO6mNxX_4Iac&s=9BZ0WF6kLEsdMhsGJOGrLjt0NZmYeAxTaA42fJq8lUk&e=) in response to a case led by the National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education, pausing implementation of EO 14173. On March 3, a federal judge in Maryland refused to halt the injunction, noting in the [**decision**](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/public/desktop/document/NationalAssociationofDiversityOfficersinHigherEducationetalvTrump/7?doc_id=X4OCBN30GUD943A2VJGNM4Q6HGO)that the Administration’s policies must comply with the United States Constitution, and particularly in this case, free speech and due process rights. The Administration appealed the ruling, and on March 14 **[a decision](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/25563130-deistay031425/)** by the 4 th Circuit Court of Appeals lifted the preliminary injunction on the order while litigation continues, enabling the NEA to reinstate a requirement for grantees to certify compliance with the order. **On June 10, the NEA posted an [FAQ explaining more detail on how it plans to administer EO 14173](https://www.arts.gov/grants/legal-requirements-and-assurance-of-compliance/frequently-asked-questions) related to diversity, equity, and inclusion activities.**

On[](https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.aclu.org_press-2Dreleases_court-2Drules-2Din-2Dfavor-2Dof-2Dartists-2Dfree-2Dspeech-2Din-2Dcase-2Dagainst-2Dthe-2Dnational-2Dendowment-2Dfor-2Dthe-2Darts&d=DwMF-g&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lm92070dTuqXDsUL9e7GQK1mqZLFuSaBRt-ClIOhxxo&m=NZZmHV9go-FXvKMXKyXlOUJSinR92rqy0yFzh7gJSJ7Hqtg3Jm2VzAU_dmOXqQpM&s=0j-J7TnhQoq-PFVB2KnK2WQqO2XH8U0Dqx6MvDfcCoU&e=)**[September 19, 2025](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/court-rules-in-favor-of-artists-free-speech-in-case-against-the-national-endowment-for-the-arts)**, a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down the NEA’s policy disfavoring grant applications deemed to “promote gender ideology.” The decision comes after months of court action that has unfolded throughout 2025. On March 6, the American Civil Liberties Union[**filed a federal lawsuit**](https://www.aclu.org/cases/rhode-island-latino-arts-v-national-endowment-for-the-arts?document=Complaint)against the National Endowment for the Arts, on behalf of Rhode Island Latino Arts, the Theater Offensive, National Queer Theater, and Theatre Communications Group, challenging the requirement that all grant applicants certify that “federal funds shall not be used to promote gender ideology,” citing violations of the First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, and Administrative Procedures Act. On April 3, the U.S. District Court for Rhode Island denied the motion to block NEA implementation of the[**executive order on “gender ideology**](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/defending-women-from-gender-ideology-extremism-and-restoring-biological-truth-to-the-federal-government/).” The court noted that the NEA had already suspended implementation of the executive order and the agency planned to consider if and how it may take further action on the order by April 30, 2025.**On April 30, the NEA issued a[memo outlining its plans](https://americanorchestras.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Final-.Notice.Implementation.EO14168.20250416-as-implemented-MAC-signed.pdf)for implementing the Executive Order on “gender ideology.”**On June 30, the ACLU filed a motion for summary judgment, arguing that the NEA is violating the First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, and Administrative Procedure Act in its implementation of an executive order that prohibits federal funding for “gender ideology.” The court ruled in September that the NEA’s plans to disfavor such projects in the grant review process violated the First Amendment as a viewpoint-based restriction on private speech. It also found the policy arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, noting there was “zero explanation” of what the term meant or how it related to artistic merit, excellence, or respect for diverse beliefs. The NEA has not yet made a statement following the court ruling.

Additionally, on February 19, the Legal Defense Fund and Lambda Legal filed[a federal lawsuit](https://www.naacpldf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025.02.19-ECF-1-Complaint.pdf)on behalf of the National Urban League, National Fair Housing Alliance, and AIDS Foundation of Chicago challenging the two executive orders related to diversity, equity, and inclusion as well as the EO 14168 on “gender ideology.” 

The full Assurance of Compliance includes prior rules regarding anti-discrimination requirements. Applicants should review the following U.S. code language, which includes more detailed information on how the NEA implements the terms of nondiscrimination in federally assisted programs. [**eCFR :: 45 CFR Part 1110 — Nondiscrimination in Federally Assisted Programs**](https://www.arts.gov/grants/grant-review-process).

As of November 2025, the Assurance of Compliance no longer specifically mentions EO 14168 and “gender ideology” but prospective grantees should review the posted FAQ on certification requirements relating to DEI:
