--- SOURCE 10: When Art Meets Building: A Primer on the Visual Artists Rights Act ---
URL: https://www.olshanlaw.com/when-art-meets-building

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, written by Thomas D. Kearns and Carolyn Sha of Olshan Frome Wolosky's real estate department (reprinted from the New York Law Journal, June 30, 2014), provides a comprehensive primer on the federal Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990 (VARA) as it applies to landlords and tenants of real property.

**Overview of VARA:** VARA protects visual artists' "moral rights" by prohibiting the destruction of "visual art" (paintings, drawings, sculptures, or photographs) of "recognized stature." Art of "recognized stature" is that viewed as possessing stature by art experts, the art community, or society in general. Qualifying artists can sue to prevent destruction or recover actual or statutory damages ranging from $750 to over $30,000 (up to $150,000 for willful infringements, down to $200 for innocent infringements). VARA rights are non-transferrable, exercisable only by the artist, and last for the artist's lifetime (or the last surviving artist's life for joint works).

**Key for Property Owners:** VARA protects works "incorporated in or made part of a building" where removal would cause destruction, distortion, mutilation, or modification (e.g., murals, frescoes, affixed sculptures). Relevant cases include *Carter v. Helmsley-Spear* (sculptures, glass mosaics, and permanent installations affixed to building) and *Board of Managers of Soho International Arts Condominium v. City of New York* (aluminum bars attached to steel reinforcement braces).

**Three Ways Landlords Can Protect Against VARA Liability:**

1. **Explicit Waiver:** For art that cannot be safely removed, the artist's rights must be waived (or the artist consented before June 1, 1991, VARA's effective date). The waiver must be a written instrument signed by both artist and building owner that: (a) specifically identifies the work and uses to which the waiver applies, and (b) specifies that installation may subject the work to destruction, distortion, mutilation, or modification by reason of removal. For joint works, a waiver by one artist waives rights of all. Waivers survive the sale of the property.

2. **De Facto Waiver:** For art of "recognized stature" that can be safely removed, building owners must make a "diligent, good faith" attempt to notify the artist of removal intention (presumed if sent by registered mail to the artist's most recent address on record with the Register of Copyrights). No claim exists if contact attempts fail, or if the owner provides notice but the artist fails to remove the work or pay for removal within 90 days. Alternative: require art installations be crafted for safe dismantling and removal.

3. **Work for Hire:** VARA rights do not apply to works "made for hire"—either prepared within the scope of an employee's employment, or commissioned as part of a collective work/compilation agreed in writing by both parties. Courts use a multi-factor balancing test (right to control production, requisite skill, employee benefits, tax treatment, assignment of additional projects). Mere use of the words "work for hire" without supporting factors is insufficient.

**'Surprise' Art:** VARA may protect work not obviously art when installed, including graffiti. In the 5Pointz case (Long Island City), 17 graffiti artists sued after the owner decided to raze the factory housing their works. Though the injunction was denied for lack of demonstrated irreparable harm, the court held "VARA protects even temporary art from destruction" and the defendants could face "potentially significant monetary damages" if works were of "recognized stature." Graffiti at 5Pointz was consented to by the owner—VARA protects only art legally placed with the owner's consent. Commercial signage may also gain "recognized stature" over time (per a Second Circuit concurring opinion), though advertising/promotional material is expressly excluded from VARA.

**Models and Unfinished Works:** Unfinished works are subject to VARA protection, per *Flack v. Friends of Queen Catherine*, where a partially completed sculpture was protected since "'preliminary' work of painters—drawing and sketches—[were] covered by VARA."

**Practical Suggestions:** Obtain artist waivers for any work installed that may be considered art; consider waivers for all art not simply affixed by a nail; include specific lease provisions requiring landlord consent and artist waivers (with sample waiver language provided, including indemnification); keep records of creator names/addresses for de facto waivers; educate building personnel; properly document work-for-hire relationships; and add VARA analysis to real property purchase diligence checklists.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: The Development of Art Projects in Japan: Policy and Economic Perspectives – FIELD ---
URL: https://field-journal.com/issue-8/the-development-of-art-projects-in-japan-policy-and-economic-perspectives

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article by Nobuko Kawashima (Professor of Economics, Doshisha University, Kyoto) examines the institutional and economic factors—specifically Japanese cultural policy and its broader economic context—that have driven the remarkable growth of socially engaged art and new public art in Japan over the last two decades. The paper defines 'art project' as art exhibitions and social practices located outside museum galleries, often participatory and involving local citizens, volunteers, and students, focused on process rather than artistic object. It notes that unlike Western socially engaged art, Japanese art projects tend to engage social issues for inclusion and well-being rather than adversarial political causes.

KEY FACTS ON CULTURAL POLICY:
- Japanese cultural policy has historically been very limited in scale; government had little interest in cultural matters until the early 1990s, letting arts operate within the market economy. In the late 1980s, reliance on earned income for Japanese theater companies was over 90%, versus about 60% in the U.S. and 50% in the U.K.
- The Agency for Cultural Affairs (ACA), created in 1968, is the main national cultural policy actor. Its 2017 budget was about 100 billion yen (0.11% of public spending), far below France (0.87%) and South Korea (0.99%). About 45% goes to heritage preservation and 30% to national institutions; less than a quarter supports contemporary cultural activities.
- Local government cultural spending peaked at 955 billion yen in 1994/5 but fell to 340 billion yen by 2010/11. Cultural facility numbers grew from ~800 in the late 1970s to ~3,200 by the late 1990s (fourfold increase), funded by local bonds subsidized by central government (1978-2001). Programming and art production received the lowest priority in local spending.

DEVELOPMENTS SINCE THE 1990s DRIVING ART PROJECTS:
1. Cultural policy became positioned alongside education, health, welfare, tourism, and regional revitalization, using instrumental justifications. Japanese policymakers are more positive about this than European researchers.
2. Growing emphasis on cultural/arts management: the Japan Foundation for Regional Art-Activities (JAFRA) was established in 1994 to train arts managers. New generations of arts managers are more supportive of art projects.
3. Corporate support shifted toward grassroots and experimental creative activities (e.g., Asahi Breweries, Chishima Real Estate, Benesse's Sōichirō Fukutake supporting Naoshima and Setouchi Art Triennale since 2010).
4. Museums' roles changed toward outreach, arts education, and workshops; ACA began competitive project-funding for museums in 2014 (e.g., enabling partnerships like Towada Oirase Art Project).
5. The 1998 Promotion of Specified Nonprofit Activities law made it easier for grassroots organizations to obtain legal corporate status, though Japan's nonprofit sector remains small (0.18% of GDP in charitable contributions vs. 2% in the U.S.; ~51,600 registered NPOs in 2017).

RECENT SOCIO-ECONOMIC TRENDS:
- Japan faces an aging population, economic downturn, industrial hollowing-out, workforce casualization, and community decline. Administrative and tax reforms since the 2000s have made local authorities more independent and self-directed.
- Creative City theory (Charles Landry, Richard Florida, introduced to Japan by Masayuki Sasaki) drew policy attention. Art projects fit the discourse of 'collaborative, self-directed, creative solution' and are relatively inexpensive. The Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale received 9.4 billion yen from Niigata Prefecture over its first five festivals (2000-2012), funded under local revitalization budgets.
- NPOs have been convenient for government bureaucracy in implementing art projects that cross departmental boundaries.

FUTURE CHALLENGES:
1. Funding: art projects struggle with funding and rely on multiple sources across various budget categories (e.g., Beppu Project), risking loss of artistic vision and becoming instrumentally oriented.
2. Policy evaluation: New public management requires quantitative cost-benefit demonstration, which is difficult for art projects with multiple, intangible, long-term aims. There is criticism that Japanese art projects tend to be celebratory and apolitical, avoiding provocative or confrontational art, which might compromise aesthetic quality.

The paper concludes that art projects have developed because they fit local authorities' regeneration needs, are inexpensive and one-off, attract corporate sponsors, and benefit from changing museum roles, the nonprofit sector, and new arts managers—but face sustainability challenges from managerialism and instrumental funder demands.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Statutes of the Republic of Korea ---
URL: https://elaw.klri.re.kr/eng_mobile/viewer.do?hseq=48734&type=part&key=38

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the full text of the Republic of Korea's ARTIST WELFARE ACT (Act No. 11089, enacted Nov. 17, 2011), as amended by Acts No. 12136 (Dec. 30, 2013), No. 13970 (Feb. 3, 2016), and No. 15568 (Apr. 17, 2018).

Key provisions by chapter:
- Chapter I (General): Article 1 establishes the purpose—legally protecting artists' professional status and rights, promoting creative activities, and providing welfare support. Article 2 defines an "artist" as a person who earns a living through artistic activities and can prove activities in creation, performance, or technical assistance in culture and arts (as prescribed by Presidential Decree).
- Chapter II (Status, Rights): Artists have the right to freely engage in artistic activities, fairly enjoy benefits from their work, and not be compelled into unfair contracts (Art. 3). The State/local governments must formulate welfare policies without discrimination (Art. 4). The Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism must conduct status surveys every three years (Art. 4-2). Culture and arts service contracts must be made on equal terms and specify contractual amount, period, rights/obligations, scope of services, profit sharing, and dispute settlement (Art. 4-3). The State develops standard form contracts (Art. 5). Article 6-2 prohibits unfair practices by culture and arts planners (e.g., pressuring artists to sign unfair contracts using dominant position, refusing/distributing inadequate profits, obstructing creative activities, or unjustly using artist information). Corrective orders can be issued, and financial support from various funds can be suspended for noncompliance (Art. 6-3).
- Chapter III (Social Security): The Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act applies to artists; the Foundation may partially subsidize premiums (Art. 7).
- Chapter IV (Korean Artists Welfare Foundation): Establishes the corporate Foundation (Arts 8-15), detailing its articles of association, affairs (social security support, job security, welfare of vulnerable artists, surveys, welfare chests, mutual-aid projects, counseling/legal aid for unfair practices, education, government projects), executives (max 15 directors, one chairperson, one full-time director, one auditor with 3-year terms, one reappointment allowed), board of directors, business year, and supervision. Articles 10-3, 15-2, and 15-3 (added 2018) govern collecting financial, credit, and insurance information with consent, and requesting data through computer networks and finance companies for verifying support eligibility.
- Chapter V (Supplementary): Foundation executives/employees are deemed public officials for penalty purposes (Art. 16); authority may be delegated/entrusted (Art. 16-2).
- Chapter VI (Penalties): Up to 3 years imprisonment or fines up to 30 million won for unlawful use/disclosure of data or financial information (Art. 17). Administrative fines up to 5 million won for various violations, including failing to prepare written contracts, violating corrective orders, failing to submit data, and unauthorized use of the Foundation name (Art. 18).

Effectiveness: The original act took effect one year after promulgation; the 2013 and 2016 amendments took effect three months after promulgation; the 2018 amendment took effect six months after promulgation.
</summary>

URL: https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10375532

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Korea Herald reported on November 6, 2012, that South Korea's controversial Artists' Welfare Act (예술인복지법) will come into effect on November 18, 2012. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism announced the government would implement various policies to promote welfare for artists who typically struggle financially. Two enforcement ordinances passed the Cabinet on November 6.

Key details:
- The government earmarked 7 billion won ($6.4 million) from next year's budget for a job training program for aspiring artists and a program supporting creative activities for professional artists. A total of 2,400 people will benefit, starting early 2013 (1,500 for job training programs and 900 for creative preparation fund support linked to social contribution).
- South Korea's artist population (including movie/performing arts staff and school teachers) was estimated at 540,000 per 2008 data from the Korean Employment Information Service.
- The law allows the government to establish a welfare foundation for artists (Korean Artists Welfare Foundation, which will be created later this month) and permits employed artists to join industrial accident compensation insurance. A revision to the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act passed the Cabinet the same day.
- The law, legislated a year ago (November 2011), sparked controversy due to its vague definition of artists and failure to include artists in medical and three other major government-led insurance programs (the four major insurance programs).
- Regarding the controversial definition of "artist," the ministry proposed four criteria for verifying artist activity: ① published art activity records, ② income from artistic activities, ③ copyright (or neighboring rights) registration records, and ④ art activities supported by national/local subsidies. Meeting any one qualifies a person as an artist; those not meeting criteria can be verified through separate deliberation by the welfare foundation.
- A standard contract form will be developed and distributed to improve working environments, and an Artists' Career Information System will be built to systematically manage artists' activities and records.

Ministry official Kim Jae-won, in charge of arts policy, downplayed criticisms, calling the law "a small but important first step" and "the starting point of reflecting the contribution artists have made to society in a law," expressing hope the law would be complemented in the future. The ministry stated it would select support recipients under fair and strict criteria, recognizing a broad scope of artists under the law while considering the limited budget.

South Korea extended its state employment insurance program to artists starting December 10, 2020 (Thursday), as the first step toward expanding coverage to all workers by 2025. The Ministry of Employment and Labor announced that artists under work contracts earning a monthly income of at least 500,000 won ($460) will be eligible for coverage under the amended Employment Insurance Act. The amendment excludes artists earning under 500,000 won monthly to prevent those not working as artists primarily for a living from claiming benefits. Artists can receive an allowance equivalent to 60 percent of their income for at least 120 days if they have paid into the plan for at least nine months. The Act's purpose (Article 1) is to protect the professional status and rights of artists by law, promote artists' creative activities through welfare support, and contribute to the development of the arts. The law was prompted by the 2005 son-bae lawsuit of the late sculptor Goo Bon-ju, which publicized issues of artists' social status and livelihood, and bills were gathered by representatives including Jeong Byeong-guk, Seo Gap-won, Choi Jong-won, and Jeon Byeong-hun.

2. Fact-finding surveys: The Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism must conduct a survey on artist welfare and creative environment every three years.
3. Korea Artist Welfare Foundation: established under this Act; handles unfair act reports and other entrusted tasks.
4. Proof of artistic activity: An "artist" is defined as someone engaging in artistic activities (creation, performance, technical support) as a business, provable via an Artistic Activity Certificate.
5. Artist status and rights: Artists must be respected as contributors to the cultural nation, have the right to freely engage in artistic activities and enjoy legitimate benefits, and have the right not to be forced into unfair contracts.

8. Prohibition of unfair behavior: Culture/arts planners cannot force unfair contract conditions, refuse profit distribution, obstruct creative activities, or misuse artist information. 9. Financial support suspension: Violators of corrective orders may face suspension of film development fund, culture and arts promotion fund, broadcasting communication development fund support, and other financial support.

--- SOURCE 14: CIF_Arts and Growth_v7.indd ---
URL: https://www.artscouncil.org.uk/sites/default/files/CIF_Arts_and_Growth.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Overview
This is the second policy report from the Creative Industries Federation (produced in partnership with Arts Council England), arguing that public investment in the arts is crucial to the growth of the UK's creative industries. The report is authored by Professor Jonothan Neelands and Eliza Easton of Warwick Business School, with contributions from leading business figures including Melanie Clore (Sotheby's), Tom Weldon (Penguin Random House), Baroness Lane-Fox, Caroline Rush (British Fashion Council), Boris Johnson, and Matthew Bourne.

## Core Economic Argument
- The UK creative industries are booming: GVA grew 9.9% between 2012-2013 (higher than any other industrial sector including financial services), and returned £77 billion of direct GVA in 2012-2013.
- Employment in the creative economy grew 5% between 2013-2014 (vs. 2.1% UK average) and accounts for 5.8% of all UK jobs; creative economy jobs grew 13.7% since 2011.
- The public arts return 0.4% of UK GVA (a 19% increase vs. 3.3% UK average) with 9.2% employment growth.
- UK films generated £1.4 billion in exports with a £916 million trade surplus in 2013.
- The arts are linked to 42% of inbound-tourism related expenditure.

## Investment Gap
- The UK invests only 0.3% of GDP on arts and culture vs. the EU average of 0.5%, France at 0.8%, and Germany at 0.4%.
- Arts Council England grant-in-aid fell 29.4% in real terms from 2010/11 to 2014/15, accounting for only 0.1% of public expenditure.
- Total public spend on arts/culture in England represents just 0.7% of total public spend.
- Local government spending on arts and culture fell 25% since 2007/08.
- No other EU country benefits from the level of GVA the UK's public arts return.

## How Public Investment Drives Growth
- **R&D function**: Public investment mitigates risk at the high-risk idea development stage. The National Theatre spent ~£50,000 on experimental workshops for War Horse; its first production cost ~£500,000 but has now been seen by 5.5+ million people and earned a £12 million surplus.
- **Seedbed for commercial success**: The RSC's two years of publicly funded development enabled Les Misérables to become London's longest-running musical (70+ million people in 42 countries). Matthew Bourne's New Adventures received £3 million in grants but returned £12 million to the Treasury.
- **Leverage effect**: Orchestras leverage an additional £2 of private investment per £1 of public investment; NPOs leverage similar amounts.
- **Industry dependence**: 37% of video games businesses depend on public grants/government schemes. Software developers can claim tax reductions up to 225% of R&D investment.
- **Tax incentives**: Film, high-end TV, animation, video games, children's TV, theatre and orchestras benefit from tax reliefs (up to 25% for touring costs, 20% for other theatre productions, 25% for orchestras). Since 2007, over 1,200 film productions claimed £1.3 billion in relief.

## Diversity and Talent
- 60.5% of creative industry workers are graduates (vs. 31.8% UK average), but 92.1% come from advantaged social/economic backgrounds.
- 14% of creative media workers attended independent schools (7% of population). BAME workers increased 34.3% between 2011-2014 but remain only 11% of workforce (vs. 14.1% of the general population).
- Public investment supports 6,500 apprenticeships through the Creative Employment Programme and £32 million training support via Creative Skillset.
- McKinsey research: gender-diverse companies are 15% more likely to outperform; ethnically diverse companies 35% more likely.

## Regional Distribution
- 47.6% of creative industries jobs are in London and the South-East — the most unevenly distributed UK sector (after agriculture and finance/insurance).
- Scotland has 6.9% of creative economy jobs, Wales 2.9%, Northern Ireland 1.6%.
- Liverpool attracted 9.7 million additional visits as EU Capital of Culture, generating £753.8 million economic impact.
- Hull (UK City of Culture 2017) saw private investment follow public investment, including £15 million from Wykeland and a 15% increase in hotel income.
- Birmingham (Anita Bhalla): home to 6,000 tech firms employing nearly 40,000; 25% of UK gaming workforce; digital tech boosts the regional economy by £1.6 billion annually.

## Key Recommendations
- BIS (Department for Business, Innovation and Skills) should recognize the creative industries in its industrial growth data.
- A joined-up policy response is needed across HM Treasury, BIS, DCMS, DCLG and DfE, under leadership of the Secretary of State for Culture.
- The mixed economy model (public investment + tax incentives + private/philanthropic funding) should continue, but tax incentives cannot replace grant-in-aid for building infrastructure, education, and outreach.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Arts Council England—written evidence (CRF0043) ---
URL: https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/111119/html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the written evidence (CRF0043) submitted by Arts Council England to the House of Lords Communications and Digital Select Committee inquiry "A creative future" (September 2022). It covers how the Arts Council supports culture, disruptions facing the creative industries, skills needs, talent pipelines, R&D policy, and international lessons.

**Arts Council funding**: Between 2018-2022, the Arts Council invested £1.45 billion of public money plus an estimated £860 million from the National Lottery. During Covid-19, it awarded £1.14 billion through the Government's Culture Recovery Fund and £160 million through its own Emergency Response Fund.

**Key disruptive technologies (next 5-10 years)**:
1. **AI** – significant impact on audience data management, collections management, artistic production, IP ownership questions, and audience curation. Arts Council's 2019 commissioned research found barriers include cost/market maturity (e.g., theatre captioning) and the need for sophisticated data management.
2. **5G** – ultra-low latency will revolutionise live streaming of data-rich content, improve accessibility, and enable remote creative collaborations (e.g., 5G Festival at Brighton Dome).
3. **Virtual production, extended reality, virtual worlds** – could radically alter how work is made and where audiences encounter it. Examples include RSC's Dream, ROH's Current Rising, Tate's Modigliani VR, National Gallery's Virtual Veronese. Social forms of immersive experience are likely to evolve (e.g., Unreal City AR trail on the Thames, Unboxed StoryTrails). Online, projects like musician-led start-up Ristband are using virtual worlds.
4. **Web 3.0 technologies** (blockchain, crypto art, DAOs, NFTs) – potentially the most disruptive, with implications for how art is made, consumed, monetised and controlled. Proponents cite potential to change power structures; critics note unregulated financial speculation and IP/attribution challenges. In 2022, Italy suspended NFT creation based on Italian masterworks.

**Skills challenges**: A major challenge is inequality of access and opportunity; many lack digital devices. The 2019 Digital Culture survey (Arts Council/Nesta) found "a widening gulf between large and small organisations," organisations becoming "less experimental and more risk averse," with a downward trend in R&D behaviours. Senior management knowledge of digital technology fell from 22% (2013) to 13% (2019). Only 19% of organisations have board members contributing to digital strategy. In 2019, 70% cited lack of funding for digital as a barrier. Pandemic shutdowns accelerated digital learning, but it's unclear whether innovation will continue at scale amid economic crisis.

**Arts Council support mechanisms**: Digital Culture Network, Audience Finder, Impact & Insight Toolkit, Bloomberg Philanthropies' Digital Accelerator Programme, Creative XR, UK-Canada Immersive Exchange, Digital R&D Fund for the Arts. NPOs like RSC, Serpentine Galleries, Watershed, Furtherfield share expertise; small organisations like Collusion and York Mediale support practitioner R&D.

**Government/talent pipeline recommendations**: Continue investment in R&D and advanced digital skills; set funding criteria enabling not-for-profit arts organisations to benefit. Templates include the Creative Industries Clusters Programme (£39m, via UKRI/AHRC – XR Stories, B+B, StoryFutures) and Audiences of the Future Challenge (£33m – Dream, Dinosaurs and Robots). Programmes should run a minimum of 5 years. Supports Boundless Creativity report (2021, UKRI/AHRC & DCMS) recommendations, including considering new Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes. Combined/local authorities should engage creative stakeholders in Local Skills Improvement Plans and cultural compacts. Universities should reflect latest tech developments in curricula.

**Industry actions needed**: Tech industry should provide access to new technologies (e.g., RSC-Magic Leap fellowships, Google Arts workshops), support board-level tech expertise (with board 'banks' considered), recognise creativity as a top soft skill. Organisations need continuous digital upskilling embedded in operations (e.g., Arts Council's 'Tech Champions' recruitment model), embed digital in financial/strategic planning, and become more data savvy.

**R&D role**: Arts Council's "Dynamism" Investment Principle underpinning its Let's Create strategy emphasises "new technological opportunities," data culture, and technology adoption. New 2023-2026 NPO portfolio will include Investment Principles Support Organisations (IPSOs) sharing digital expertise. National Lottery Project Grants welcome digital/immersive projects; funds over £100,000 prioritise technology partnerships and new forms of content/audience reach.

**Government strategies effectiveness**: UKRI/AHRC industrial strategy programmes have been effective but end in 2023; future programmes should address geographical gaps (e.g., no current cluster in the Midlands), ensure not-for-profit eligibility, run 5+ years. Creative Industries Tax Relief schemes (Film, Theatre, Museums & Galleries) have shown positive impact; similar schemes should be considered for advanced tech practices.

**International lessons**: Cutting-edge innovation is highly collaborative and cross-border. The Arts Council supports international exchange via the Future Art and Culture (FAC) programme at SXSW (produced by British Underground) and the UK-Canada Immersive Exchange (UCIE). SXSW provides cross-disciplinary collaboration, investment and export outcomes. Creative XR prototypes have been selected for showcases at Tribeca, Venice Immersive and LFF Expanded.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Art Is Work | American Academy of Arts and Sciences ---
URL: https://www.amacad.org/publication/art-is-work/section/2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the "Art Is Work" report by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences' Commission on the Arts (a multiyear project with 44 members including artists, scholars, advocates, and leaders). The report addresses the central question: "How can we better recognize the value of artists in our national policy in order to enable the essential work they do?"

Key findings and statistics:
- While 81% of Americans believe the arts are "a positive experience in a troubled world," only 22% believe artists contribute "a lot" to the general good of society.
- Arts and culture supply approximately 4.3% of U.S. GDP (larger than construction, travel/tourism, and agriculture in 2019), providing a nearly $33 billion trade surplus in 2019.
- Production of arts and cultural goods/services grew by more than 35% from 1998 to 2016 (inflation-adjusted).
- Addressing barriers for Black creatives in film/TV could increase annual revenues by $10 billion.
- BLS counts 2.6 million artists (1.6% of all workers), but other estimates put creative economy employment as high as 5 million.
- 12.3% of artists held their occupation as a second job (up to 34.8% for musicians); artists are 3.6 times more likely than other workers to be self-employed (34% self-employed in 2012-2016).
- Median annual wage for arts/design occupations was $48,130 (May 2019) vs. $39,810 for all occupations; dancers/choreographers earned $31,150 while architects earned $76,680.
- Only 22.8% of actors worked full-time for the entire year.
- Women are 46% of the artistic workforce but 81% of dancers/choreographers and only 33% of musicians.
- Artists are less likely to be non-white/Hispanic (25% vs. 36% overall); 44% of dancers/choreographers are non-white/Hispanic.
- Around 40% of those on some Native reservations are practicing artists.
- In 2017, three-quarters of U.S. adults consumed artistic content electronically, and over half attended artistic activities.

The report outlines FOUR key principles for building a better system:
1. Name and include artists in federal policy (federal representation, explicit naming in legislation).
2. Recognize how creative work happens (independent contract work, multiple employers, entrepreneurship, inconsistent income as standard).
3. Center equity (anti-racist policies equitably funding, training, and supporting Black, Indigenous, and other artists of color, plus women, artists with disabilities, and rural artists).
4. Think locally, share nationally (national funding shaped to support local mechanisms).

The COVID-19 pandemic underscored artists' precarity—venues shuttered, gigs canceled, job losses—while also revealing racial and gender inequities; many artists accessed unemployment insurance for the first time via Pandemic Unemployment Assistance.

The report also includes case studies: the LA County Creative Strategist/Artist-in-Residence program (Deborah Aschheim's voting engagement work), the City Artist program at Public Art Saint Paul (Amanda Lovelee's "Pop Up Meeting"), Transportation for America's arts integration, and Christina Agapakis's role as creative director at biotech company Ginkgo Bioworks ($15 billion valuation).

URL: https://www.norc.org/content/dam/norc-org/pdf2025/National%20Survey%20of%20Artists%20-%20Findings%20Report.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report presents topline findings from the National Survey of Artists, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago with funding from The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation. The survey was designed to make visible the lives and livelihoods of artists practicing in the United States, addressing limitations in existing data sources that either only capture artists in specific occupations or use overly broad definitions. The survey used a nuanced, multidimensional screening process to identify practicing artists rather than relying on employment arrangements, considering creative practices, engagement methods, time spent, audiences, and recognition by others.

The survey was fielded September-November 2024, offered in English and Spanish, and included a final sample of 2,618 artists. It drew from three sample sources: NORC's AmeriSpeak probability-based panel, the Lucid non-probability panel, and a list sample of arts and design school graduates from the Strategic National Arts Alumni Project (SNAAP).

To qualify as an artist, respondents had to meet five screener criteria: (1) Practice—participated in at least one of 37 artistic activities across five disciplines (Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Writing, Craft Arts, Other Arts); (2) Engagement—engaged as a teacher, professional, former professional, or culture bearer (not just hobbyist or student); (3) Audience—intended audiences included their community, clients, other active field members, or the general public; (4) Recognition—others (beyond just friends/family) think of them as an artist; and (5) Hours—spent more than 0 hours per week on eligible arts activities. 97% of respondents participated in at least one activity, 29% met the engagement criterion, 46% met the audience criterion, 22% met all three criteria, and 18.38% met the recognition criterion. Design-only respondents were excluded to prioritize capturing data on artists with less traditional work arrangements.

The report includes findings across sections covering: artists' creative practices and identities; work arrangements (including up to four jobs; income sources; paid, temporary, and part-time work; self-employment; arts vs. non-arts occupations); finances (household income, assets, debts, financial support, and vulnerability); health needs and benefits (health insurance, dental and vision coverage, healthcare precarity); and artist demographics (gender, sexual orientation, age, geography, race, education, military service, and legal system experience). The report also contains detailed portraits of four specific artist groups: teaching artists, culture bearers, fully self-employed artists, and 3+ job holders.

The purpose of the report is to provide descriptive statistics to inform policies and support systems reflecting the lived experiences of the artist workforce. It does not analytically explore causes of observed patterns but offers companion resources including a technical report, public use data file, and user guide.
</summary>

The post asserts a return on investment of €4,800 in economic activity for every €1,200 received, citing the Finnish Ministry of Social Affairs & Aalto University Economic Policy Research (2024).

However, the comment section contains a critical fact-check by user Samantha Rochard (verified via Google Gemini), which identifies multiple inaccuracies:

- The €4,800 return figure is not part of the official Finnish study.
- The primary experiment concluded in 2018, with final results published in 2020.

Confirmed outcomes of the actual Finnish experiment included improved well-being, reduced stress, increased autonomy, and positive effects on creativity and entrepreneurship in qualitative interviews — but not the dramatic productivity gains claimed in the post. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the League of American Orchestras (updated July 15, 2026) provides comprehensive guidance on the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) grant process, covering recent major disruptions and changes to federal arts funding.

**FY2025 and Open Grant Awards (Terminations):**
- On May 2, 2025, the NEA terminated many in-progress FY24 and FY25 grant awards, effective May 31, 2025, and withdrew many offers of new FY25 awards that were awaiting final confirmation.
- The NEA stated it would prioritize projects that "elevate the Nation's HBCUs and Hispanic Serving Institutions, celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, foster AI competency, empower houses of worship to serve communities, assist with disaster recovery, foster skilled trade jobs, make America healthy again, support the military and veterans, support Tribal communities, make the District of Columbia safe and beautiful, and support the economic development of Asian American communities."
- Terminated grantees had until June 30, 2025 to request final payment for allowable costs incurred before May 31, 2025; Federal Financial Reports were due by July 31, 2025. Most final reporting requirements were waived, though experts recommend completion for technical compliance.
- Grantees had 7 calendar days to appeal. Approximately 100 appeals were approved over summer 2025.

**FY2026 Application Process:**
- On August 7, 2025, a new executive order on "Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking" was announced, along with a DOJ memorandum on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs.
- On February 6-7, 2025, the NEA revoked prior grant guidelines and issued revised FY26 guidelines. Initial application deadlines were March 11 and July 17.
- The Challenge America grant program was canceled for FY2026; applicants were directed to Grants for Arts Projects.
- The NEA stated in a February 18 webinar: "In accordance with Executive Orders, we will not fund projects that include DEI activities."
- Applicants must certify compliance with Executive Order 14173 (Ending Illegal Discrimination) and, previously, EO 14168 (on "gender ideology"). As of November 2025, the Assurance of Compliance no longer specifically mentions EO 14168.
- On September 19, 2025, a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down the NEA's policy disfavoring projects deemed to "promote gender ideology," finding it violated the First Amendment.
- SAM validation has returned to Grants.gov and must be active.

**FY2027 Application Process:**
- The Challenge America and Our Town grant opportunities are now embedded within Grants for Arts Projects (GAP) for FY27. Agency funding priorities now include celebrating the 2028 Olympic Games.
- Applications will be submitted as PDFs; video and audio files must be submitted as links in a PDF.
- On May 29, 2026, the OMB released proposed rules transforming federal financial assistance management (new Uniform Guidance), potentially effective October 1, 2026.
- Applicants are strongly encouraged (but not required) to align with agency funding priorities.

Key resources cited include NEA Grant Guidelines, Assurance of Compliance requirements, and application instructions for Music, Arts Education, and Challenge America disciplines. The League recommends reading guidelines carefully and consulting NEA specialists before applying. The page notes uncertainty about how new rules apply to NEA funding administered by states and localities.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: The Visual Artists Rights Act (VARA) — OVLA ---
URL: https://www.oregonvla.org/resources/the-visual-artists-rights-act-vara

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Oregon Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts (OVLA) explains the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990 (VARA), which grants "moral rights" to artists of certain "works of visual art." These rights are non-transferable (though waivable via signed contract) and exist under 17 U.S.C. § 106A, meaning artists can bring claims even after selling their work or not owning the copyright.

VARA applies only to "works of visual art" as narrowly defined under §101 of the Copyright Act. This includes paintings, drawings, prints, sculptures (in single copies or limited editions), and still photographs produced for exhibition meeting the same limited edition requirements. Excluded categories include posters, maps, globes, charts, technical drawings, diagrams, models, applied art, motion pictures, audiovisual works, books, magazines, newspapers, periodicals, databases, electronic publications, and merchandising/advertising items. "Works made for hire" are also excluded. Courts use "common sense and generally accepted standards of the artistic community" when determining coverage.

VARA grants two key rights: (1) the right of attribution, which protects the artist's reputation by allowing them to claim authorship or prevent their name being used on works they did not create or works modified in a prejudicial manner; and (2) the right of integrity, which prevents intentional distortion, mutilation, or modification prejudicial to the artist's honor/reputation, and prevents destruction of works of "recognized stature" (intentional or grossly negligent destruction is a violation).

Exceptions to VARA include ordinary wear-and-tear from environmental factors and passage of time, modifications from conservation or public presentation (placement/lighting) unless caused by gross negligence, and VARA rights apply only to originals, not copies or reproductions.

Section 113(d) addresses works incorporated into buildings (e.g., murals). The right of integrity doesn't apply if the artist consented to installation before VARA's effective date (December 1, 1990), or if after the effective date when both artist and property owner signed an agreement specifying the work may be damaged during removal. For works incorporated into buildings after the effective date with no written waiver where the work can be removed without harm, the building owner must: (1) make a "diligent, good faith" attempt to locate and notify the artist, and (2) if located, provide notice with 90 days for the artist to remove the work or pay for its removal. If the artist removes the work, they regain title to it.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: An Artist's Reflection on Visual Artists' Rights (Sec. 106A) ---
URL: https://www.authorsalliance.org/2026/04/10/an-artists-reflection-on-visual-artists-rights-sec-106a

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a guest post by Anne T. Gilliland, a longtime Authors Alliance member and former Scholarly Communications Officer at UNC Chapel Hill, published as part of the series marking the 50th anniversary of the Copyright Act of 1976. The post reflects on Section 106A of US copyright law, which confers moral rights (attribution and integrity) on creators of certain types of visual art.

**Key points covered:**

- **Moral rights concept**: Unlike most of US copyright law which treats author rights in terms of economic gains, moral rights relate to personal autonomy and the individual relationship to one's work, regardless of money involved.

- **VARA passage (1990)**: The Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990 (VARA), codified in Section 106A, was the first time moral rights entered US copyright law. The impetus was the desire for the US to join the Berne Convention, whose signatories must recognize some form of moral rights. There was opposition from the motion picture industry and other stakeholders who feared moral rights would give creators control over works made for hire.

- **Scope of VARA**: Narrowly written to apply only to "fine" art — unique works and limited edition prints (signed, numbered editions of 200 copies or fewer). A photograph qualifies only if produced for exhibition purposes. Excluded from the definition: posters, maps, technical drawings, motion pictures, applied art, periodicals, electronic publications, merchandising/advertising items, works made for hire, and uncopyrightable works.

- **Two moral rights granted**: (1) Right of attribution — the right to claim authorship, disclaim works not created, and prevent attribution after modifications prejudicing honor or reputation; (2) Right of integrity — the right to prevent prejudicial modifications and destruction of works of "recognized stature." Section 113 addresses situations where visual art (like murals) is incorporated into buildings scheduled for demolition or remodeling.

- **Historical context**: The post recounts an Alexander Calder mobile at Pittsburgh airport that was painted green and gold (then pink) to match Allegheny County branding, motivating the need for such protections. Modifications due to passage of time or preservation needs are not actionable, and rights do not apply to reproductions (like mass-produced posters).

- **Key limitations**: Rights cannot be transferred and survive transfer of other rights or the physical object; however, they can be waived. For works created on/after VARA enactment, rights run for the author's life (or last surviving co-author). For pre-VARA works, rights last as long as other Section 106 rights if title hasn't been transferred.

- **Author's personal reflection**: Gilliland discusses her journey from art student in 1978 (when the new law took effect, establishing copyright upon creation without registration) through law school, comparing her experience as a visual artist to other creative work. She argues visual art presents an acute case for moral rights because reproductions lose qualities of originals (textures, light reflections) that text or video reproductions don't lose.

- **Debate on expansion**: The question of expanding attribution rights beyond visual works is debated, as highlighted in the Copyright Office's 2019 attribution study and the Copyright Principles Project (which recommended consideration of extension while noting it would be neither straightforward nor easy).

The post includes images of Gilliland's own artwork (Worried Eyeball, Radio, Women Alone) and notes she has never planned to make a living as an artist, yet finds the moral rights concepts "valuable and true" about her life as a creator.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: When Art Meets Building: A Primer on the Visual Artists ... ---
URL: https://www.olshanlaw.com/when-art-meets-building

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, written by Thomas D. Kearns and Carolyn Sha of Olshan Frome Wolosky's real estate department (reprinted from the New York Law Journal, June 30, 2014), provides a comprehensive primer on the federal Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990 (VARA) as it applies to landlords and tenants of real property.

**Overview of VARA:** VARA protects visual artists' "moral rights" by prohibiting the destruction of "visual art" (paintings, drawings, sculptures, or photographs) of "recognized stature." Art of "recognized stature" is that viewed as possessing stature by art experts, the art community, or society in general. Qualifying artists can sue to prevent destruction or recover actual or statutory damages ranging from $750 to over $30,000 (up to $150,000 for willful infringements, down to $200 for innocent infringements). VARA rights are non-transferrable, exercisable only by the artist, and last for the artist's lifetime (or the last surviving artist's life for joint works).

**Key for Property Owners:** VARA protects works "incorporated in or made part of a building" where removal would cause destruction, distortion, mutilation, or modification (e.g., murals, frescoes, affixed sculptures). Relevant cases include *Carter v. Helmsley-Spear* (sculptures, glass mosaics, and permanent installations affixed to building) and *Board of Managers of Soho International Arts Condominium v. City of New York* (aluminum bars attached to steel reinforcement braces).

**Three Ways Landlords Can Protect Against VARA Liability:**

1. **Explicit Waiver:** For art that cannot be safely removed, the artist's rights must be waived (or the artist consented before June 1, 1991, VARA's effective date). The waiver must be a written instrument signed by both artist and building owner that: (a) specifically identifies the work and uses to which the waiver applies, and (b) specifies that installation may subject the work to destruction, distortion, mutilation, or modification by reason of removal. For joint works, a waiver by one artist waives rights of all. Waivers survive the sale of the property.

2. **De Facto Waiver:** For art of "recognized stature" that can be safely removed, building owners must make a "diligent, good faith" attempt to notify the artist of removal intention (presumed if sent by registered mail to the artist's most recent address on record with the Register of Copyrights). No claim exists if contact attempts fail, or if the owner provides notice but the artist fails to remove the work or pay for removal within 90 days. Alternative: require art installations be crafted for safe dismantling and removal.

3. **Work for Hire:** VARA rights do not apply to works "made for hire"—either prepared within the scope of an employee's employment, or commissioned as part of a collective work/compilation agreed in writing by both parties. Courts use a multi-factor balancing test (right to control production, requisite skill, employee benefits, tax treatment, assignment of additional projects). Mere use of the words "work for hire" without supporting factors is insufficient.

**'Surprise' Art:** VARA may protect work not obviously art when installed, including graffiti. In the 5Pointz case (Long Island City), 17 graffiti artists sued after the owner decided to raze the factory housing their works. Though the injunction was denied for lack of demonstrated irreparable harm, the court held "VARA protects even temporary art from destruction" and the defendants could face "potentially significant monetary damages" if works were of "recognized stature." Graffiti at 5Pointz was consented to by the owner—VARA protects only art legally placed with the owner's consent. Commercial signage may also gain "recognized stature" over time (per a Second Circuit concurring opinion), though advertising/promotional material is expressly excluded from VARA.

**Models and Unfinished Works:** Unfinished works are subject to VARA protection, per *Flack v. Friends of Queen Catherine*, where a partially completed sculpture was protected since "'preliminary' work of painters—drawing and sketches—[were] covered by VARA."

**Practical Suggestions:** Obtain artist waivers for any work installed that may be considered art; consider waivers for all art not simply affixed by a nail; include specific lease provisions requiring landlord consent and artist waivers (with sample waiver language provided, including indemnification); keep records of creator names/addresses for de facto waivers; educate building personnel; properly document work-for-hire relationships; and add VARA analysis to real property purchase diligence checklists.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: Waiver of Moral Right in Visual Artworks ---
URL: https://www.copyright.gov/reports/exsum.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Copyright Office's final report to Congress on the impact of waiver provisions in the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990 (VARA), which for the first time legislated limited moral rights of attribution and integrity to authors of narrowly defined visual artworks. VARA rights can only be waived by a signed, written agreement specifying the work and precise uses to which the waiver applies.

Key findings include:

**Background:** Nine states had enacted moral rights legislation before VARA, following either a "preservation model" or protecting rights of attribution and integrity for works of recognized quality. A tenth state's law, enacted after VARA, applies only to works in state buildings. Moral rights are also protected indirectly by state tort, privacy, defamation, and unfair competition laws, as well as the Lanham Act and Copyright Act.

**International context:** Member nations of the Berne Convention must meet minimum protection under Article 6bis, but the treaty does not address waiver. The Office surveyed 14 nations and the European Community; France provides broad protection while the UK relies more on contract law. Pre-VARA case law (Vargas v. Esquire, Granz v. Harris, Gilliam v. ABC, Wojnarowicz v. American Family Association) provided moral rights protection through contract, copyright, and unfair competition theories. Carter v. Helmsley-Spear was the only case awarding relief under VARA, but was reversed on appeal because the work was deemed a work made for hire.

**Survey results:** More than 1,000 written responses were received from 47 states and the District of Columbia, with 955 self-described visual artists. About three-fourths knew of moral rights, but fewer than half knew they could be waived. Seven percent said waiver clauses were routinely included in contracts, but nearly 40 percent said they were part of commissioned work contracts. Nearly a quarter of artists covered by VARA knew of artists asked to waive rights; 13 percent had refused contracts with waivers. More than half of those who rejected a waiver said rejection voided the deal. Over half who experienced waivers said they complied with specificity requirements; about one-third said contracts contained a separate price for the waiver. Most art contracts remain oral and thus cannot contain valid waivers.

**Public hearing (June 21, 1995):** Participants noted waivers are rare because written contracts are rare. There is a distinction between "moveables" and works incorporated into buildings (sec. 113). Many believed the sec. 106A waiver should be repealed or modified for moveables, while most saw the need for sec. 113 waivers for building-incorporated works. Recommendations included that one joint author should not be able to waive for all co-authors, and VARA should apply to print and broadcast reproductions.

**Sample contracts:** Examples included a Campbell's Soup Art Contest requiring all moral rights waivers, a Seattle Transit Project contract allowing removal with right of first refusal, and a Los Angeles County transit agreement permitting removal even with physical defacement.

The report concludes that because federal moral rights legislation is young and artists and users are often unaware of the Berne Convention standard, accurate predictions about the impact of VARA's waiver provisions are difficult to make at this time.
</summary>

"After hearing testimony from artists' representatives, commercial users and other interested parties, Congress determined that the artists' rights should not be absolute, but that they should be tempered by commercial realities, provided that provisions were enacted to insulate authors from being unduly influenced to give away their new-found rights."

This webpage presents the full text of 17 U.S. Code § 106A, the section of U.S. copyright law (from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute) establishing rights of certain authors of visual artworks to attribution and integrity, enacted via the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990 (VARA, Pub. L. 101–650, Dec. 1, 1990).

Key provisions of the statute:
- (a) Rights of Attribution and Integrity: Subject to section 107 (fair use) and independent of exclusive rights in section 106, the author of a work of visual art has the right to (1) claim authorship and prevent use of their name on works they did not create; (2) prevent use of their name where the work has been distorted, mutilated, or modified in a way prejudicial to their honor or reputation; and (3) subject to section 113(d) limitations, prevent any intentional distortion/mutilation/modification prejudicial to honor or reputation, and prevent destruction of a work of recognized stature (with intentional or grossly negligent destruction constituting a violation).
- (b) Scope and Exercise: Only the author has these rights, whether or not they own the copyright; joint work authors are co-owners of these rights.
- (c) Exceptions: Modifications from passage of time or inherent nature of materials are not violations; modifications from conservation or public presentation (including lighting/placement) are not violations unless caused by gross negligence; the attribution rights do not apply to reproductions of works in the items listed in the section 101 definition of "work of visual art."
- (d) Duration: For works created on/after VARA's effective date, rights last for the author's life; for pre-existing works where title wasn't transferred by the effective date, rights are coextensive with section 106 rights; for joint works, rights last for the life of the last surviving author; all terms run to the end of the calendar year of expiration.
- (e) Transfer and Waiver: These moral rights may NOT be transferred, but may be waived only by express written agreement (signed by the author, specifically identifying the work and uses covered). A waiver by one joint author waives rights for all. Ownership of these rights is distinct from ownership of any copy or copyright; transferring a copy or copyright does not waive these rights.

Editorial and statutory notes:
- The section was added by Pub. L. 101–650, title VI, §603(a) (Dec. 1, 1990, 104 Stat. 5128).
- VARA took effect 6 months after enactment (June 1, 1991), applying to works created on/after the effective date and pre-existing works whose title had not been transferred by that date, but not to destruction/distortion/modification that occurred before the effective date.
- The Register of Copyrights was directed to study the extent of waiver of author rights (report due within 5 years) and the feasibility of resale royalty rights for visual artists (report due within 18 months).

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

**Round 1 – Germany, France, Netherlands/Ireland:**
- Searched: "Künstlersozialkasse Germany artists social insurance system", "France intermittent du spectacle artist welfare status", "Netherlands basic income experiment artists cultural policy"
